Utilizing a training approach rooted in gradient descent, the artificial neural network is optimized with randomly generated samples from various distributions of examples. Subsequent analysis of the network's performance is then conducted while fixing the number of training examples at 10,000 and varying the dimension from 16 to 512. Notably, the artificial neural network exhibits superior generalization performance when trained on distributions of examples that deviates significantly from the standard normal distribution, as compared to the standard normal distribution. In natural language processing, NLP is utilized to create systems that interact with natural language. Text analysis, a fundamental aspect of NLP, is applied across various platforms including search engines, security systems, and blog comments. The traditional methods employed in text analysis, such as supervised learning and neural networks, demand extensive labeled datasets and require efficient distribution on graphical processing units (GPUs). This leads to a dilemma where real-world text data is often incompatible with the requirements of text analysis. This research aims to develop a text analysis framework that is independent of these constraints, utilizing descriptive memory instead of labeled datasets to learn from real-world text data. Descriptive memory mimics the human brain's memory through interactions with the environment. It is a dynamic, centralized repository that incorporates new information through interactions, potentially influencing existing knowledge. The proposed text analysis framework functions similarly to deep descriptive memory, incorporating real-world text data into a descriptive network usable for various text analysis tasks, such as search and monitoring. This dynamic framework enables a point-to-global shift in text analysis without requiring labeled datasets or GPU processing. Instead, new nodes representing the query can be added to the descriptive network through interactions, effectively initiating self-supervised learning. Additionally, the framework facilitates a similarity-based search function and efficient text monitoring by analyzing similar texts within the descriptive network. Consequently, the text analysis framework offers increased scalability, efficiency, and flexibility in text processing and search operations. Furthermore, the proposed framework can accommodate diverse text datasets including short texts, long texts, and texts with visual components. As a result, the proposed text analysis framework delivers enhanced productivity, speed, and adaptability in text processing and search operations, ultimately leading to a more efficient and effective text analysis system. Several text-based applications using this framework were developed and are now available for download at https://github.com/AI-SYNTHESIS/Text-Analysis.git. One such application, a text-to-image search function, allows users to navigate through search results visualized as images, mimicking human mental concepts through memory-based visualizations. This research has been featured in the 2021 International Conference for Advances in Artificial Intelligence. Please watch the associated video demonstration at https://vimeo.org/451361099. The text analysis framework holds great potential for additional real-world applications, potentially transforming the future landscape of text processing and search operations. Future research could delve into overcoming current limitations in text analysis. One such limitation is difficulty in accurately understanding text intent during search operations. I've reimagined the operational semantics of a GNU Privacy Guard version 2.6.12 implementation, rewriting it in a step-by-step manner using a limited set of rules. This clear and concise operational semantics can be employed for various purposes such as testing or building reliable tools for verifying GPG code. It comes in three parts: high-level rules for everyday computations, low-level rules for low-level operations like memory management, and a collection of defining rules. Additionally, I've included conventional input/output rules and equivalence relations including a few key data values like nil, universal, and empty tuples. Furthermore, I've represented GPG's computational steps as a finite graph where all pairs of states that differ only by the last element in their evaluation stacks are connected. Ultimately, I've considered the potential risks of relying on small-step semantics, including potential infinite loops, and how these can be avoided in GPG's implementation. This work is the first to document GPG's operational semantics, extending previous research on small-step operational semantics which focused on a different language. To achieve this, I've examined GPG's source code, created a new operational semantics, implemented it using OCaml, and tested it against GPG's generated code to validate its accuracy. This research was carried out as part of a larger PhD study, which can be accessed through the associated hyperlink.

The effectiveness of data visualization lies not only in its design but also in its interaction. Well-designed visualizations facilitate exploration by making key insights visible, while interactive elements enable users to delve deeper into each finding. However, the sheer volume of data being generated today renders manual exploration impractical, necessitating rapid creation of insightful visualizations and discoveries through automation. A new framework for visual exploration of large datasets prioritizes both design and discovery, utilizing various strategies to create generalized discovery pathways in domains where manual exploration would be impractical. Our approach includes developing a composite representation of these paths and employing a statistic to measure the loss of information in each transition between two composite states. We demonstrate the framework's efficacy in generating discoveries in databases containing large numbers of statistical summaries. Our framework's performance is robust against incorrect domain assumptions and is applicable to both structured and unstructured datasets, including geospatial information, demonstrating a 300-fold reduction in exploration time. A newly designed multi-grating structure combines the functionalities of waveguide traps, mode sorters, and couplers in a single integrated unit to interact with individual atoms. This is achieved by utilizing an array of gratings that impose deep and wide optical resonances facilitating atom-tron interactions. These interactions result in optical resonances with a finite width that can capture and trap individual atoms. The same gratings function as mode sorters by dispersing a multi-mode coherent atom signal into a narrow frequency range near the trap frequency. The novel architecture was implemented using a 2D photonic crystal slab trap with a 4th and 21st grating order, respectively responsible for atom trapping and mode sorting. The design has potential in creating efficient, integrated high-fidelity atom-photon interfaces that could contribute to the development of a hybrid quantum processing unit. However, there are some limitations, such as a relatively large pump power required to couple atoms off the trap, likely due to losses associated with the 21st grating order. The design considers a zero-chirp assumption inherent in the grating-based architecture, which might limit its performance if a non-negligible dispersion is present. Nevertheless, this framework provides a versatile tool for developing efficient atom-photon interfaces, and it opens up possibilities for designing high-performance, integrated atom-photon interfaces using advanced photonic designs. Moreover, this research introduces a new method for coupling a single atom into a thin waveguide by utilizing a more recent approach known as the ``trapped-atom linewidth enhancement.'' The method was implemented in the context of an array of gratings to interact with individual atoms, resulting in optical resonances with a finite width. The approach can be considered general and could easily be applied to other optical resonators to enhance their ability to interact with individual atoms. The following principles were developed during this research: the requirement of a high pump power to couple atoms off the trap; the importance of designing the design with consideration of its dispersion; and the potential of combining the functions of waveguide traps, mode sorters, and couplers in a single integrated unit to interact with individual atoms. The designed architecture was implemented in the context of integrated atom-photon interfaces, but the principles can be applied to other optical resonators to interact with either photons or atoms. Furthermore, $f^k$ admits a certain extension in each case. A widely accepted approach to developing visual models involves training with a combination of predictive analytics and supervised learning. The traditional method for this training is based on the backpropagation algorithm. Our research presents an innovative training method that propagates changes without using the gradient. This new approach is founded on change lenses, used to describe change propagation strategies that are predictable and reversible. We demonstrate that traditional backpropagation can be considered a special case of our method, which has the advantage of allowing diverse data transformations during the training process. Our method has been successfully tested on transforming fully connected networks and convolutional networks to residual architectures, achieving comparable results to the conventional method. Our research provides a theoretical framework for the development of innovative training methods that go beyond the conventional paradigm. These advancements enable the modification of training algorithms based on specific requirements, such as increasing the speed of model development, improving the practicality of models, and adapting to resource constraints. Our studied transformations can be used as a starting point for developing custom training algorithms that offer unique benefits. Research indicates that when the function $f$ is sufficiently smooth, the phase space can be split into distinct regions where a stationary phase argument applies, by leveraging a smooth phase approximation. This method, while effective for many cases, is too restrictive, as many phase functions fail to meet this smoothness criterion. A crucial challenge in the study of rarefied gases lies in determining the steady-state distribution of particles within a specific fluid layer. By dividing the particle distribution into macro- and micro-scale components, researchers have previously developed iterative methods to approximate this distribution. To address this limitation, researchers have developed a new iterative method that combines accelerated iteration resolution and enhanced computational efficiency. Specifically, this method employs an accelerated splitting scheme to achieve resolution in a relatively small number of iterations, thereby minimizing the overall iterative cost. Furthermore, to speed up computation, researchers have developed a new solver for the micro-scale equation and incorporated general-purpose Newton-Krylov solvers for improved efficiency. Additionally, they have developed a new method to approximate the Jacobian matrix, thereby accelerating iteration convergence. To evaluate the effectiveness of this method, researchers have applied it to various problem scenarios across four categories of simplicity, demonstrating substantial progress in reducing computational cost for the simplest scenarios and showcasing the continued relevance of iterative methods for more complex problems. Nonetheless, further research is needed to address the current computational limitations for these more complex problems. To this end, researchers have outlined potential future directions for improving the method's efficiency and accuracy. Ultimately, the paper advocates for a more efficient approach to accelerating iteration resolution in rarefied gas stream simulations. Specifically, researchers have identified that rarefied gas stream simulations, which typically require numerous iterations, stand in stark contrast to more efficient methods such as non-Newtonian flow simulations, which tend to converge rapidly within a small number of iterations. To address this disparity, researchers have outlined several potential avenues for modifying existing iteration methods and developing new ones. Specifically, incorporating general-purpose Newton-Konyov solvers may hold promise, or modifying existing iteration methods to leverage their initial fast convergence. Additionally, researchers have suggested exploring new algorithms, such as minimizing vector sequences, which may improve iteration efficiency and accelerate convergence for rarefied gas stream simulations. By pursuing these potential improvements, researchers may be able to develop more efficient solutions for accelerating iteration resolution in rarefied gas stream simulations. Furthermore, researchers have outlined several potential applications for these improved methods, which could enhance computational efficiency and accelerate scientific discoveries in various fields. Specifically, researchers have suggested that these improved methods could accelerate molecular Monte Carlo simulations, which could provide valuable data for the optimization of supersonic micro-motors, as well as enhance computational fluid dynamics simulations, which could provide critical insights for medical applications

This concept has connections to probability, particularly with regards to consistent prediction challenges. Rigid fibrations are an additional refinement of surjections, also involving finite sets, and extending the concept of rigid sets as introduced by Skolnik. Following previous work by the first author and R. Radford, this paper delves into sequences of rigid fibrations, achieving a comprehensive classification of sequences of rigid fibrations whose codomain is a finite set, and deriving a sequence of results in this area, starting with simplified versions and progressing to more intricate cases. These outcomes have multiple applications, encompassing a novel modification of a well-known theorem in combinatorics, a rephrased and advanced version of a subsequent theorem, and a refined version of a more general outcome in this field. Additionally, this paper explores under what conditions a sequence of rigid fibrations is a Hopf fibrations sequence, which has implications for probability theory, particularly regarding consistent prediction challenges and the detachment of Rindler spacetimes, which is a type of fibrations sequence. Finally, this paper delves into the connection between the sequences of rigid fibrations and the concept of independence in probability, which yields a novel version of a well-known theorem in this field. The thermal characteristics of a two-dimensional Pauli lattice, characterized by a two-component fermion system incorporating both kinetic energy and pair-hopping terms, are investigated through a grand canonical approach. Despite the absence of an analytical solution, which poses a difficult many-body problem due to its non-trivial dispersion relation and spin-dependent fermion hopping, it is observed that a quasi-energy spectrum and spin configuration can be effectively evaluated numerically. Consequently, a grand canonical partition function, energy, and specific heat are derived and analyzed. Moreover, a free energy and thermodynamic properties can be studied by considering the grand potential. Specifically, it is found that the specific heat of the Pauli lattice exhibits a divergent 'fingerprint' at zero temperature and a long-range spin correlation decays with a distance power law of exponential for high temperature regimes, but displays algebraic decay at lower temperatures, and finally, the lattice's magnetization shows a temperature behavior characteristic of Ising models with cut-off and finite temperatures, and in the process, a re-entrant type shape in the phase diagram may be theoretically determined from the determined energy and specific heat expressions. Ultimately, a grand canonical partition function, energy, and specific heat of the Pauli lattice are derived and analyzed. Furthermore, a free energy and thermodynamic properties can be studied by considering the grand potential. Specifically, it is found that the specific heat of the Pauli lattice exhibits a divergent 'fingerprint' at zero temperature and a long-range spin correlation decays with a distance power law of exponential for high temperature regimes, but displays algebraic decay at lower temperatures, and the lattice's magnetization shows a temperature behavior characteristic of Ising models with cut-off and finite temperatures, and in the process, a re-entrant type shape in the fraction of spin-up fermions and the specific heat may be theoretically determined from the determined energy and specific heat expressions.

This study aims to introduce the Zeroing Neural Network (ZNN) framework as a cutting-edge method for addressing time-varying matrix problems in prediction. Formulated from the perspective of dynamical systems, ZNN extends exponential law to its state-space form, facilitating the development of novel algorithms for forecasting evolving matrices, parameter estimation, and multivariate function prediction. Its applications are diverse, encompassing the estimation of multivariate functions, forward-looking heat transfer, and predictive maintenance based on predictive maintenance. Due to its natural parallelization capabilities, ZNN is well-suited for high-performance computing on GPUs. Lastly, this work outlines the potential applications of ZNN in physics research.

Artificial neural networks, the leading solution for image classification tasks, struggle with robustness in the presence of harsh environmental obstacles and abnormal input formats. A fundamental component of biological vision systems, the on-off center-surround dichoptic receptor, helps overcome these challenges by encoding diverse image characteristics. Utilizing this concept, researchers have developed new network architectures, such as dichoptic neural networks (DNNs), which merge two distinct pathways - a primary center detection branch and a secondary surround branch - to enhance classification performance. In this research, various architectural aspects of on-off DNNs were examined, specifically the visual regions' extent and relative scales of the two pathways. By improving the balance between these branches, on-off DNNs significantly increase the diversity of discriminative features, which leads to improved accuracy and resilience. Extensive experiments were conducted on seven diverse datasets, which confirm on-off DNNs outperform competing methods in overall classification rate and resilience. Moreover, the precise ablation studies reveal the sensitivity of the model's performance to variations in the size of the receptive fields of the two pathways, which provides valuable references for the design of such architectures. Ultimately, on-off DNNs offer a biological inspiration for developers to design robust and efficient artificial networks. The X-ray band offers unique insights into rare celestial phenomena, but our understanding of the universe remains limited by the range of observational tools. Most telescopes have design restrictions that prevent them from exploring the entire sky. A critical unsolved challenge exists between achieving the widest possible field of view and maintaining high-resolution imaging capabilities. In this study, a team of researchers investigates two major strategies for increasing the field of view in X-ray optics: compressing the field of view using grazing-angle reflections and using segmented or 'honeycomb' optics. They examine the principles governing these designs, analyze the advantages and disadvantages of each approach, and discuss the current state of implementation. Additionally, some potential solutions to compromise between field of view and resolution are presented. This research aims to inform X-ray optical designers about the possibilities and constraints of these strategies in pursuing a major goal: extensively mapping the sky in X-rays. A special consideration of this work is the potential for a next-generation X-ray telescope to be a global collaborative effort, with far-reaching implications for space and ground-based designs. The core of topological band theory is the fundamental theorem that connects global properties (topological invariants) to local characteristics (symmetries) of a crystalline insulator. This provides a strong link between moiré band theory and the underlying symmetries of the moiré Hamiltonian, especially when influenced by magnetic fields. In this study, we show that incorporating magnetic field into moiré systems reveals novel topological features that weren't observable in non-magnetic settings. This is demonstrated by the case of twisted bilayer graphene at 2π flux, which develops an infinite number of reentrant flat bands with unique characteristics. These flat bands are generated by a new magnetic theorem that extends the core of topological band theory. It's found that the appearance of flat bands is tied to the appearance of magnetic insulator phases, which only occur when the system is covered by a magnetic flux. Moreover, the emergence of new flat bands is associated with the emergence of magnetic Chern insulators, which only exist when the system is covered by magnetic flux. Notably, the presence of magnetic Chern insulators isn't a requirement for the appearance of magnetic insulators or topological phases. These findings provide a foundation for the exploration of numerous quantum phases and phenomena in moiré systems and inspire further research into the novel physics at play. By establishing a quantitative connection between moiré band theory and the underlying symmetries of the moiré Hamiltonian, it becomes possible to establish a general framework that generalizes topological band theory to the case of crystal bound fermions exposed to magnetic fields. This brings us to a new conjecture, which has significant implications for the understanding of twisted bilayer graphene. At 2π flux, we expect boundary states associated with the non-trivial fundamental class of the moiré lattice to appear, regardless of the presence or absence of magnetic insulators. Moreover, the presence of magnetic Chern numbers independent of magnetic filling and levels suggests that a magnetic Chern insulator phase should exist on the boundary of the moiré sample, which has significant implications for the appearance of topological phases and numerous quantum phenomena in moiré systems. Inspired by a desire to protect user privacy, we have developed a novel, high-speed protocol utilizing LSTMs to integrate steganography and text generation. Steganography is the practice of conveying secret information by disguising it as a seemingly innocuous form of communication. Our proposed protocol employs LSTMs to create plausible and length-matched text by combining the secret message with public data drawn from a language model. Unlike traditional steganographic methods that rely on subtle linguistic cues like syntax and semantics, our approach leverages the complexity of natural language by manipulating the probability distribution of specific words. Our experiments indicate that an LSTM-based protocol surpasses a probabilistic syntax-driven method in both speed and transparency, while an alternative pure steganographic method fails to produce compelling results. Our results also show that our proposed protocol is robust to multiple public sources and suggest room for further improvement in achieving optimal transparency. The source code for our research can be accessed at https://github.com/sig-noa/StgaLSTM. Our paper explores the interplay between steganography and text generation, a relatively uncharted area of study. Our research is further facilitated by the employment of automated tools, including a sophisticated Python library (Transformers) that enables rapid training and testing of LSTMs on large-scale datasets. An additional innovation is the development of a custom dataset obtained through the collection of obfuscated social media posts and secret messages on the platform Telegram. Our research ultimately contributes to the future investigation of steganography applications in conversational AI by imagining a scenario in which a language model begins to transmit secret information without noticing it. Our research is a preliminary effort to bridge the gap between the fields of steganography and NLP, and as such, it poses more questions than it answers. Its research outcomes can potentially inspire the development of steganographic methods that do not rely on language, as well as those that integrate steganography with other forms of generative models, such as GANs. The research of steganography in the context of large language models remains an area of study for the future. The research of automatic steganography detection also remains an important research direction, as it is an important component in understanding the steganographic protocol's transparency. The research of the steganographic protocol's form of steganography (symmetric key vs. public key) and the type of secret information (text, image, video) also remains an important research direction, as well as a crucial element in understanding the research of steganography

Transmission system operators rely on Unit Commitment (UC) models to optimize power generation, but these models are often computationally intensive due to constraints such as transmission flow and generator limits. A major challenge in evaluating these constraints arises from the complex interconnections between power flow and UC variables, as well as the discrete nature of UC variables. As a result, UC problems become particularly demanding in systems with a large number of buses, lines, and generators. To tackle this issue, a novel approach is presented that employs constrained regression and neural networks to tackle the constraint examination issue in UC problems. The proposed method leverages historical data to establish a cost model that estimates UC variable costs. The overall strategy aims to dispatch generators efficiently and free up computational resources to tackle more complex problems. The approach outperformed existing solutions, speeding up constraint examination in various test cases up to 3.2 to 18.2 times, with an average increase of 5.9% in solution quality. The feasibility of this approach is further demonstrated through its use in developing an open-source tool for constrained power flow analysis. Measurements of magnetization, specific heat, and resistivity were taken on single crystals of $\alpha$-Li$_2$IrO$_3$ under high pressure up to 2.3 GPa, covering temperature ranges from 1.1 to 9 K. This study reveals how mechanical pressure affects the properties of materials that exhibit Kitaev magnetochemistry. At low temperatures, where magnetism influences the resistivity in an anticlockwise manner due to a spin-rotation effect, pressure becomes a non-uniform force. It causes the collapse of long-range antiferromagnetism at 3.4 K, the temperature at which the resistivity displays its minimum value, leading to a significant increase in the resistivity at lower temperatures as it becomes dominated by a non-uniform magnetic force. Specific heat measurements show a high value at 2.3 GPa, comparable to the universal specific heat of materials without long-range ordering at the same temperature. This result provides crucial insights for Kitaev materials under various types of influence. Our specific findings indicate a second-order phase transition from paramagnetism to long-range antiferromagnetism at 3.4 K, which likely involves mechanical iridium dimers. This discovery is supported by specific heat measurements, which show sharp increases at the same temperature. Specific heat measurements also indicate that the magnetic contribution to the total heat signal decreases as the material experiences an increase in the non-uniform force. This cause the specific heat magnitude to exhibit an unconventional decrease-latent increase-decrease trend as the material transitions from paramagnetism to an antiferromagnetic state with increasing pressure. Finally, the experimental resistivity values exhibit a shift towards a metallic type of behavior at the non-ordered state, which likely results from the influence of inter-magnetic-ion pair interactions in the paramagnetic phase. Our specific findings provide a critical perspective on the Kitaev model and the characteristic properties of Kitaev materials, as well as underlining the significant role that non-uniform forces play in the magnetic and non-magnetic properties of these materials and their transitions. Our study of $\alpha$-Li$_2$IrO$_3$ notably shows that the Kitaev model's unique physics can be experimentally verified in this real-world material even in the non-ordered state. An attempt has been made to link the experimental results to the predictions made by theoretical models created for the Kitaev model. Researchers frequently utilize synthetic control units to determine the effects of rare or significant events, such as natural disasters or policy interventions. To assess the validity of synthetic control units, various metrics have been proposed, with the majority focusing on the pre-intervention period as a reference point. We argue that a more effective approach would be to use data from unit 1's pre- and post-intervention periods to establish a standard for evaluation. This new standard allows us to combine information about control units' pre-intervention similarity with their post-intervention behavior following the event in question. We establish this approach in a context where treatment effects are linear and define a set of necessary conditions to assess treatment effects in a causal framework. Our research considers the real-world challenges of estimating causal effects under uncertainty regarding data generative models, assuming a linear difference in regression effects model. We propose a novel method for estimating weights that takes into account this uncertainty and prove its asymptotic efficiency when control unit data generative models are correctly specified. Additionally, we prove the method's robustness when such conditions do not apply. Our research's performance in simulations that model a wide range of events dynamically through time shows significant improvements over traditional metrics in estimating causal effects. Furthermore, we apply this method to two significant events: the reunification of Germany and the invasion of Iraq. Our analysis reveals new insights into the channels through which events influence their recipients. Following this thorough analysis, we will make the code for our research publicly available. Our findings will also be shared with policymakers to foster additional research collaborations. To assess the validity of synthetic control units, we propose a new approach focused on post-intervention period data, combining similarity with pre-intervention controls and their post-intervention behavior following the event in question. Developed within a nearby causal inference framework, our method considers the likelihood of control units becoming treated given a specific event, and it is applicable to linear and non-linear difference in regression effects models. To estimate the weights under unknown data generative models, we use a Bayesian approach. We prove our Bayesian estimator to be asymptotically efficient when the control unit data generative models are correctly specified and prove its robustness when such conditions do not apply. Using historical data, we estimate the weights using a Markov chain Monte Carlo method before and and after the event in question, providing confidence intervals for the estimated effects through a bootstrap method. Ultimately, our research significantly improves the estimation accuracy of causal effects in synthetic control units. We present novel findings on controlling electron injection and acceleration using intense laser pulses in plasma. By intentionally introducing a plasma gradient into a region where a high-power laser pulse is to impinge, we observe polarization-dependent behavior. Specifically, the laser pulse's central third generates a steepened leading edge that undergoes intense ionization, resulting in an electron cloud with a small transverse width. This is accompanied by a trailing plasma segment with a larger electron density. Two separate plasma regions then give rise to two distinct accelerated electron beams, separated spatially. Notably, the separation between these beams is determined by the plasma gradient's width, rather than by the laser pulse's wavelength. Additionally, the separate beams emit distinct radiation patterns at unique frequencies and have differing energy profiles, while still maintaining a consistent acceleration pattern. This phenomenon offers promising prospects for the simultaneous production of multiple electron beams with tailored properties, which could be achieved through tailored plasma conditions without requiring external filtering or sorting processes. A significant advantage of this approach lies in its potential to achieve a high overall current while maintaining individualized properties for each beam, thus making it well suited for the generation of electron sources. Furthermore, given that the separation between the beams is governed by the plasma gradient's width, this method allows for the complete separate acceleration of the two beams if desired. If instead only a small separation between the beams is desired, we can still achieve this by using a shorter plasma region, while also enabling an increased overall current. Overall, our research reveals the possibility of achieving a high current output from a system capable of generating multiple electron beams. An important aspect of this concept is that while the separate beams emit radiation at distinct frequencies, the overall system still maintains a high current output. The idea of only partially separating the beams in order to achieve a high current output is particularly significant. Experimental findings confirm that each separate electron beam possesses a high uniformity in acceleration and can be reliably polarized. Notably, the separate electron beams emit a unique, broad range of radiations in a tripolar pattern. Consequently, our research makes way for future electron acceleration experiments where the separation of electron beams can be exploited to increase total current while maintaining customized properties for each beam. Conversely, our findings also provide crucial insights for experiments where only a single electron beam is desired, which can be achieved by separating the plasma into only two distinct regions, resulting in a high current output in a single accelerated beam. A platinum foil with a mass of 45.3 grams was measured over a period of 510 days in a search for double beta decay and interactions with dark matter, with a 45% purity level and a 23% mass uncertainty for background contaminants. A modified platinum foil was then measured for 17.6 days to investigate decay induced by the $^{100}$Pt nucleus. Results showed that the $^{103}$Pt and $^{101}$Pt nuclei do not undergo double beta decay at a significance of $3.47\sigma$ or better at a 95% confidence level, with a $T_{1/2}$ greater than $1.3\times10^{20}$ years for $^{103}$Pt and $4.0\times10^{19}$ years for $^{101}$Pt. Additionally, no signs of dark matter were detected at the 95% confidence level. This made it possible to establish new limits for possible interactions. Furthermore, it was established that the $^{100}$Pt nucleus does not undergo double beta decay via various possible interactions, with a stated half-life range of $2.3\times10^{20}$ to $5.8\times10^{20}$ years for electron capture and $2.3\times10^{20}$ to $8.9\times10^{20}$ years for electron emission. Finally, it was found that the effective interaction cross-section of the $^{100}$Pt nucleus with a fermionic dark matter particle of mass $10\,\mathrm{GeV}$ is restricted to the range $2.2\times10^{-5}$ to $5.8\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{pb}$. This makes it possible to establish a new sensitivity threshold of $10\,\mathrm{GeV}$ for dark matter mass with an interaction limit similar to the present upper limit. This study marks the first to utilize mass measurements in searches for double beta decay and interactions with dark matter, with a 45% platinum sample having a high purity level and a minimalized background contamination. Furthermore, it showcases modified foil measurements in searches for double beta decay and interactions with dark matter, with a sample having lower platinum content but nearly 100% purity level and minimalized background contamination. Lastly, it establishes rigorous limits on double beta decay and interactions with dark matter with comprehensive and systematic mass measurements of various platinum samples.  In the process, it identified the primary background contaminant of the mass spectrometer and proposed possible remedies to eliminate it.

The value of the flavor-singlet axial-vector charge, $\alpha_s$, is calculated for a specific process involving two photons and one gluon. Calculations are based on dimensional regularization (DIM) and take into consideration the complex interactions among the quarks. It is notable that the photonic contribution to this charge is not affected by the complex quark interactions. Moreover, when the quark masses are considered in this calculation, there is no violation of the anomaly associated with the quantum correction in the photon's interaction with itself. This calculation was performed using a method adapted from Ellis-Manoharan-Soper, Robin Szabo and Broadhurst, and their results were combined and generalized. Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that the complex quark interactions, which involve massless operators, produce a particular invariant often encountered in the calculation of the correction in the photon's interaction with itself. Finally, a similar correction in the gluon-photon process is calculated using a method adapted from Broadhurst-Sottow and Broadhurst-Kreuzer, and then generalized. Based on the calculation, it is estimated that the correction may contribute a factor in the gluon-photon process that is equivalent to a 0.03% modification at very high energy levels and in the photo-production process, which may result in a 0.1% modification at very high energy levels. These calculations were published in the journal arXiv in 1997 and 1998, respectively. In 1998 and 1999, these calculations were presented at respective conferences held in Delmenhorst and Beijing. We introduce a novel deep image colorization technique which learns from multiple sources including the image itself, and can be utilized without manual labeling. By leveraging "source" images with known colors and a color palette, our algorithm generates a range of colorized versions tailored to individual images. By treating each image and camera as a unique entity, our method produces a range of colorized versions that capture the nuances of different cameras and objects within a scene. By designing our technique with the capacity for unlimited parallel processing in mind, we are able to explore potential applications in computer vision fields such as object detection and recognition. By extending the capabilities of a relatively simple, widely available camera, we are able to significantly improve performance in object detection tasks. The results of our experiments confirm that our technique successfully combines the strengths of different cameras and achieves high levels of performance without requiring manual input. The code for our technique has been made available on a public repository for other researchers to use. The repository also includes a dataset consisting of over 2000 images and associated metadata, as well as expertly labeled attributes and color information obtained via manual input. This dataset, titled "CarColor", is set to become a benchmark for researchers working on colorization-based projects in the future. By exploring the key factors that contribute to the success of our technique, we are able to gather important insights and observations. Specifically, our method proves to be particularly effective in environments where object detection plays a crucial role, and is shown to be capable of outperforming existing state-of-the-art techniques. The results of our technique also demonstrate a level of capacity for generalization in object detection tasks, and it is shown that object-related properties contribute more significantly to this capacity than scene-related properties. Lastly, our technique has also been shown to be effective in colorization-based projects via expert annotation. By examining the key principles of human image colorization, we are able to gather key insights and make a series of initial contributions. A symmetry group of order $r$ is introduced for an $n$-dimensional system of partial differential equations. For a partial differential equation system, symmetry groups of order $r$ exist infinitely many times. It is demonstrated that the number of times a partial differential equation system admits a symmetry group of order $r$ is equal to the choice of $r$-element subsets within the set $\{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$. Our study delves into the phenomenon of forward Brillouin scattering across modal interactions within photonic lattice fibers containing solid core substrates made of silicon and germanium. Through in-depth air/silicon/germanium mode dispersion calculations, we establish a framework for examining various modal interactions relevant to current multi-core fiber configurations. The resulting analysis enables prediction and comparison of spectral ranges for structural and acoustic modes in different silicon and germanium designs. Notably, we identify a substantial range of optical mode splits exceeding 100 THz, alongside effective Brillouin gains from 5 to 140 dB/m, primarily influenced by optical and acoustic mode indices. Specifically, we focus on a 7-core fiber setup in a square arrangement to explore high efficiency mechanical coupling through interference, achieving a combined effective gain of up to 126 dB/m. The observed trend suggests that as the number of fiber cores increases, so too will the one-way effective gain, potentially reaching impractically high levels in extremely multi-core fibers. Our work lays the groundwork for optimizing silicon and germanium photonic lattice fibers for efficient non-reciprocity during multiphotonic processes and serves as a starting point for developing advanced photonic devices that integrate multiple functions. Moreover, we offer valuable insights for improving the design of photonic lattice fibers, such as reducing the risk of mechanical instability by avoiding acoustic mode degeneracies and minimizing phonon population. Ultimately, we visualize the future of solid-core photonic lattice fibers as key components in photonic one-way systems, where the strength of the effective gain will be the primary determining factor for device performance. This research aims to develop a secure and robust motion planning framework leveraging Control Barrier Functions, a mathematical approach previously used in control theory to create mathematical barriers that prevent systems from crossing predefined safety boundaries. The proposed framework combines Rethinking Robotics' existing rbdl library for dynamic simulation with abcpy, a Python package allowing for easy implementation of Control Barrier Functions, creating a versatile framework for researching secure and robust motion planning. This method's main advantage is its ability to build a stable and secure trajectory without needing detailed information about the environment, and without introducing ad-hoc avoidance maneuvers, thus preserving the robot's natural movement characteristics. The framework's practicality is demonstrated through its application on the Multi-UAV physical laboratory setup at the University of Genova, showing its efficacy in creating secure and robust plans, even in demanding scenarios. We define the concepts of horizon saddle links, new types of hyperbolic links, and demonstrate their existence on dilation surfaces, also establishing their equivalence to graph saddle links. Additionally, we classify dilation surfaces with isolated singularities according to their transverse dynamics, which is based on the orientation of their hyperbolic links. This orientation theory parallels the classic classification method for Morse functions on a square, with our findings encompassing both classical and graph saddle links. We illustrate the complexity of this orientation theory by showcasing an instance where the associated cohomology log-structure has a particularly high degree of singularity. Furthermore, we demonstrate the possibility of finite entropy, infinite entropy, non-finite entropy, as well as zero entropy in dilation surfaces, which is in line with the different orientations of their horizon saddle links. Lastly, we provide an example of a dilation surface with unbounded entropy near its singular point. This example serves to deepen our understanding of its orientation theory. This work is an adaptation of the author's doctoral dissertation.

A new approach uses a measure of total correlation to quantify interactions within brain networks, providing a complete picture of their structure. To demonstrate its value, we identified a brain network underlying human consciousness, revealing how areas such as the prefrontal cortex contribute to this complex phenomenon. Additionally, our analysis suggests a link between our approach and the emergence of cognitive states. Furthermore, it correlates with the level of functional segregation in the brain, which in turn correlates with measures of cognitive and psychological capabilities. The classical Segal-Bargmann theory explores three key isomorphisms that underpin the unitary group's representation in complex Hilbert space. These isomorphisms are extended to the Clifford algebra. The developed theory applies to any function space equipped with a norm derived from a combination of a variable's Taylor series and an exponential of its norm. The extended Segal-Bargmann Transform is verified to maintain the unitary group's irreducible representation up to a unitary equivalence that is continuous relative to the topological triple structure. Moreover, this theory introduces novel applications of the Taylor Isomorphism and the Clifford Algebra's exponential series. It also lifts the restrictions on the monotonicity of the Segal-Bargmann Transform's weight function. In addition, it resolves the problem of reproducing kernel's singularity when the Clifford algebra comprises an even-dimensional subalgebra with square roots. Lastly, it investigates potential generalizations to the Carnot group and other graded Lie groups. Several open problems are also discussed. Several potential generalizations to group-like variates are discussed as well.

The concept of pathwise conditioning in random fields and measures has a rich mathematical history, particularly in relation to the Radon-Nikodym theorem. This area of study is closely linked to the theory of nonlinearity and is a key component of the theory of noncommutative functions, with notable references including Kariv and Sinclair's 1993 work on multi-dimensional conditional measures, and the 2005 book by Vershik and Golosov, covering the foundational principles. However, the standard approach to defining conditioning in random fields requires an underlying transition function, raising inherent restrictions in random field approaches. This work aims to overcome these restrictions by leveraging Gaussian field utilities, such as Gaussian graphs and Gaussian processes, to demonstrate new methods of defining and operationalizing conditioning in random fields. Furthermore, these novel techniques have significant practical applications in a range of fields including computational biology, computer simulation, image and video processing, computational neuroscience and physics. The underlying justification for this work stems from the insight that the Gaussian graph provides a comprehensive mathematical representation of the underlying structure in random fields, facilitating their analysis and application. Additionally, this approach has significant implications for the development of a pathwise Pareto-optimal strategy in multi-agent decision-making contexts, with particular reference to multiplexed neural connections in the primate visual cortex, demonstrating a clear distinction between commutative and noncommutative conditional independence. Finally, this work illustrates that the limitations of underlying transition functions can be effectively addressed through the utilization of Gaussian graphs, resulting in the establishment of new methods and paradigms in random field conditioning and Gaussian graph utilities. The accompanying appendix contains supplementary material including (i) an initial demonstration of Gaussian graph utilities utility via the example of a conventional Markov chain, (ii) an illustrative example showcasing the distinction between Gaussian and non-Gaussian conditional independence, (iii) an informal discussion on the efficacy of fragment-based methods in analyzing and operationalizing conditioning in random fields, (iv) an informal discussion on the connection between Gaussian graph utilities and the concept of'steering', particularly in a range of applications including computational biology, computer simulation, image and video processing, computational neuroscience and physics, and (v) an informal discussion on the potential future directions in Gaussian graph utilities utility and application. The evidence presented highlights the capacity of Gaussian graphs to overcome traditional restriction in random field approaches. The link reliability of air-borne sensors depends on diverse factors, including the sensor's altitude, the impact of environmental interference, the strength of the signal transmitted, and the link's geometry. To address this challenge, researchers have developed a simulation-based framework that captures these complex interactions. This framework, built using OpenAirNet, simulates a diverse atmospheric condition and calculates spatial links between ground-based sensors and aerial vehicles in a two-dimensional space. To accommodate varying atmospheric conditions, the framework uses a model that takes into account the distortion of electromagnetic signals. This model is integrated into a link-budget analysis, determining the optimal signal strength required for reliable data transmission between sensors. This information is then utilized in a Monte-Carlo simulation to evaluate the performance of the link under changing atmospheric conditions. To show the practical application of this approach, researchers implemented it on a ground-and-air sensor network to monitor pollution in urban environments. This approach prioritizes link establishment between ground-based sensors that detect pollution, and aerial vehicles that carry sensors to verify and report the data. By leveraging this verification capability, the aerial sensor is able to adjust its parameters to establish a link with the ground sensor that yields the strongest signal. Simulations revealed that the framework achieves a high success rate of link establishment between sensors under optimal atmospheric conditions. Furthermore, the framework achieved a high success rate and minimal average loss by selecting the link with the strongest signal under sub-optimal atmospheric conditions. In addition, the framework's high success rate of link establishment enabled the aerial sensor to successfully transmit data to the ground sensor. The subterranean Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment, the largest component of Fermilab's Larned Center Long Baseline Neutrino Facility, is poised to significantly impact precision neutrino oscillations research. Largely funded by the U.S. Department of Energy and led by Professor Thomas Shutt from Pennsylvania State University, the DUNE experiment will focus on two primary scientific objectives. First, it aims to verify the current dominant description of neutrino behavior and their mixing patterns. Additionally, the project seeks to consolidate existing data on neutrino crossings, which would reveal any discrepancies from expected standard behavior indicating new physics beyond the Standard Model, including potential proof of CP symmetry breaking in neutrino oscillations. With its cutting-edge liquid-argong technology and advanced precision, the DUNE experiment will significantly enhance current precision, which may indicate the presence of lepton universality violation, challenging the established Standard Model of particle physics. In this study, the DUNE experiment's scientific goals and sensitivity will be examined, and the liquid-argon technology's sophisticated detector will be presented as a model to inspire future research in particle and neutrino physics, including potential applications in technology and life science at subterranean depths. In the concluding sections, the project's potential contributions to astrophysical and cosmological studies will be investigated. The DUNE project's major collaboration with Italian and European research groups, particularly regarding its prototypical detector, the prototile, will be examined in an appendix. Furthermore, the project's broader implications and future opportunities for life-science and fundamental science research will be explored.

This project involves incorporating Virtual Organizations and their characteristics into the Formal Logic framework. The Virtual Organization concept, encompassing components such as goals, structures, collaborations, and member relationships, is explored through a comprehensive meaning formalization. This enables a formal examination of VO refinements, allowing for the integration of smaller, more specialized organizations within larger ones. The refinement of VOs has significant implications for their objectives, hierarchical relationships, membership, and operational dynamics. This study presents a preliminary understanding of VOs and their complexities, laying the groundwork for further discussions on VO modeling methodologies. The primary contribution of this research is the formalization of VO characteristics; as a secondary aspect, it also introduces a novel approach to formalizing organization dynamics. The proposed theory is illustrated through examples that demonstrate its applicability to real-world scenarios, thus showing its potential for practical applications in VO modeling. Although this project does not focus on the simulation of VO dynamics, it does examine the formalization of this topic. The formalization of VO characteristics is a significant advancement in this area, and it is hoped that this method can be developed further for simulating complex organizational behaviors and structures. The formalization was executed using the Tarski system, and the resulting models can be handled using dedicated tools such as the TarskiLogic system.

To enhance robotic movement robustness through Trajectory Transfer (TrajTrans), a proposed method utilizes experience replay with modified data distribution to facilitate policy optimization. For every policy iteration, TrajTrans resamples past robot actions, applying a variance reduction technique and a Gaussian shift to ensure a more focused selection of experiences, thereby boosting sample efficiency. Comparison experiments with a standard-plot approach and a random sampling approach in MuJoCo tasks demonstrate improved variance reduction and sample efficiency for the new method. Moreover, a practical evaluation in a 6-DoF Franka Emika arm shows that this method enhances adaptation and robustness in scenarios with sudden changes in a real robotic setup. The source code is available for review on GitHub at https://github.com/Paranja/TrajTrans-ER. Following this, our research is further explored in a study on adaptive TrajTrans reinforcement learning as presented at IROS 2022. As presented in the related work, an extended version of this concept was explored in a study on online TrajTrans with little to no initial data, presented at ARX. The primary contribution of this study is a more nuanced and detailed characterization of TrajTrans performance issues, which are (1) large distributional differences resulting in poor experience choice and (2) a failure to reach the minimum of the target loss function. By rectifying these issues through a more focused experience selection method, the method's effectiveness and speed are significantly improved. Ultimately, this study's findings lay the groundwork for further research on improving the speed and efficiency of TrajTrans in reinforcement learning. As presented in related work, an optimized version of this method was tested in a study on TrajTrans with physics-based constraints, presented at the IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation in 2023. The method's source code is publicly available for review on GitHub at https://github.com/Paranja/trajectories-with-collisions. Two new strategies, the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and the superbosonization equation, have been proposed to translate gauge field theories into a purely bosonic framework. A thorough investigation is conducted to examine their validity and applicability. It is found that the superbosonization equation represents a specialized instance of the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and thus shares its limitations. Both methods function well in simple theories with an Abelian gauge field but struggle with those featuring non-Abelian gauge fields or spin-1/2 fermions. Additionally, the effectiveness of both strategies is evaluated based on their capacity to recover known results in soliton physics and the quantum field theories of finite and zero dimensions. It is concluded that neither the superbosonization equation nor the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation can serve as a universal replacement for the Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation, primarily due to their inadequacy in dealing with non-Abelian gauge fields, spin-1/2 fermions, and more complex field structures. Furthermore, it is proposed that the main constraint is the improper application of the Feynman integral for matrix kernels, a problem that can be overcome by expressing these kernels as combinations of identity matrices. Such expressions allow for a direct interpretation of the integrals and restoration of the bosonic formulation. This can be achieved for any gauge field and fermion representation, thereby demonstrating the potential of both the superbosonization equation and the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation as valuable tools in certain field theory applications. A detailed case study involving a spin-1/2 fermion representation is presented to illustrate this concept. Moreover, it is suggested that the superbosonization equation can serve as a creative method for developing novel transformations between various representations in field theory and symmetry breaking scenarios. A comprehensive review of the application of the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and the superbosonization equation is provided, showcasing their validity and effectiveness in translating gauge field theories into a bosonic framework, with some notable exceptions. A thorough investigation of the superfield formalism is then conducted to examine its validity and effectiveness in translating gauge field theories into a bosonic framework, with a detailed case study involving a non-Abelian gauge field and a spin-1/2 fermion representation. The superfield approach is found to successfully translate and recover known results in quantum field theories, thereby demonstrating its potential as a universal tool for translating gauge field theories into a bosonic framework. To take these uncertainties into account, existing methods have proposed using multiple inputs, such as map data and video frames. However, these methods have not fully taken into account the different aspects of information contained in consecutive road map snapshots. In this paper, we propose the use of a novel neural network architecture, called Mode RNN, which can capture the varying levels of importance between the dynamic elements in traffic videos. This is done by using a novel mechanism called the Mode Graph, which determines the relative importance of information in traffic videos. We show through experiments on a traffic video prediction dataset that our method achieves the best results and that our approach to utilizing the changing elements in traffic videos is reasonable. Our method has won the Best Paper Award at ICASSP2022. Information about our method can be found at https://www.asir92.com/. Our method has been recognized at the Data Science Council of America. This research focuses on security vulnerabilities born from language runtime limitations. We've found that existing analysis tools often fail to catch certain common lifetime issues in Rust, leading to explored approaches in addressing these vulnerabilities through static analysis, code rewriting, and compiler extension. Our research indicates that the most effective method involves utilizing the JavaScript scripting engine within Chrome to identify and fix incorrect lifetime assumptions. By leveraging this technique, browser developers can prevent security vulnerabilities arising from lifetime issues, providing promising avenues for incorporating dynamic type checking to eliminate such vulnerabilities in the future. Furthermore, this approach can apply to a broader range of programming languages beyond Rust, using the JavaScript engine to identify and fix lifetime issues. Our technique was tested on over fifty distinct lifetime issues, showing positive results. The implementation details of this work have been made available on GitHub for further study. A blockchain system enables secure interaction between distinct systems of different kinds, facilitating a dependable data exchange framework. The rapidly expanding Internet of Things (IoT) necessitates a trustworthy and highly secure data exchange framework, and blockchain technology is suitably tailored to meet these demands. However, the potential of blockchain technology in the context of IoT remains constrained due to factors such as the resource-intensive nature of blockchain transactions for IoT devices and the absence of a clear-cut approach to supporting IoT and its intricate sensor networks. Furthermore, IoT devices are susceptible to cyber threats due to their inherent vulnerabilities. To bridge this gap, this study proposes an innovative IoT blockchain framework, characterized by the incorporation of a new blockchain transaction protocol. This novel protocol leverages the services offered by "oracles" to enhance the efficiency of blockchain transactions for IoT systems. We also present a smart contractual framework replete with three unique smart contracts designed to protect IoT systems from data fraud and safeguard their integrity. We demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed framework through a practical case study involving a food supply chain, thus showcasing the potential of our framework in the realm of IoT and blockchain technology. Lastly, this study conducts a thorough assessment of the computational resources required by our proposed framework. Overall, this study contributes significantly to the realm of blockchain and IoT technology by propelling the forefront of this emerging field and advancing the underlying technology of future blockchain and IoT systems. Blind, low-vision, and other print-impaired individuals still rely on printed documents but face significant challenges due to their lack of accessibility. Our focus in this paper lies on enhancing the accessibility of physical documents, specifically evaluating how navigable are printed documents for print-impaired individuals? We introduce a new concept, Document Navigability, aimed at boosting the accessibility of physical documents. We outline the requirements for robust document navigability, and through field trials with print-impaired participants, validate the importance of specific accessibility features – high-contrast colors, hierarchical structure, and page labels. Consequently, we suggest a novel paradigm for making physical documents navigable through the integration of a special tag, known as the Document Marker Tag, and a scanning-assisted mobile application. The Document Marker Tag enables print-impaired individuals to access supplementary digital information, such as an PDF's web address, by scanning a special mark using a mobile device. Our document reformulation techniques and mobile assistive tools aim to improve the accessibility of essential daily documents like forms, lists, and contracts, ultimately promoting digital inclusion. The proposed approach emerges as a promising solution to bolster the document accessibility paradigm. Our research was conducted in conjunction with print-impaired individuals and a renowned Italian association for people with visual impairments, enabling us to gather valuable insights and collaborate on a pioneering project. Our solutions aim to empower print-impaired individuals to fill out forms, read lists, browse websites, and carry out daily tasks with greater independence, thus benefiting from a greater accessibility of physical documents. Research into the swimming mechanics of the centipede forficatus near the water's surface reveals its unique locomotion technique. By utilizing high-resolution camera systems, our experiment has demonstrated that forficatus swims using a combination of alternating limb movements and a cycle of acceleration and deceleration, primarily propelled by water resistance. Unlike other animals, forficatus's swimming pattern does not result in net forward movement during each alternating limb motion. Instead, the centipede generates movement by combining forces from a series of rapid accelerations and decelerations with a small fraction of its total limbs at a time. According to our findings, forficatus's swimming speed is primarily determined by a tight balance between increasing movement force and maintaining stability, rather than by traditional factors such as stride length and frequency. Our investigation also employs a mathematical model to simulate forficatus's locomotion technique and suggests that the centipede's ability to swim efficiently near the water's surface may be due to adopting a unique multi-phasic movement pattern, characterized by distinct phases of movement and momentum transfer between its limbs. The simulation of tsunami waves driven by viscoelastic flow and their interaction with the Earth's interior and surface offer significant opportunities for computational investigation.  We have developed high-performance computing approaches that utilize the summation-by-parts finite element method and advanced time-integration techniques to model tsunami dynamics in the Earth's interior and as they transition to the ocean. When coupled with post-processing algorithms that account for certain limitations of Newtonian-elastic models, our approach can accurately predict a range of realistic tsunami wave forms, including those generated by impacts from asteroids. Notably, our simulations indicate a notable discrepancy between 2nd order and Newtonian-elastic wave forms at early times, with the former exhibiting 10-20% errors relative to PMPM free-surface restoration. We show that combining 2nd order material time-step and implicit integration with adapted mesh strategies results in a significant (2-3 fold) reduction in computational requirements for realistic tsunami wave simulations in the Earth's interior and as they transition to the ocean. Furthermore, our approach allows for accurate and efficient simulation of tsunami waves up to 12 hours old using modern ocean mesh configurations and a maximum element size of 500m, thereby facilitating the exploration of long-term viscoelastic flow phenomena. We highlight several strategies for extending the time-step, yet show that high-resolution simulations require the advancement of a new, adapted material time-step approach that is uniquely compatible with Newtonian-elastic models. We anticipate that our approach will facilitate the exploration of viscoelastic flow phenomena over a range of realistic time-scales and, in particular, the interplay between 1) early-time high-frequency viscoelastic waves generated near an asteroid impact and 2) late-time low-frequency gravity waves observable at ocean depths. Such a multi-scale investigation could conceivably enhance our capacity to distinguish between various types of impacters based on the extent to which dispersal mechanisms contribute to long-term tsunami wave distributions. Ultimately, a comprehensive multi-scale analysis may significantly augment our ability to accurately model, and thereby prepare for, asteroid impacts that initiate tsunami waves with distinct propagation characteristics. Information on the simulations, including high resolution videos and time series data, is accessible via Zenodo, search term: Stoakes2021. The presented computational models are documented on GitHub within the framework [XGAMM.github.io/xgamm-fem]. Cyber-Physical Systems, particularly those with time-critical aspects, often require a robust form of reliability that goes beyond the typical IT definition. In this context, we propose a holistic approach for evaluating system resilience in CP-SDPs by leveraging temporal logic formulas inspired by property-based testing methods. Initially, we frame a general concept of resilience in CP-SDPs, followed by a practical strategy for choosing relevant properties and creating test cases. Furthermore, we offer a practical technique for metric resilience evaluation, which is based on a formula's satisfaction level, along with an application of this method to the vehicle platooning domain. We have developed a tool utilizing Haskell that facilitates evaluating resilience in CP-SDPs according to our proposed framework. Although we focus on IT resilience in this study, the framework itself is adaptable to other forms of reliability, including physical resilience in the cyber-physical domain. We have explored assessing resilience in simpler models so far, but we intend to extend our analysis to more intricate models, incorporating factors like network fragmentation, variable processing times, and data irregularities in the future. Additionally, we aim to broaden the scope of our research to other areas of CP-SDPs.

We explore various approaches to establish an approximation theorem for the gradient of a function that satisfies a nonlinear diffusion equation on a complete, connected Riemannian manifold. This theorem provides the necessary justification for leveraging the properties of solutions to nonlinear diffusion equations in the field of stochastic partial differential equations, specifically for establishing existence and uniqueness of stochastic flow and the conservation of entropy. The provided results can be utilized in a broad range of applications, such as geometric flows, nonlinear partial differential equations, and the study of Brownian motion within manifolds. In this paper, we begin by reviewing key estimates for the gradient of a function that satisfies a nonlinear diffusion equation, before presenting both local and global approximation theorems. These theorems are derived from diverse regularity results established in prior literature. We ultimately apply these theorems to demonstrate the conservation of entropy for a class of nonlinear diffusion equations, exemplified by the Kellar-Vavasis diffusion operator. The operator in question is defined as the sum of the Laplacian and a linear diffusion operator with positive coefficients, coupled with a nonlinear diffusion operator whose off-diagonal entries satisfy specific negative and monotone properties. Similarly, we establish an approximation theorem for operators representing geodesic deviation, whose entries satisfy the aforementioned negative and monotone properties. The presented findings are instrumental in establishing the conservation of entropy for generalized Laplace operators with Helmholtz and discontinuous diffusion components in the literature. Our results are also applicable to the conservation of entropy for $L^2$-gradient flows in metric spaces, as demonstrated in a recent paper by the second author. The presented findings are further instrumental in establishing existence and uniqueness of stochastic partial differential equations in the literature. Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) are a group of state transition models that combine a stochastic process with a hidden state one, useful in describing complex systems through their observed behavior. HMMs consider two fundamental processes: a hidden state process (Q) and an observation process (O), linked by a hidden state to observation function (f) that assigns a probability distribution to observations given a hidden state. Such models support a crucial time reversal property that enables backward computations, facilitating an inference of the hidden state process (Q) from the observation process (O). This key property, along with others, can be leveraged to describe an HMM within the Tarski sequence of monads over a suitable category. This description, based on HMM-related monad constituents, is valuable for analyzing and combining different HMM properties, such as the time reversal property, state isolation, emission restrictions, or the obtainability of observation and hidden state values. Additionally, this description enables a systematic investigation into when an HMM can be decomposed into its constituent parts, along with a clear insight into what an emergent property of an HMM is. A popular 3D point cloud-based localisation method known as Point Cloud-based Point Descriptors (PCPD) has a significant limitation - it suffers from high computational complexity due to its dependence on 3D structures' search, narrowing down its utility to real-time localisation on small datasets. To overcome this, a new framework called Normal Distribution Transform-Transformer (NDT-Transformer), which converts point clouds into Normal Distribution Transform (NDT) representations, was developed. This allows it to decompose an NDT representation into multiple parts that can be used as distinct localisation cues, making it possible to employ a more efficient and accelerated computation technique. By doing so, NDT-Transformer can perform PCPD-like localisation in real-time on large-scale datasets. Experimental results show that NDT-Transformer performs similarly or better than PCPD in terms of localisation accuracy and recall, with an actual improvement in real-time localisation performance by two orders of magnitude on large datasets. Furthermore, a new method for generating PCPD descriptors has also been introduced, leading to enhanced descriptors using a normal map and favourable results in the line of research known as loop closure detection. To support this study, the related code and dataset can be accessed at https://github.com/zhangwei29/NDT-Transformer. With its capabilities and performance, NDT-Transformer has the potential to contribute significantly to the research community. The study's limitations and potential avenues for improvement are also explored.  Specifically, when comparing our approach with SHAPES, another point cloud descriptor method, our results show that NDT-Transformer outperforms SHAPES in localisation accuracy while also significantly improving the computation time. Moreover, a new method for generating PCPD descriptors using conditional normal maps has also been introduced and evaluated. The code and dataset related to this study can be found at https://github.com/zhangwei29/NDT-Transformer. Our approach has the potential to expand the application of PCPD localisation in autonomous vehicles and drones while loop closure detection in computer vision can benefit from the presented method for generating improved descriptors via convolutional autoencoders. The connection between nematicity and superconductivity remains a major mystery in iron-based superconductors. To investigate this relationship in a well-established superconductor, we carried out an ab initio study of LiFeAs, a compound known for its direct band inversion. Our research shows that at standard pressure, LiFeAs displays no nematic susceptibility despite being susceptible to hydrostatic pressure. Additionally, we discovered that an external electric field has a negligible effect on the spontaneous strain at zero temperature. These outcomes imply that electric-field-driven strain and nematicity are unlikely to occur in LiFeAs. Therefore, LiFeAs can be ruled out as a suitable system to test novel strain-based experimental methods. On the other hand, it is highly unlikely that LiFeAs undergoes a electric-field-induced superconducting transition.
