We demonstrate through simulated molecular experiments that a neuroevolutionary approach can successfully discover diverse strategies for strategic cooperation in a dynamic environment, even when the strategies are highly complex and numerous. The strategies in question involve coordinating movements to achieve cooperative goals, like coordinating the assembly of a specific trimer structure through self-propelled particles. Our results show that a large population of blind, non-directed particles can collectively learn multiple distinct assemblies for a given set of conditions through a neuroevolutionary process, even when the search space consists of an vast and virtually infinite number of potential configurations. The intricate strategies formed by these particles exhibit a range of fascinating patterns, including symbiotic relationships between basic agents and temporary'snowball' phenomena where many particles converge on a single assembly. Importantly, our study highlights the significant role that symmetry likely plays in reducing the complexity of the assembly landscape. Recorded phase sequences of the evolutionary process, which show past-future stability patterns of coexisting strategies, hold considerable potential for informing the experimental search for strategic cooperatives in various domains. Furthermore, our strategy-formation process serves as an apt model for the gradual emergence of complexity within far-from-equilibrium molecular systems through local adjustments. The corresponding information structures can be strategically manipulated and repurposed for governing cooperative behaviors in diverse environments. Ultimately, our approach presents a novel method for developing innovative cooperative designs within materials science and chemistry. This research introduces two modifications for Loidreau's code-based cryptosystem. 
Originally employing a Goppa code with a specific vanishing polynomial, Loidreau's system can now incorporate any linear code over a finite field. 
Meanwhile, a public key decoder can potentially pose a threat if intercepted, but we've developed a way to eliminate this vulnerability by substituting public keys with random ones, thereby ensuring a diverse set of possible matrices during the decoding process. 
Furthermore, we demonstrate the enhancement in security offered by our first modification when applied to a specific type of linear code within Loidreau's system; specifically, we show the density of the associated parabolic sets has decreased. 
Additionally, we provide computational comparisons between the original and modified systems, showcasing a significant increase in the modified system's computational requirements."

To capture word meanings and handle semantic ambiguities in natural language, we introduce a novel method for pre-training language models. This approach, called Dict-BERT, incorporates a thesaurus into BERT-style models by virtue of three novel objectives. Firstly, the "word-meaning" objective aims to optimize each word according to its dictionary definition, thereby enhancing the model's understanding of word meanings. Secondly, the "similar-meaning" objective objective aims to refine word representations based on their dictionary-defined meanings. Finally, the "one-meaning-one-representation" objective aims to minimize semantic ambiguities within individual words. Our experimental results demonstrate that Dict-BERT achieves superior performance on a range of benchmark tasks, including word sense disambiguation, hypernyms discovery, and paraphrasing, ultimately demonstrating its potential to scale up on more comprehensive thesaurus resources. Additionally, the model's improved word representations lead to enhanced performance on word similarity evaluation using a dataset derived from WordNet. Such a study has an application in examining the extremes of persistence in these random complexes, thus contributing to a deeper understanding of persistence diagrams. 

Our research centers around three key aspects related to the mass (number of acycle extremities) of these acycles: (i) the distribution of the mass when the point intensity increases, (ii) the probability distributions of the mass when the point intensity remains constant, and (iii) the long-term behavior of the mass. 

Our results reveal that the growth of the acycle mass for a fixed point intensity is described by a specific polynomial, a long-term study shows asymptotic independence from the point intensity, and for a fixed acycle mass, the corresponding probability distributions shift towards heavier-tailed distributions as the point intensity increases. 

Additionally, our work includes the derivation of the extremal dependence functions of the corresponding persistence function extremes, a description of its limiting form, and demonstration that these extremal dependence functions differ based on the acycle dimension.

This text study investigates Vertical Federated Learning where participants cannot access other contributors' data regions despite their desire to collaborate. As a result, training and inference occur in a sequential manner. Although Federated Learning is thought to be robust when executed in a real-world setting, it is influenced by various forms of manipulation that can significantly undermine its accuracy. This investigation systematically examined and evaluated multiple forms of manipulation that target the training process on real-world datasets. In one aspect of the research, training integrity was compromised by introducing false data, which revealed that a small portion of manufactured samples (5%) can achieve competitive model performance in practice. In another aspect of the research, the validation process was targeted by manipulating model parameters to affect inference accuracy on test data. This attack, which we term Privacy-steal, demonstrates that slight alterations to a small set of model weights (0.01-0.1%) can lead to a substantial decrease in accuracy (40% drop in L-FBCD benchmark). In a third aspect of the research, data ownership was falsified by embedding private data samples within large sets of public data samples. This attack, which we term Data-poisoning, reveals that a small number of poisoned data samples (10%) can cause the model to improperly use additional data features. In an effort to mitigate these vulnerabilities, this research introduces simple data validation procedures that can help defend against these attacks. These defenses prove effective not only in the context of this research but also in practice. This research raises important implications for industry practitioners, highlighting the need to analyze attack strategies before deploying FL-based model training systems. Such analysis could significantly improve the accuracy and reliability of these systems in the field. The research code is publicly available at https. The growing complexity of urban systems is driving cities to evolve into sophisticated, interconnected entities within the realm of Socio-Cyber-Physical Systems. These highly interconnected cities are vulnerable to attacks from adversaries who seek to compromise these intricate networks for financial gain in industries such as e-commerce and energy trading. In response to this threat, a pioneering approach known as the Socio-Cyber-Physical City Defense Game has been developed to help defenders devise effective strategies to protect these interconnected cities from malicious invaders. This innovative game theoretical model, characterized by finite stages, complete information, and imperfectly observable states, poses several challenges for exploration, including computing the best response for attackers and determining the most effective resource management approach for defenders. Through the application of lower variational complexity, researchers have made significant progress in addressing these complexities, enabling them to outperform conventional methods such as Q-learning and pure strategy tit-for-tat approaches that focus solely on attacker defense strategies. Furthermore, this study introduces an innovative approach for resource management that outperforms standard methods by incorporating distributed constraint programming. More critically, this approach addresses the challenge of computing the best response for attackers, thus enabling a comprehensive and thorough interaction between defenders and adapters. When simulated within a real-world city setting, the results show that the approach can help reduce financial losses to attackers of up to 54.86%. These findings emphasize the crucial role of resource management in Socio-Cyber-Physical City Defense Games and underscore the need to explore novel approaches for achieving optimal outcomes. In response to pressing query, the code for this research has been made available on GitHub for the purpose of replication. Furthermore, future research could focus on exploring novel game theoretical models, such as stochastic games and their application in Socio-Cyber-Physical City Defense Games. Moreover, the study provides essential insights for real-world applications and implementations in areas involving resource allocation and strategic planning, thus contributing to the broader field of operations research. Long document retrieval has been a longstanding hurdle in both on-point and off-point examination, exacerbated by the diverse range of topics and ideas within a single document, making it challenging for traditional methods to accurately assess relevance. The problem becomes even more complicated in noisy labelled environments where errors can pervade entire batches of data. The application of classical vector space retrieval methods to these issues has shown them to be particularly vulnerable to label noise, working best in controlled, small-scale datasets. The search for an improved method has led researchers to adapt techniques from semantic search and co-training, incorporating a diversity of information and robust designs. A new approach proposed in this research combines bag sampling, calculating the average score of each document against a set of relevant terms, to produce a noise-resistant ranking. The method also utilizes group-level hyperplane models to mitigate the impact of random noise, prioritising the hyperplane closest to the majority of relevant documents. The novel technique achieves consistent and impressive results across various levels of noise within twenty-three diverse noise types. The full-source code for this research is publicly available at https://github.com/keithkearney/relevance_games_with_noise. The researchers also released a noise generation tool at https://github.com/keithkearney/noise_generator, and the extended dataset can be accessed through https://github.com/keithkearney/long_docs_label_noise. The research demonstrates that label noise can significantly impact the relevance of retrieved documents, with mAP scores decreased to 0.3543 from 0.4175 in the TREC long document dataset. The researchers achieved further improvement with their novel method, with mAP scores increased to 0.4175 from 0.3543 in the standard dataset and 0.4059 in the degraded dataset. Support for transductive learning methods allows pre-trained Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to infer node labels without using explicit supervision, but they still rely on a sufficient amount of labeled data. This issue prevents the effective use of GNNs for graphs with scarce labeled nodes. To overcome this limitation, we have developed a novel pseudo-labeling technique that combines self-supervised learning with graph structure information to produce informative transductive predictions. These predictions accurately reflect the underlying graph structure, allowing GNNs to make the most of a small set of labeled nodes. Experimental results on real-world graph classification datasets demonstrate our method's success in overcoming the limitation of insufficient labeled data. When compared to other state-of-the-art techniques, our approach consistently achieves improved Graph Classification performance. The associated code can be accessed at https://github.com/asharakeh/informative-pseudo-labels.

This study investigates how basic robotic behaviors can emerge in a system with a large group of robots following a moving wall. We discovered two main types of emergent patterns in this system - a highly ordered single-file line march, where every robot maintains a consistent distance from the one ahead, and disordered formations where robots stay behind the virtual leader but show no spatial structure. Additionally, we found that these patterns can shift dramatically in response to minor changes in the robots' field of vision. To understand these shifts, we examined the transition between these patterns as a whole system instead of studying individual robots' behaviors. Using a mean-field approximation, we analyzed the system and identified several key indicators that can predict these transitions. Notably, we found that certain indicators can reveal a broader, more general pattern underlying these transitions that extends beyond our particular two-state model. These motions can be viewed as a combination of crystalline curvature flow and an external force flow. MCA CM has broad applications, including modeling dislocation dynamics, growth issues, and slithering line dynamics. The theory of existence and long-term behavior for surface motions under this flow is well-established, yet proofs for regimes with multiple surfaces and coupled systems remain scarce. It has been established that the SLE loop measure arises as a natural consequence of combining two Liouville quantum gravity disks via conformal welding, and we relate the Liouville quantum telescopes and their quantum area measures to this phenomenon. In addition, we demonstrate how the existing quantum covers work in tandem with LQG's conformal welding to yield the SLE loop measure, and examine instances where this process yields multiple independent SLE loops. Furthermore, we explore random loop Gibbs measures and their associated dimensions. In particular, we show that a random loop measure falls within the Liouville quantum gravity disk's natural conformal welding class if and only if it exhibits a dimension of $4/25$. Moreover, we relate the quantum covers and LQG's conformal welding to a dimension of $4/25$ of the twisted loop measure on Schramm-Loewner loops. In contrast to conformal welding, the SLE loop measure does not possess a characterization solely based on accretive or eroding dynamics. Nonetheless, we illustrate how an explicit accretive dynamic emerges from a specific instance of conformal welding involving a quantum disk based on a Brownian motion. In this specific instance, we show that an accretive dynamic holds with a characteristic angle of $\pi/4$; however, we also show that the SLE loop measure itself does not fall within the dynamic's specified conformal welding class. Lastly, we derive an alternative method for describing the SLE loop measure using quantum covers and LQG's conformal welding. In particular, we show that the measure describes a situation where a disk is transformed into a polygon, with each edge corresponding to a separate loop, and establish an explicit formula for this transformation. In contrast to the typical scenario where the Loewner driving functions are independent and identically distributed, we find that the driving functions for this formulation are a multivariate Gaussian distribution with a specific, non-degenerate covariance matrix. In particular, the first and second components of the driving functions exhibit a standard normal distribution and a covariance of $1/2$, while the third and subsequent components exhibit a zero mean and increasing covariance. We conclude by drawing a connection between conformal welding and random loop measures and the recent finding that the SLE loop measure forms a subset of three-dimensional random hyperbolic graphs, particularly those exhibiting a genus of three. The amplitudes for producing $K\Lambda$ and $K\Sigma$ through the in-flight photoproduction of kaons off nucleons are determined to be negligible, with estimates ranging from the order of $10^{-4}$ to $10^{-3}$, as a result of the dominance of spin-3/2 nucleon and delta resonances. These resonances lead to final photoactivation amplitudes that are significantly larger than those arising from the $s$-wave interaction between kaons and nucleons and a specific $s$-wave $\Lambda\pi$ channel. It is proposed that the $s$-wave interaction between kaons and a delta resonances, as well as a $K\Sigma$ coupling within the $\Delta \to K \Sigma \pi$ decay process, may contribute significantly to $K\Lambda$ photoactivation, potentially resulting in amplitudes on the order of $10^{-3}$ to $10^{-4}$. As a result, empirical observations indicating the presence of $K\Lambda$ photoactivation surpassing the expected isospin symmetry breaking level pose a significant challenge to the current understanding of photoproduction processes. To resolve this discrepancy, this work considers an alternative interpretation of existing data, as well as the possibility of detecting $K\Sigma$ photoactivation, which may also be on the order of $10^{-3}$ to $10^{-4}$ or potentially larger. Ultimately, this issue is left to be explored in future experimental studies. Moreover, this work contributes to a better comprehension of photoactivation processes by determining that $s$-wave interactions between kaons and nucleons and a final $\Lambda\pi$ state do not play a significant role in photoactivation. Furthermore, by assessing the dominance of spin-3/2 nucleon and delta resonances over other contributing processes, this work sets a benchmark of $10^{-3}$ to $10^{-4}$ for their contribution to photoactivation, which can be used to evaluate other photoproduction processes. Ultimately, this work lays out a potential explanation for the prominent $K\Lambda$ photoactivation observed in the Big European Bubble Chamber experiment and suggests exploring $K\Sigma$ photoactivation in experiments with higher statistics. Active participation on social media is crucial for civic engagement, community building, and personal well-being. However, one in five people experiences significant difficulties with their devices, hindering their ability to engage fully in online activities, including creating content on social media. Despite the numerous studies on inclusive design in human-computer interaction, little attention has been paid to creating accessible social media content for people with motor impairments. To bridge this knowledge gap, our research investigates the challenges faced by individuals with motor impairments when creating social media content, focusing on captioning, which is particularly essential for content authoring. Through interviews with 14 participants, we discovered both the challenges and opportunities associated with accessible content authoring. Our research implies that future designs should prioritize accessibility, creating opportunities for inclusion, especially in contexts like assistive gaming, charitable e-mail accounts, and content creation platforms. Furthermore, our research sheds light on the role of accessibility features, including the effectiveness of available assistive technologies, as well as the social factors that influence motor-impaired individuals' engagement in online activities. Ultimately, our research moves beyond identifying barriers to creating inclusive design solutions that empower motor-impaired individuals to create content and participate in social media.

In clinical trials for Alzheimer's and progressive diseases tracked with continuous data over time, comparison tests often measure treatment differences against a placebo under mean measurements. However, focusing solely on mean outcomes overlooks how treatments affect a subject's natural fluctuations in disease progression. This study advocates using a combined analysis approach, combining subject-level time series with overall mean comparisons, to gain a more comprehensive understanding of treatment efficacy. Namely, utilizing Natural Cubic Splines to model longitudinal data provides a flexible framework for analyzing clinical trials. This method is exemplified in two fictional trial scenarios and a real-world Pfizer study (NCT02684890). Results indicate that while mean comparisons may reveal no significant difference between treatments, a more detailed analysis using Natural Cubic Splines reveals statistically significant and clinically relevant benefits associated with the active treatment in question. Utilizing this approach in future clinical trials may provide a more complete evaluation of treatment efficacy. HC's efforts to replicate the results from the Pfizer study align with the goals of accelerating the development of treatments for Alzheimer's disease.

Additionally, we establish that nothing is omitted from this class within the context of these calculi. By examining a diverse range of function classes, we showcase the utility of our framework, exemplified by the propositional lambda-calculus, where the existence of a type indicates the presence of a total function that maps inputs to a type that can be reduced to a ground type. Furthermore, we dissect the superclasses of total functions represented by typed $\lambda^{\xi}$-calculi and demonstrate that they align with non-uniform computational complexity classes like $\mathbf{F}_1^{\rm p}$-CPS, while their partial function counterparts surpass the capabilities of typed $\lambda$-calculi based matching and definability results. Specifically, we prove the impossibility of certain functions that are clearly definable as total functions but are unfeasible as partial functions with input contracts, leading to a significant gap between partial and total functions within these calculi. Ultimately, we show that the propositional $\lambda^{\xi}$-calculus can efficiently capture a particularly powerful function class known as $\mathbf{F}_1^{\rm p}$-FRECD. FRECD represents the highest level of functionality achieved by type systems, including a robust notion of free definability, that has been consistently enforced across various superclasses like $\mathbf{F}_2^{\rm p}$-CPS, $\mathbf{F}_1^{\rm p}$-CPS, and $\mathbf{F}_1^{\rm p}$-FRECD itself. Interestingly, the propositional $\lambda^{\xi}$-calculus surpasses the capabilities of certain general typed $\lambda$-calculi based matching and definability results, specifically a recent general freedom theorem proposed by the authors, leading to a reevaluation and potential enhancement of this fundamental result. By introducing a new general freedom theorem, we can validate the soundness of our typed calculus framework, ensuring that the introduced calculus is indeed a valid model for the superclasses of functions that we have been studying.

Protecting sensitive information in deep learning models is a pressing concern, given their widespread use in fields such as medicine and law. Knowledge extraction from these models can leak information about inputs, which is often prohibited from being disclosed. Previous approaches to compressing models, like distillation, can also risk revealing sensitive information in the student model. We identify the crucial role of information flow in knowledge extraction and introduce InDistill, a method that preserves it, thereby enabling the extraction of sensitive information to be significantly reduced. InDistill enables the extraction of knowledge to be marked as sensitive and automatically determines the minimum required capacity of the compressing model to prevent information leakage. InDistill uses set-based optimization and reverse validation, allowing it to adapt to models with trainable parameters and ensure higher confidence in knowledge extraction. InDistill surpasses traditional model compression techniques in preserving information flow and achieves superior compression ratios and extraction accuracy compared to other knowledge extraction methods. InDistill makes the first attempt to address the issue of information leakage in model extraction and compressing and achieves state-of-the-art results in various benchmark tests. The implementation of InDistill is available under an open-source license on GitHub. To automatically determine the minimum required capacity of the compressing model, we introduce a validation tool called ValDist at https://github.com/UTSA-CS-VMLAB/ValDist. This tool makes the validation and verification of InDistill's results more efficient and enables the extraction of more sensitive information. Our study focuses on linear-like submotions, a category that encompasses singularities from the bifurcation theory, including those in the Arnold's Classification. It has been discovered that two linear-like submotions share equivalent topological properties if and only if their corresponding vector fields are locally equivalent. Moreover, we developed a clear, algorithmic method to determine the topological equivalence of foliations. Furthermore, we demonstrated that non-trivial cases of submotions in $\mathbb{R}^2$ and maps from the Arnold's Classification cannot be topologically equivalent. This theoretical framework has significant practical implications, as it allows researchers to establish a collection of distinct topological properties for specific types of dynamical systems, as seen with the case of 1-forms on 2-torus and their associated vector fields. It is also noteworthy that a similar distinction between submotions cannot be made based solely on the properties of their level sets. Finally, through our findings, we established that the set of all local bifurcations that occur in smooth 2-dimensional dynamical systems, without explicit constraints, possess distinct topological properties and are therefore impossible to categorize using any single parameterizing method. The presented theories and results have significant implications for the study of topological properties in 2-dimensional dynamical systems and provide a foundation for future work in this field. The CountSketch algorithm offers an efficient solution to fast, low-memory counting of general functions. Its resilience to withstand carefully crafted inputs that exploit its weaknesses has long been a crucial consideration. Research conducted more than a decade ago established the limitations of how well it can learn certain types of self-modulating functions. Subsequent studies have improved our understanding of these restrictions in certain scenarios, but only when dealing with non-adaptive input environments. This study breaks new ground by providing the first performance guarantees for function counting on the "learned" class of functions under an adaptive setting. We developed a new technique that enhances our theoretical knowledge of this domain, while also revealing a surprising connection between the resistance factor and memory usage. Furthermore, our research introduces the concept of 'high-mixing functions,' and demonstrates that CountSketch's performance on these types of functions significantly surpasses that of the 'uniformly mixed' variant. Finally, our mathematical analysis also highlights a critical memory-based threshold that determines the feasibility of achieving a certain level of performance in the adaptive setting. We show that CrossEntropy, another prominent function counting method, falls short of this threshold, and thus cannot guarantee the same level of performance in the adaptive scenario. This last finding underscores the critical importance of developing methods that can effectively resist carefully crafted, adaptive inputs. By establishing tight performance bounds for the adaptive setting, our research significantly advances our theoretical knowledge of this domain. Our research also showcases a novel practical implication, as we demonstrate that the resistance factor can effectively be used as a basis for selecting functions with superior properties. This study's groundbreaking discovery of the feasible performance range in the adaptive setting opens up new avenues for investigating CountSketch's performance, while our extensive experiments reveal crucial, previously unexplained patterns underlying its behavior. Our research sheds new light on these findings, while our analysis provides an insightful explanation for why the resistance factor serves as a effective performance predictor. We predict that our study's performance analysis will hold up well against future research, and our investigation into these unknowns may uncover new insights to advance the field. Last but not least, we reveal an unexpected connection between our research's ideas and a classic concept from number theory, while our analysis provides a thoughtful discussion on how this connection might lead to future breakthroughs. High-frequency trading could greatly benefit from quantum computing, as it leverages parallel processing and the quantum principle of superposition. A modified version of the game theory's Prisoner's Dilemma, suitable for a quantum environment, was introduced by Pitowicz using quas-classical operators in 2006. This paper builds upon that concept, using Grover's matrix to create a basis state, and employs the resulting operator philosophy to develop a new game theory model with a quas-classical approach, along with a corresponding quantum algorithm. Additionally, a simulation of this game theory model on a quantum network is demonstrated, showing that a non-tractable classical problem becomes tractable on a quantum network. This research also examines how a quantum-based Prisoner's Dilemma game can reduce risk and increase return rates in the context of high-frequency trading. Furthermore, as a testament to the algorithm's performance, a simulation was conducted with 100,000 games, providing concrete results. These outcomes suggest that a quantum-based approach to the game could yield better financial returns than a traditional classical based strategy. Finally, a discussion on potential applications and challenges associated with this algorithm is presented. These concepts, although still in their early stages, may contribute to the development of a more robust quantum-based financial system in the future. Let $\mathcal{D}$ represent the domain of a function $f:, \mathcal{D} \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ where $m \geq 2$, with $f(u)$ taking values in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ for every $u \in \mathcal{D}$. Assume that for each individual component $i$ from 1 to $m-1$, the function $f_i$ is continuously differentiable within the domain $\mathcal{D}$. Under these assumptions, it can be proven that the function $f: \mathcal{D} \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is also continuously differentiable, with its partial derivatives specifically defined as $\frac{\partial f_i}{\partial u_j} = \frac{\partial f_{i+1}}{\partial u_j}$ for all $i, j = 1, 2, \ldots, m-1$. This result specifically means that the partial derivatives of a function can be consistently extended to its higher-order counterparts, which has significant implications in various applications across both pure and applied mathematics. As a result, it is evident that a function's differentiability within a particular domain can be leveraged to infer the differentiability of a more complex, extended function that incorporates additional variable components. Furthermore, it is significant to note that even if a function is defined through its computational iterations, its differentiable properties can be inherited by its more complex, higher-order partial derivatives. Interestingly, this result bears resemblance to a fundamental theorem that was initially discovered by Augustin Cauchy and later widely popularized by the mathematician Lipkin, which deals with the theorem of mean value. As an application of this new approach, it is now possible to enhance and generalize the classical Legender's mean value formula. Furthermore, it will also be possible to generalize the requirements for the theorem of mean value by replacing the traditional non-degenerate convex sets with alternative set definitions that lack the property of being non-degenerate but still satisfy the conditions of the coordinatewise convexity. Human vocal behaviors in social interactions are regulated by complex psychological, social, and environmental factors. Entrainment, a phenomenon where people synchronize their voice patterns, is particularly important in understanding these interactions, yet detecting it in everyday contexts is challenging due to the lack of suitable measurement tools and difficulties in distinguishing it from other potential regulating factors, such as the presence of other sounds. To address these limitations, we developed a new computational method for measuring entrainment in conversations that is informed by high-quality dialogue datasets and utilizes a multi-faceted approach to define and quantify entrainment in diverse settings. We tested our method in two studies, one of which analyzed monologues and dialogues from a large dataset and found that entrainment is strongly linked to interpersonal connections and observed in various contexts, including alone and in crowded environments. A second study conducted in a driving simulator showed that individuals engage in dialogical entrainment even in situations not previously observed in the dataset, while also finding distinctions in entrainment behavior. Overall, our research demonstrates that with the correct tools, entrainment is a ubiquitous feature of human social interactions. These findings have implications for a wide range of psychological and social theories, and our method provides an accessible way for researchers to measure entrainment in a growing range of domains. Our method is available for download at https://github.com/AArtificialIntelligence/dialogical-entrainment. estimating depth from a single image can simulate the type of multi-view
information found in common depth datasets. We investigate whether training
neural networks on depth estimation rather than categorization offers an improvement
for subsequent tasks and whether depth estimation provides an advantage over
other established pre-training methods. The study reveals that employing depth
estimation pre-training yields superior results for downstream tasks than
traditional categorization pre-training, and that using depth estimation with
random labels offers a notable improvement over supervised pre-training in
semantic segmentation. The code for this research is publicly accessible at https://github.com/apiccioni/noisy_depth_pretraining. The finding suggests that depth estimation can be an effective pre-training approach
for downstream tasks beyond depth prediction. Moreover, while depth estimation
pre-training considers the geometric aspect of images, which may not fully
capture the image's semantic content, it appears to be beneficial for tasks
involving semantic segmentation. The study also sheds light on the notion that
training a network with partially corrupted depth maps can be advantageous for
taking full advantage of the learned geometric information. Ultimately, the
research indicates that cross-domain pre-training can be a valuable tool for

We offer an innovative solution to test Kendall's tau rank correlation coefficient's significance without explicitly estimating the rank correlation. This solution develops a asymptotically correct statistical test by considering a linear relationship between two random variables' ranks, resulting in a straightforward and efficient test that surpasses conventional methods like the student's t-test. Additionally, our method results in a more reliable p-value. Notably, when the data is normally distributed, this test becomes a conservative yet powerful alternative that achieves an optimal result, often outperforming the t-test. On the other hand, when the data does not follow the normal distribution, this test becomes more powerful and reliable, showcasing its robustness in a simulation study. A real-world case example from the field of psychology further illustrates the effectiveness and practical application of our method. A related R software package called 'kendall-test' facilitates the use of this test in a typical statistical analysis. Lastly, our method's theoretical validity is established through a series of rigorous mathematical proofs and modeling. A related Python package 'kendall-test' is included in the GitHub repository 'kendall-test', where the code is made openly available for readers to reproduce the results and embark on similar research. The rapid advancement of automotive information and communication systems has driven the development of intelligent driving and active safety features, leveraging collected sensor data about traffic and driving conditions. With a central control system, automotive companies can ensure seamless integration, but this raises concerns about data security and privacy. To address these issues, we're developing a decentralized system for collecting and processing data within an automotive network, minimizing the need for data transmission to a central location. This enables various intelligent applications to run autonomously on edge nodes, while maintaining the privacy of individual vehicles. Our framework uses advanced techniques like federated learning, multi-party computation and secure encryption to protect confidentiality and integrity of data, and prevent privacy breaches that could compromise a vehicle's location or driving history. Instead, each edge node processes only general traffic data like speed or position information, maintaining a balance between ensuring safety and privacy's top priority. This robust architecture maintains compatibility with existing systems and can coexist with current network structures without difficulty. Furthermore, we explain the concepts behind ML model development, processing, and distribution at the edge, outlining the benefits and trade-offs of this decentralized approach in comparison to traditional centralized methods. This comprehensive framework addresses various challenges at the edge, focusing on how to leverage aggregated data effectively and mitigate issues like overfitting, data imbalance, and ML model non-convergence. In addition, we highlight the importance of establishing and maintaining trust among interconnected vehicles through a reputation system that deals with issues like cheating, data sharing, and model collaboration. Our simulation results provide insight into the performance and challenges of collaborative learning among a dozen vehicles under different circumstances. In one instance, we observed that collaborative training can improve accuracy by nearly 100% when a majority of vehicles participate, while notable improvements in accuracy and convergence rate were observed across a wide range of vehicles. This large participation threshold ensures minimal overhead and resource usage. Moreover, we found that the decay factor has a considerable impact on the convergence speed: a fast decay rate leads to faster convergence but may result in lower average model quality, whereas slower decay allows vehicles to contribute more to collaborative learning. This trade-off can be mitigated by adjusting the time-to-live for aggregated data. This research lays the groundwork for future studies in the realm of edge intelligence, focusing on scalability, security, privacy, and reliability aspects of decentralized machine learning. Ultimately, it serves as a starting point and inspiration for future work in intelligent systems and communication, empowering vehicles with self-governing intelligence that maintains privacy and resilience. This work reveals that the Euler characteristic serves as an intrinsic, topological invariant capable of offering valuable information on a specific manifold. We take advantage of its robustness to permit variations in the manifold's topology, making it useful for identifying the underlying topology from a complete metric. The paper begins with an examination of its practicality in determining the topology of small-dimensional manifolds, before exploring its applications in higher dimensional cases, where the topology cannot be determined solely by the Euler characteristic. The efficacy of this approach is demonstrated through analysis of specific, high-dimensional soliton-type metrics. The conclusion features a discussion on potential limitations of this approach, along with suggestions for further modifications to extend its reach into regions with more negative curvature and narrow necks. Finally, we identify an open question concerning the use of Euler characteristic in determining the topology of Reissner-Weyl solutions with finite energy. An accompanying notebook delves into the mathematical applications of the Euler characteristic in PyTorch, using Geometric Deep Learning as a reference. Evolutionary algorithms have seen significant advancements in recent years through parallel computing, resulting in Parallel Evolutionary Algorithms with remarkable performance. However, this parallelization comes with a drawback: some generations may remain unresolved for an extended period. To address this inequality, parent selection strategies have been developed to boost convergence by eliminating the 'evaluation time bias.' This paper presents an innovative solution to this issue by introducing a frequency-based parent selection approach, which assigns a more representative parental role to individuals who have been evaluated less frequently. The mechanism involves tracking the evaluation frequency of individuals and using a sorted parent pool to improve solution convergence. The solution is versatile and adaptable, making it suitable for Asynchronous Parallel Evolutionary Algorithms. Our experiments conducted across multiple high-dimensional functions and scenarios demonstrate that this parent selection strategy consistently delivers high-quality solutions and enhances convergence by maintaining a balanced parent pool. Notably, our proposed solution matches or surpasses the performance of current best-asynchronous-PMA algorithms in several functions while outperforming them in others. This paper presents an innovative approach to blind image restoration, a family of problems that encompass related tasks such as blind deblurring, super-resolution, and blind de-noising, the common goal being to amplify the clarity of a damaged image by restoring its intensity and sparsity within a given frame size. We delve into these problems by extracting relevant information from the Fourier transform of the image without any additional references, the approach involving extracting sparsity in the form of localized data within a specified radius. We utilize the kernel mixture model to represent this localized data, demonstrating that the dimensions of a kernel representation are sufficient for extracting key features of localized data. This insight enables us to develop a universal solution framework for blind image restoration, the effectiveness of which is demonstrated through successful applications in blind deblurring and super-resolution. Experimental findings confirm that the method performs favorably when compared to leading non-blind solutions in terms of restoration quality. Additionally, the findings highlight the versatility of the kernel mixture model in representing localized data at various scales. Furthermore, the approach is successfully evaluated on a state-of-the-art task, the creation of a high-resolution image from a sub-resolution image, where the method exhibits superiority over existing techniques. The implementation details and source code for the methods are available online for further investigation. The research demonstrates that the Fourier transform domain is well-suited for extracting sparsity in the form of quasi-local data, a finding that is consistent with existing knowledge. The method is founded on the concept of approximating the spectrum of an image using a kernel mixture and is subsequently applied to various image restoration tasks. The research showcases the effectiveness of the kernel mixture model as a robust tool for understanding image properties and extracting meaningful structure, particularly in blind image restoration. The application of the model is a finding that is unique in the research on this topic. The ideas presented in the paper are the foundation for a broader range of applications of the kernel mixture model and signal processing tasks involving image restoration. The research sheds light on the significance of leveraging structured data, such as pseudo-circle data derived from the kernel representation, for enhancing the clarity of a damaged image. The findings illustrate the effectiveness of approximate localization in achieving superior restoration quality when compared to exact localization. The research highlights the potential of leveraging the Fourier transform as a useful tool for deriving additional information from images. The research is founded on the concept of utilizing the kernel representation as a compact way of capturing localized data. We introduce a new associative Yang-Baxter equation type, referred to as the nonuniform associative Yang-Baxter equation (nuybe), that is in line with the associative Yang-Baxter equation (ybe) but doesn't follow the algebraic closure principle. It's proven that any solution to the nuybe can be viewed as a weighted sum (or more specifically, a finite combination of complex weights) of solutions to the ybe. Furthermore, we explore various categorical aspects related to the nuybe, including the instances of uniqueness for up to isomorphism nuybe solutions, the extension of these solutions to the nuybe through convolution, and the Upmeier-Lenard-Snider theorem. Examples of nuybe solutions are given based on the twisted nilpotent Yang-Baxter equation and the algebraic torus. It's also shown that the inverse of an nuybe solution, defined as its 'conjugate', exists under specific algebraic and associative conditions and that the nuybe solution's conjugate can be obtained directly from its twisted form. Lastly, we give conditions under which the nuybe solution's conjugate corresponds to an ybe solution. Additionally, we provide the rigorous proof of a property related to the nuybe solution's convolution, which was previously given heuristically in another study. Distributed consensus is crucial for a broad range of distributed systems, such as distributed databases and blockchains, to function effectively. The implementation of consensus algorithms in practice is hindered by a variety of failures and more challenging when considering the occurrence of such failures. Traditional consensus algorithms often lack a comprehensive failure model, making them less applicable in practical scenarios. A consistent consensus model called Canopus has been developed to address failures such as network faults and node misbehavior, allowing it to achieve high performance through elective consensus establishment. The Canopus model effectively handles various types of failures; however, it lacks support for network failures that can lead to permanent consensus impossibilities. To address this gap, we introduce RCanopus, an extension of the Canopus model that accounts for network failures to ensure correctness in such failure scenarios. The integration of network failures in RCanopus is achieved through the concept of irrecoverable failures, enabling it to ensure that no participant can establish an incorrect majority, thus ensuring consistency. The implementation of RCanopus is demonstrated using the eDLC consensus algorithm, which attains a 37% performance improvement over the original Canopus model. The results demonstrate that RCanopus, when compared to other consensus algorithms, offers a 37% performance improvement, which is up to a 5x factor compared to failure-prone baselines. Specifically, for failure-free environments, RCanopus outperforms Canopus by 9%, which is also up to a 2x factor compared to failure-tolerant baselines. Moreover, RCanopus, when compared to the failure-tolerant RLiar consensus algorithm, shows a 37% performance improvement in failure-free environments. Finally, RCanopus, when compared to the failure-prone DLedgerBOP consensus algorithm, shows a 5x factor performance improvement in failure-free environments. The results of this study demonstrate that RCanopus's unique mechanism to ensure consistency offers a 37% performance improvement, which is up to a 5x factor compared to failure-prone baselines. Prior experiments examined soybean phospholipid bilayers under a solution containing polycarbonate, however, found inconsistent results. To verify the source of the inconsistency between studies, our experiment compared the mechanical behavior of soybean phospholipid bilayers and a mixture of soybean phospholipid and cholesterol, both under a solution containing water and a non-polar solvent. Despite our expectations, both systems failed to display a typical Young's modulus found in a previous study using a different substrate, however, we did observe a non-linear relationship between the measured deformation and the applied force. While our experiment uncovers the origin of the inconsistent previous results, our experiment was not able to determine the effective Young's modulus of the bilayer because of the non-linear relationship. Most current object detectors lack a method to accurately gauge their uncertainties, a crucial consideration for numerous applications. This research introduces an end-to-end approach called BayesOD, comprising classifier and regression probabilistic modules, which can be easily incorporated into any existing object detector. This leads to improved uncertainty estimation. Two key factors contribute to the efficacy of BayesOD: a standardized prediction distribution to minimize the variance of predictions and a modified training method to enhance the alignment of predictive distributions with the data's posterior uncertainty. Experiments using Standard Train and Valid and Adversarial Train and Valid protocols on the COCO dataset demonstrate that BayesOD yields uncertainties that closely match the actual distribution of labels while demonstrating robust resistance to noise. Additionally, it outperforms current best practices in reduced variance on the entire range of COCO challenges. Lastly, demonstrations of plausible applications of the methodology include active learning and adversarial training, and they show a significant increase in performance compared to the baseline. Code for the methodology can be found at https://github.com/asharakeh/bayesod. A related video illustrating the methodology can be found at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GLH2Gj_I6Uo. A graphical presentation of the methodology can be found at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=P2G_2joDQ9E. A more detailed explanation of the methodology can be found at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UQ8PZ9_2wBM. The methodology is applied to 19 challenges of the ILS dataset in an Adversarial Train and Valid setting, showing a marked increase in performance over the baseline. This research demonstrates that the reliability of the methodology in the face of noise is, in part, due to the stability of the training process. A model trained using Standard Train and Valid protocols exhibits a measure of uncertainty that closely matches the distribution of labels but demonstrates a lower degree of robustness to noise as evidenced by an evaluation using the Adversarial Train and Valid protocol. Conversely, a model trained using the Adversarial Train and Valid protocol exhibits a measure of uncertainty that closely matches the distribution of labels at lower thresholds and exhibits a significant decrease in accuracy in the face of noise as evidenced by an evaluation using the Standard Train and Valid protocol. This dichotomy highlights the importance of considering the particulars of the application in the selection of the methodology. This difference in behavior is likely due to a discrepancy between the data's posterior uncertainty and the predictive distribution, each estimated by a evaluation of the Standard Train

We re-examine the phenomenon of transversal modes in wave-plate experiments and apply this understanding to interpret the results of the double-slit experiment and the six-box experiment within the framework of quantum mechanics, thereby demonstrating how the pigeonhole effect can simplify explanations of apparent non-locality. By recognizing transversal modes as a manifestation of the pigeonhole effect, which becomes evident when multiple wave amplitudes converge, we can avoid confusing this phenomenon with genuine non-locality and instead see how it can simplify the explanation of quantum phenomena that have often been mistakenly attributed to non-locality. For instance, in the case of the double-slit experiment, treating the particles as having a narrow distribution in momentum components along a specific transverse direction enables the application of the pigeonhole effect to conserve probability and describe the emergence of an interference pattern without requiring phase relations between experiments. Similarly, for the six-box experiment, treating it as a variant of the double-slit experiment allows for an explanation via the pigeonhole effect, effectively eliminating the need for Erwin Schrödinger's eigenstate collapse notion. Furthermore, we highlight instances where measurements related to transversal modes exhibit randomness due to the pigeonhole effect, which potentially utilizes the Zeno effect to explain such phenomena. Our reinterpretation of these experiments also reveals implications regarding macroscopic observability, experimental design, and the commonly misconstrued notion of quantum mechanical collapse in multiple parallel measurements. Moreover, we consider various other wave-plate experiments and discuss a range of modifications to these experiments that could serve to further elucidate the underlying principles governing these phenomena. Ultimately, we conclude that many quantum paradoxes can be reconciled through the incorporation of the pigeonhole effect into our understanding of quantum mechanics. Cosmic Ray Backgrounds produced by interactions of Galactic Cosmic Rays with Earth's atmosphere are a significant disturbance for gravitational wave instruments due to their widespread and variable output. Another significant source of noise, significant at low orbital altitudes, is the Cosmic Ray Background generated within Earth's magnetic field by interactions between Galactic Cosmic Rays and the magnetosphere. This note outlines a simulation study examining the characteristics of particles produced by collisions between Galactic Cosmic Rays and the Sun's solar wind as they are trapped in Earth's magnetic field at lower orbital altitudes. This simulation was conducted using the FLUKA particle transport code and reports on the distribution of deposited charge, energy, and direction of particles produced in collisions at the surface of Earth's magnetic field. Furthermore, it details the distribution of genetically linked particle generations confined within the Earth's magnetic field. Lastly, it discusses an assessment of the resulting noise produced by these particles on GW detectors such as LIGO and VIRDI, highlighting their potential for deeper analysis of transients and broad-band signals. Nevertheless, it presents challenges for analyzing GW signals themselves due to the uncontrolled variability of the Galactic Cosmic Ray input flux. Analysis focused on low-frequency spectra and found the emergence of a noise plateau for particle mean-life above ~10 s due to a substantial accumulation of genetically linked particles. Furthermore, it was determined that the total deposited charge increased almost directly in proportion to the incident Galactic Cosmic Ray flux. Consequently, if the Galactic Cosmic Ray input flux were to increase following a burst, the number of trapped particles would initially rise before reaching a peak and then return to pre-burst levels as the flux returns to normal. Analysis suggested this peak could occur roughly 40 minutes after the burst, a time-frame tied to the time needed for particles to be diffusely transported away from the impact site and for Earth to rotate out of the P-III wind sector. One of the crucial factors for identifying the source of these signals could be a correlation with the phase of the Galactic Cosmic Ray 26 meV neutron abundance variation. Nevertheless, such an identification would be complicated for the GW community due to the need for data spanning multiple solar cycles. Furthermore, such a characterization could be complicated for any event featuring a sudden increase in the Galactic Cosmic Ray input flux, with respect to identifying its source. Consequently, such an identification would require a prior understanding of the underlying cause for the increase, which could be more easily achieved during events tied to shock fronts propagating cosmic rays towards Earth. Finally, it was noted that the phenomenon itself could serve as an tool for monitoring

Network traffic forecasting is a crucial issue. The underlying graph describing traffic patterns is intricate and dynamic, which is often overlooked in many machine learning models. These models fail to capture a graph's local topology and adaptive changes over time. In response, this paper introduces a novel framework incorporating a sequence of interpolation layers to address the forecasting of a target road on a graph by leveraging historical data from surrounding roads. This framework consists of two main layers. Firstly, it devises a universal skeleton detection model using a deep learning approach, capable of identifying the relevant roads' spatial distribution during forecasting. Secondly, it designs a localized link revaluation model to effectively determine the relative importance of these roads over time. Experimental results reveal significant improvements in forecasting accuracy for this road forecasting framework, with only slight resource consumption. Its efficacy is proven through thorough experiments on real-world datasets. The framework achieves outstanding performance with 16.5% increased MSE and 91.7% increased correlation coefficient compared to other models. In addition, its computational expense is remarkably low with only 1.35% increased time consumption. The method outperforms other models in dealing with link dropout, with robustness reaching 75.2% and only mild fluctuation at 18.9%. Consequently, this framework exhibits tremendous potential in handling a diverse array of road forecasting scenarios. Its superiority over other models is further highlighted by its achievement of 0.987 correlation coefficient when provided with complete data, with minimal deterioration in this metric when dealing with partial data. Therefore, this approach exhibits massive practical applications and investigative value in dealing with diverse graph-based issues. Analysis of this framework further sheds light on the importance of a graph's local topology in traffic context. The design of this model reveals that graph adaptation has a significant impact on traffic pattern evolution. After adjusting some of the model's key parameters, such as the average density of small grains, we found that our model accurately reproduces a wide range of astronomical observations and can effectively predict the characteristics of dust in different environments within the interstellar medium. The model suggests that small grains play a more important role in determining the optical properties of dust in sparse environments, whereas larger grains dominate in denser conditions. A variant of the Lights Out game is examined, involving a graph with distinct nodes representing states and edges resulting from pressing buttons. Unlike the original, this version incorporates nodes with multiple buttons that can be operated simultaneously. Research into the minimum number of operations required to return the graph to its initial state is called the Lights Out problem. A key concept in this context involves tap sets, which are configurations reached by sequential operations and cannot be reversed. A tap set is considered maximal if adding any node to it results in a new set that can be reversed. We investigate the maximum size of these sets, referred to as the $t$ value, in all graphs. A key finding relates to regular graphs: for these, a general lower limit for $t$ has been established, standing at $\frac{d}{2}$, and specific instances can easily reach this threshold. Moreover, general lower and upper bounds for $t$ across all graphs have been achieved, and certain instances reach this threshold. However, the problem remains largely unsolved due to unclear $t$ values in most graphs; thus, a key question has been proposed - what regular graph type has the largest $t$ value?; this question seeks an example where $t$ is less than $d$, a value that would clarify many of the Lights Out problem's uncertainties. In addition to regular graphs' investigation, the problem has been analyzed in terms of its Cayley graphs. This research uses set-valued numerical domains in the context of Abstract Interpretation to examine the limits of existing state-of-the-art tools. To address this, the proposal suggests a novel technique aimed at enhancing the precision of numerical domains during the upward phase of analysis by leveraging more information from the downward phase. This is achieved through a two-step approach. Firstly, the precision during the upward phase is increased by utilizing a "best guess" obtained from the downward phase. Secondly, the accuracy of the "best guess" is verified through a correlation analysis. This method enables the use of more sophisticated numerical methods from the class of set-valued numerical domains, resulting in higher precision. Initial experiments conducted on real-world programs have shown that Decoupling leads to significant increases in precision of numerical domains. Excessive outliers in training data are a common issue that can lead to suboptimal model performance. A reliable approach to mitigating this problem involves utilizing techniques such as outlier detection and data balancing. Such methods are widely applied in various machine learning settings, including the training of nearest neighbor models. Among these nearest neighbor methods, proximity graphs are particularly effective due to their ability to utilize multidimensional distance information. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to utilizing proximity graphs in outlier detection. Specifically, we begin by demonstrating the superlinear complexity of this task in universal spaces where p is greater than or equal to 1. We then introduce a novel dataset representation in the form of a vertex-weighted long-range-delta graph, which allows for the exact solution of the outlier detection problem with a reduced O(n (1/s^2)/alpha) complexity when n represents the dataset size, s is the desired sensitivity, and alpha is a constant scalability factor. We expand upon this concept with an algorithmic improvement that approximates the optimal outcome with a predetermined level of tolerance while achieving a time complexity of O(n (1/s^2)/alpha^5). Notably, we enhanced the efficiency of the outlier detection process with a technique called cluster-based sparse, which can significantly speed up the problem resolution for datasets with pronounced clusters. Furthermore, we propose a method for accelerating the search process in the graph using approximations, resulting in a time complexity of O(s^2 log^3 s m +m^2), where m is the number of vertices in the graph. We tested and validated the effectiveness of our proposed method on diverse datasets with varying levels of complexity, observing notable improvements in performance compared to existing methods. We are made the code available on GitHub at https://github.com/krishnanr/proximity-plot-outlier-detection. The code can be executed via a jupyter notebook. The simulation of a rapidly moving atom, facing a stationary wall in Stochastic Quantum Mechanics, yields two distinct scenarios.  By calculating the electromagnetic radiation emitted, it's found that when the atom's velocity is slow, velocity-dependent Stirling Electromagnetic Radiation is produced, similar to the Casimir-Polder force.  Conversely, at higher velocities, a continuous stochastic spectrum is observed, indicating unresolvable elastic collisions between the atom and the wall.  These findings demonstrate an intriguing connection between spontaneous radiation and the mechanisms of stochastic quantum collisions.  Moreover, these results also reveal an analogous relationship between Stirling Electromagnetic Radiation and the mechanisms driving superconducting junctions, which may have practical implications for devices using quantum coherence.  Our simulation suggests that a device consisting of a rapidly moving atom at the quantum spinantipode, facing a conductive surface, may offer a useful prototype for experimenting with quantum coherence in superconducting junctions, without requiring intricate quantum circuit designs.  Finally, these physical phenomena could inspire innovative concepts in quantum optics and electromagnetic radiation-based experiments.  Our work offers a new perspective on electromagnetic radiation as a potential approach for investigating the quantum aspects of collision physics between atoms and solid-state surfaces.  In addition, we present a novel idea for discovering and characterizing phenomena related to quantum coherence within superconducting junctions using an atom-optics approach, which can be considered an interesting form of quantum interference.  Ultimately, these research findings may pave the way for further developments in quantum mechanics and electromagnetism as well as physics-based computer science concepts, notably in the realm of quantum optics and electromagnetic radiation physics.  Our simulation contributes to a more tangible and comprehensive understanding of quantum mechanics and electromagnetism by incorporating stochastic boundary conditions into atomic motion simulations.  Depending on the velocity of the atom, our calculation results in either low-intensity, zero-average electromagnetic radiation resembling Stirling Electromagnetic Radiation near a mirror, characterized by a 1/r potential, or high-intensity, broad-band electromagnetic radiation indicating a violent collision between the atom and the wall, which cannot be resolved.  These findings offer an original link between spontaneous radiation and stochastic quantum collisions within superconducting junctions, and the associated simulation may facilitate experimentation with quantum coherence in superconducting junctions using an atom-optics approach.  To the best of our knowledge, our calculation contributes an innovative connection between stochastic quantum collisions and electromagnetic radiation, which could inspire a new perspective on electromagnetic radiation as a potential approach for investigating the quantum aspects of collision physics between atoms

The representation learning approach with community awareness has become increasingly prominent in graph embedding, yet its state corresponds to early advancements that depend on predefined community structures. In response, this paper proposes a novel fairness-focused representation learning strategy, named $\textit{LocalCFA}$, with the aim of addressing the constraints associated with predefined community structures. $\textit{LocalCFA}$ represents a hierarchical fair sharing framework composed of a central node, its neighbors, and their immediate surroundings. It proposes a comprehensive theoretical framework to capture Local Community Fairness and leverages this concept to design an effective objective function. Further, $\textit{LocalCFA}$ is implemented using a combination of autoregressive functions and graph neural networks, achieving improved effectiveness according to experiments conducted on both synthetic and real-world data. Beyond its superior performance, $\textit{LocalCFA}$ offers notable advantages in fairness, complexity, and controllability. Ultimately, $\textit{LocalCFA}$ presents a groundbreaking strategy for fair representation learning that goes beyond the conventional group-level approach by promoting local community fairness. It also promotes innovative research avenues in fairness-focused representation learning. The code for $\textit{LocalCFA}$ is available at https://github.com/MITIE-LID/LocalCFA. As a form of contribution to the graph learning community, this paper conducts a systematic evaluation of the effect of community size on the performance of $\textit{LocalCFA}$, revealing a size-sensitive attribute discrimination characteristic. Therefore, this research offers valuable insights into the design of fairness-focused representation learning methods, inspiring the graph learning community to consider the impact of community size on the effectiveness of representation learning models. Lastly, to facilitate the interaction between the community structure and the learning process, this paper proposes a novel strategy, allowing $\textit{LocalCFA}$ to adaptively select community sizes and adapt to their inherent properties, thereby enhancing its effectiveness. The learned representations are available at https://github.com/MITIE-LID/LocalCFA/commits/main. This research focuses on kinetic models for reversible enzyme reactions and their dynamic systems models, with the goal of developing efficient computational tools for approximate solution calculation. We derive and justify non-local hybrid and time-stepping schemes that can be integrated with existing numerical methods, such as the Dirichlet problem's finite element approach. We establish the validity of these schemes through theoretical proof and demonstrate their efficiency through numerical demonstration. Furthermore, we explore the possibility of adapting established simulation software for our newly developed schemes. Two key aspects, of reasonable size, are computationally tested to evaluate the effectiveness of our solutions in practical applications. The first test examines the speed of reaction in a small sphere and the second examines the effect of ultra weak formulation implementation in a more complex model. We successfully implemented the described schemes in Python and Mathematica and achieved the desired results, with validation through comparisons with established software such as COMSOL and FreeFem++. The outcomes reveal that the employed time-stepping method enhances computational performance and surpasses conventional solution methods like implicit Euler or Crank-Nicolson in various key metrics. Additionally, the employed non-local scheme offers an improved error rate of O(h^2 + \Delta t). Ultimately, the obtained results in comparison with exact solutions show an average error rate of around 4.7%, while showing considerable potential for optimization through more precise modeling. Nonetheless, in comparison with implicit Euler method, our approach has demonstrated a reduction in the error rate of at least 50% with an additional 9% compared to Crank-Nicolson. Interestingly, the time-stepping method enabled a 2-fold acceleration in computational speed while allowing a 4 times larger time step compared to the implicit Euler method. Interestingly, the observed results suggest that the most time-consuming aspect of our algorithm, the non-local finite element method, for solving kinetic models for reversible enzyme reactions, is the solution calculation rather than the problem definition or the global procedure. Therefore, to enhance computational performance, fine-tuning these aspects is necessary. In terms of optimization, one promising strategy is to apply the solution-adapted scheme, which has the potential to offer a more error-resistant solution. In summary, the described schemes for kinetic models of reversible enzyme reactions have proven effective and show considerable potential for further improvement, especially with regards to expanding their applications to modeling types that co-associate linear and non-linear transport mechanisms. Ultimately, the success of these schemes in efficiently computing solutions to these complex models may facilitate the establishment of a quantitative relationship between enzyme structure and function. The models are classified as mild or severe bubbles based on the duration of their optimistic phase. The price distribution in both types of bubbles follows a log-normal pattern. A mixture of two normal distributions better differentiates mild and severe bubbles, with the mixture components corresponding to the optimal parameters for each type. These findings provide valuable tools for assessing financial instability. The research has practical implications, as its findings are intended to assist officials in determining when intervention is necessary to prevent a catastrophic collapse. By aligning the oscillator's equilibrium position with the laser, the path integral formulation is simplified. Utilizing the Markov-chain Monte Carlo method, specifically the Metropolis algorithm, the quantum state of the oscillator can be represented. This approach allows a semi-classical interpretation of the oscillator's behavior. The influence of laser intensity and frequency, oscillator mass and spring constant, and path-length discretization on oscillator populations and autocorrelation times are also examined. Moreover, the effects of laser intensity on oscillator occupation numbers are compared to established numerical and asymptotic results. The methodology presented here can be easily extended to multichromophoric systems, making it suitable for use in complex systems where a cumulant expansion would be impractical. As such, this method offers a promising means of modeling nonlinear optical materials, despite the associated computational cost. To mitigate this issue, we suggest employing specific strategies to reduce computational costs, such as employing multiple-time-step integrators and merging Monte Carlo and Verlet algorithm steps. The combination of these algorithms significantly reduces computational costs by an order of magnitude, bringing it into a feasible range for use on individual chromophoric systems. The methodology is therefore presented as a versatile tool for exploring the interactions and behavior of complex systems involved in chromophoric dynamics. Developing CS NLP systems is obstructed by the scarcity of CS data. Researchers attempt to alleviate this issue through data augmentation by utilizing monolingual data, yet substitutions of single words result in minor enhancements and are not very natural. This study explores the effect of exchanging word sequences within sentences by applying sequential substitutions to CS sentences. By accomplishing this, it has been demonstrated that natural-looking data augmentation boosts a CS BERT model's performance on both CS sentence classification and CS word language model tasks. Moreover, it has been proven that utilizing a superset of single-word substitutions leads to decreased performance in CS sentence classification. Interestingly, it has been discovered that including artificially generated sequences in CS data yields improved performance in CS sentence classification. These achievements are credited to the enhanced contextual understanding enabled by the added word sequences. It is anticipated that these models will also prosper on other tasks such as machine translation and named entity recognition. The source code for this study is available at https://github.com/amirveyssieh/LexSub. We also release an Arabic-English CS sentence language model. An evaluation of this model reveals a 23.6% improvement in LL8 on the EN-AR-EN Wiki data set, yet the model exhibits confusion between the two languages, often choosing the less common term. Consequently, it can be inferred that the model is able to grasp some CS knowledge. The effect of the linguistic properties of the two languages, such as morphological complexity and word order, is explored. It is discovered that these characteristics pose challenges for the model's comprehension of the less dominant language. Consequently, suggestions are provided to aid future CS NLP systems in understanding less common language words. Ultimately, it is believed that with additional data and a more thorough word disambiguation process, future CS NLP systems will be capable of tackling challenges alone. The study also reveals a 23.6% improvement in LL8 on the EN-AR-EN Wiki data set. The source code for this study is available at https://github.com/amirveyssieh/BERT-Arabic-English-CS-LM.
