For efficient partitioning of large hexahedral meshes, high-performance computing (HPC) practitioners rely on pre-defined, user-specified partitioning schemes. These typically involve uniform sectoral divisions but can also incorporate customized segmentations like reflecting and rotating half-cubes. Nonetheless, current methods fall short in addressing segmented meshes resulting from cutting operations within Hexahedral meshes, which are commonly employed in HPC domains. To address this limitation, we propose a method for automatically generating partitioning schemes that incorporate tets resulting from hexahedral mesh cutting. We achieve this by introducing a new type of sector consisting of multiple tets, which allows for increased flexibility in partitioning designs. Furthermore, this method enables the incorporation of reflecting and rotating half-cubes, thereby reducing the total number of sectorial elements required. We demonstrate an extensive evaluation of our approach, which showcases its efficacy by comparing the number of sectorial elements needed to partition a given hexahedral mesh with and without incorporating cutting tetrahedra. Specifically, our approach allows for reducing the number of sectorial elements by a factor of 2 to 58, which substantially decreases the time and effort required to generate partitioning schemes in practice. To showcase the applicability of our approach, we utilized a computation involving cutting simulations on a Boeing Cessna aircraft model, which demonstrated a notable reduction in partitioning complexity. We successfully partitioned the resulting large hexahedral mesh with cutting tetrahedras using a relatively coarse 16^3 sectorial partitioning, which yielded results concordant to those obtained using finer 40^3 sectorial partitioning designed without cutting tets. We implemented the proposed approach using the ifcart HPC tool and publicly released a accompanying Python module titled "cart_py". Furthermore, we released a given cutting simulation dataset "cut_sim_data" on GitHub, which serves as a comprehensive test case for evaluating partitioning schemes. We intend to continuously expand the cut_tet_hex.py module to widely available partitioning schemes. A future extension of this work will involve developing algorithms within the cart_hpc framework to generate partitioning schemes from any mesh, regardless of its topology or origin. Moreover, we will leverage advanced geometric analysis techniques to optimize cutting tetrahedras for efficient partitioning. By promoting efficient partitioning schemes through cart_hpc, we aim to empower HPC practitioners to achieve better outcomes in domains such as cutting simulations and physics-based rendering. This study introduces an innovative numerical approach for accurately describing the behavior of power conversion equipment, including solar inverter lag, through analytical inverter lag modeling. Currently, available models relying solely on simulation or measurement-based data are often cumbersome and impractical. In contrast, this methodology leverages measured or simulated data in a convenient manner to derive a closed-form equation representing the characteristics of the power equipment under examination. Utilizing the Matlab Curve Fitting Toolbox, the proposed method enables a straightforward fitting process for most common power equipment profiles, including step response data. As a result, the derived model can be easily employed in a wide range of applications, including predictive maintenance, parameter estimation for power system models, and closed-loop digital controller design, showcasing its potential through the design of an optimal linear controller for solar inverters. In particular, the proposed linear controller is shown to be effective in overcoming the inherent nonlinearities of solar inverter dynamics. Moreover, the study assesses and compares the proposed model with a data-driven approach based on neural networks, highlighting the proposed method's advantages in terms of implementation simplicity, model reduction, and computation efficiency. Notably, the proposed method requires only a small fraction of the data required by the neural network approach while maintaining comparable accuracy. Extensive numerical results validate the proposed method for various profiles with diverse initial conditions and delay values, effectively addressing the continuous issue of delay compensation in control engineering. In addition, the study considers the impact of measurement uncertainty on the accuracy of the fitted models, highlighting the need for delay measurement via established methods to ensure practical model accuracy. Ultimately, the proposed method serves as a versatile tool for characterizing a broader class of power equipment, including those exhibiting significant nonlinearity. It is well understood that such behavior typically arises from the internal conversion or modulation process but does not necessarily stem from that behavior; for instance, the gearless wind turbine employs a nonlinear control strategy yet exhibits linear behavior in its downwind region. In such cases, the proposed method can effectively describe typical power equipment behavior, including the fundamental characteristics of variable-speed solar inverters. In particular, the study demonstrates that the proposed model can accurately capture the dynamics of variable-speed solar inverters when employed as a linear model, which is shown to be effective for most solar inverter response profiles. One of the significant challenges in reinforcement learning is dealing with tasks in complex, high-dimensional or even infinite-dimensional spaces for state and action variables. Current RL theories largely ignore the mathematical properties inherent to these tasks, particularly continuity, which is essential for developing theoretical foundations for reinforcement learning. This research introduces a concept of coarse-grained continuity, tailored to the Euclidean metric, and demonstrates its practical application in developing a broad framework of RL algorithms. We show that our continuity notion aligns with intuitive principles when applied to Markov decision processes. This involves developing dynamic programming algorithms with value and policy iteration, proving their convergence, and exploring connections with existing RL works, while also providing theoretical justification for the selection of learning rates. We evaluate the effectiveness of our algorithms through comprehensive experiments on various tasks, even extending to those with non-Euclidean features. Furthermore, we integrate our Coarse-GCN approach with the state-of-the-art SARSA and TD3 algorithms, achieving significant improvements in performance on continuous control tasks. This research utilizes the Euclidean metric to define the continuity notion, resulting in its potential generalization to other metrics through the use of generalized distances. Consequently, the notion of coarse-grained continuity can be applied to a broad range of RL tasks and settings. Lastly, the code for our algorithms has been made publicly available at the repository https://github.com/andreabassi/coarse-grained-continuity. This work is an adaptation of my original PhD thesis. The original PhD research was conducted at Paris Science and Technologies (UMR 8623) and submitted in 2021. The primary contribution of my thesis is the development of a novel notion of coarse-grained continuity for metric spaces applied to reinforcement learning and markov decision processes. Following the validation of my thesis, several notable breakthroughs have been achieved: The utilization of our Coarse-GCN approach led to the development of the first RL algorithm to achieve near-optimal performance for tasks with a non-Euclidean feature, namely the computation of the optimal mean reward rate under linear functional constraints. Moreover, the efficacy of our Coarse-GCN algorithms was further supported by the accomplishment of the first generalization of the off-policy TD learning algorithm to general Borel spaces and the Euclidean metric. Finally, the following experimental results, not present in the original thesis, show the effectiveness of our algorithms on the game of chess. Animacy is a fundamental concept in understanding behavioral responses towards various animals. Research has demonstrated that the likelihood of an animal species being targeted in a transplants study correlates with its animacy score, which is calculated as the proportion of studies focused on that species (de Waal et al., 2019). The defining characteristic of animacy is difficult to quantify, making it an enigmatic aspect of human perception. Recent findings indicate that the animacy organization in the human brain is evident in the patterns of functional brain activity, specifically in the ventral temporal cortex (Amorim et al., 2014), where distinct pathways and modules process different aspects of visual stimuli, such as objects and individuals. The present study aims to shed light on the underlying neural mechanisms of the animacy organization in this cortical region. To achieve this goal, we developed a novel stimulus set featuring a variety of animal faces and body parts to serve as a basis for identifying the animacy-related responses in animacy-sensitive brain areas. The data collection process consisted of three experiments conducted independently, which revealed distinct animacy-related responses in two specific brain regions. The first experiment categorized the stimuli based on a gradient of animacy, which evoked distinct neural responses in both regions, with more animacy-conferring stimuli eliciting greater activity. The second experiment focused on the semantic representation of animacy, which revealed separate neural modules for distinct aspects of animacy within both regions. The third experiment demonstrated that the animacy-related responses in both brain areas were highly selective, distinct, and organized in a hierarchical manner. Our findings imply that the animacy organization in the human brain is highly specialized and targets specific facial characteristics. Furthermore, we propose that the unique, detailed, and highly distinct animacy-related responses in the VTC subnetwork reflect the highly distinct animacy categories, such as primates, dogs, and cats, which are widely recognized by primatologists, dog owners, and cat lovers. The distinct animacy categories in the VTC subnetwork may offer a possible explanation for the species-specific transplants studies, such as those targeting primates, dogs, and cats. The present research provides fundamental insights into the unique animacy-related responses in the VTC subnetwork, which can shed light on the overall animacy organization in the human brain. The distinct animacy categories in the VTC subnetwork further justify the use of animacy scores, which group species according to their animacy values, to explain the targeted species in the transplants studies. In social collaboration with an intelligent system, having the capacity to adapt one's behavior in response to its actions is crucial for effectively engaging in cooperative and competitive interactions. However, existing reinforcement learning approaches that tackle scenarios with multiple optimal ends often fail to identify these responses due to their limited ability to coordinate with the system's actions, which are typically modeled as stochastic events. By leveraging the potential of probabilistic representation learning, our proposed transfer empowerment representation (TER) offers a fresh perspective on how an agent can interact with the system through empowered representations of the agent's actions. With the integration of a novel intrinsic motivation that measures the empowerment of the agent, our technique allows the agent to adapt to diverse goals by means of a goal-related exploration strategy, facilitated by a goal-exploration potential (GEP) network. By assessing various scenarios, including a controlled laboratory setting and a real-world application of using an intelligent assistant in a job search process, our method demonstrates its superiority in producing a wide array of behaviors that consistently align with the system's expected actions, thus leading to more beneficial outcomes in comparison to traditional training methods. Our research aims to modify a classic computer vision technique called "contrastive learning" to identify materials from single images, utilizing physics-based rendering to create realistic synthetic data for the algorithm. By training the algorithm on a small number of data samples, it can then successfully identify materials in images it hasn't seen before. Our work applies contrastive learning to a dataset of single images of materials, with the images being simulated using laws of physics to account for variations in macroscopic properties. By doing so, the algorithm learns robust features that aren't susceptible to changes in material properties such as shape, as it trains on physics-based simulations rather than real-world images of materials. Our novel approach allows the algorithm to specialize in material identification and can one-shot learn to recognize a wide range of materials, such as metals, plastics, and glasses, based on real-world images of materials. Our evaluation shows that our algorithm successfully identifies materials in real-world images with high accuracy, surpassing alternative techniques such as based on deep learning. Our results confirm the potential for scale-up to identify multiple materials with the same approach. Our software is available for immediate use. As a result, the proposed technique has various potential applications such as in augmented reality and robotics. Our evaluation also explores potential limitations and extensions of the algorithm, such as the identification of characters in movies. Our work is the first to demonstrate a comprehensive material recognition system and open a new research pathway to combine physics-based rendering with contrastive learning. As a result, the algorithm can extend to other domains such as detection and recognize 3D objects from single images by modifying a few parameters, thus reducing the requirements to create a model for each object category. Our algorithm allows the identification of a nearly infinite number of object categories by modifying a few parameters, thus opens a new research pathway to automate the process of data collection and reduces collection time to a few hours. Our evaluation shows that our algorithm successfully predicts unknown material categories with high accuracy, thus demonstrating a significant advancement in research. Our work also leads to a major shift in research from the current state-of-the-art in material recognition and object detection. Our algorithm is currently limited in its application to a limited number of 3D categories, thus we also outline a new research pathway to extend the identification of 3D categories with a limited number of known 3D shape data and reduce the time of data collection to a single video. We introduce a novel method for matching local features without a detector, in a category-level retrieval context, by directly comparing the spatial relationships of points within a query image to those in a dataset of candidates. Our approach, LoFTR, utilizes self- and cross-attention mechanisms to identify corresponding areas and calculates a category-level score based on spatial coherence across all categories and the query image. Unlike traditional deep learning-based retrieval methods, LoFTR does not require pre-trained detectors to extract local features, leveraging the stability of the transformation of local points instead. This allows our method to run significantly faster, be relatively lightweight, and robust to poor illumination and noise. We demonstrate LoFTR's efficacy on the FLIR dataset and achieve state-of-the-art performance. Furthermore, we showcase the efficacy of LoFTR under uniform illumination conditions and highlight its ability to effectively localize objects of minimal length, such as handgun grips. Code and pre-trained models are available at https://github.com Research com/LoFTR. Our method won the Utility Track first prize in NeurIPS 2021. We've conducted an extensive examination of eight distinct methods for quantifying the morphological intricacy of languages. These measures have different bases for evaluation, such as word formation types, word structures, and lexical densities. We've obtained data on eight languages from the Wittenberg Language Resource Database. We've applied correlation-based techniques to the phenotypic scale, and our results show that most measures are highly correlated with each other, suggesting they're evaluating similar aspects of morphological complexity. We've discovered significant linear connections between these measures and aspects of corpora-based measures of morphological complexity. Notably, our results also reveal that some language typology-based metrics, including Saffart's morphological complexity index, don't correlate with the other measures, indicating they may be capturing a distinct aspect of morphological complexity. We've also found discrepancies between our results and previous empirical connections established in the literature. Our analysis highlights the importance of validity in establishing correlations between complexity measures. We've also defined and established a new metric for lexical density based on collocations. The paper concludes with recommendations for future research and practical applications of our findings, such as informing language teaching and learning. Although ar-K-FIA achieves comparable results with the current state-of-the-art Freed-Beta ICA method, its convergence speed remains a limitation. In order to address this limitation, our paper presents an efficient variant of ar-K-FIA called M-ar-K-FIA, which reduces the time complexity from O(K^3.5) to O(K^2.5). In addition, our paper validates the effectiveness of M-ar-K-FIA through both theoretical proofs and empirical simulations. Specifically, our method significantly reduces the computational time for analyzing large datasets comprising hundreds of variables. In particular, our method accelerates the computational time by factors of 3.5 to 4.5 when compared to the original ar-K-FIA approach under two diverse dataset scenarios. Furthermore, our method preserves the generalized freshness degree, which is a vital advantage for analyzing time-series data. Ultimately, our method maintains comparable freshness degree to the ar-K-FIA method after applying our modifications. For fast-moving data like social media updates that arrive in rapid succession, determining when an incident has occurred becomes a complex problem. To solve this issue, we suggest an innovative approach that involves using a distributed memory architecture to develop a real-time system capable of identifying incident start times based on geolocated tweets. By spreading calculations across multiple layers, the system can minimize computational overhead. Once an incident is detected, it uses a robust algorithm to determine the time and location at which it likely occurred. To ensure accurate results, the system utilizes a sophisticated mechanism for validating data quality and mitigating potential errors, taking into account factors such as the speed at which information spreads on social media and possible inaccuracies in the locations associated with the tweets. By leveraging a dataset that includes nine hundred and fifty-one incidents, each spanning an hour in duration, we can confidently report that our method outperforms existing solutions. Through thorough experimentation, we validate the system's ability to accurately identify incidents in a real-world setting, successfully detecting over eight hundred incidents out of the total one thousand and twenty five incidents, with the remaining two hundred and twenty five incidents being false positives. In addition, our experimental findings reveal that the social media platform, Twitter, constitutes our primary source of information, providing a significant portion of the data used to determine the locations associated with the incidents. Overall, the system's unique architecture, combination of computational tasks, reliance on geolocated social media data, and thorough methodology contribute to its exceptional performance, effectively demonstrating its ability to accurately detect incidents in a timely and location-aware manner. Experimental results, including visualizations and data analysis, are provided in support to illustrate the credibility of our findings. The system's source code is publicly available for the purpose of dissemination and research. Recent studies indicate a strong connection between quantum steering and Wigner negativity, revealing Wigner function's negative values to be a precise measure of quantum guidance. Notably, research reveals both indicators to be highly correlated in various systems, sharing the same features and behaviors. As a result, analysis of Wigner negativity may offer a convenient replacement for research on quantum steering without compromising the underlying insights. The main objective of this thesis is to explore recent findings regarding the connection between quantum steering and Wigner negativity, with particular emphasis on their respective roles in assessing non-local properties of quantum systems. In the course of this study, it becomes evident that odd-symmetric states possess distinct properties compared to other general mixed states, with certain subspaces holding special significance. The study concludes by drawing parallels between recent research on nonlocal properties of quantum systems, including quantum steering and Wigner negativity, as well as the distinct properties of real vector states. Accurate analysis of quantum key distribution performance is crucial, yet traditional methods often oversimplify by focusing on uniform random seeds, while real-world assessments necessitate non-uniform seeds. We introduce a more general approach to quantum key distribution performance analysis, applicable to various schemes, that considers non-uniform random seeds. We demonstrate the application of this method to multiple quantum key distribution scenarios, showcasing its utility. For the absolute Q-entropy, a detailed analysis is provided, detailing how to calculate key rates as well as practical, roundingly obtained estimates. We examine how traditional methods compare to our approach for Sunaputra-Sasaki, fast random encryption, and fast random encryption protocols, revealing substantial gains in key rates achievable with uniform seeds, yet also highlighting cases where the optimal key rate with non-uniform seeds either surpasses or falls short of the uniform seed outcome. Furthermore, a general approach for the log-average Q-entropy is developed, offering roundly obtained estimates. We apply this method to the Fast Random Encryption protocol and Free Space Quantum Key Distribution, illustrating its effectiveness. We conclude that while traditional methods may attain optimal key rates with uniform seeds, a more comprehensive approach, considering non-uniform seeds, can lead to greater success in practical scenarios, as demonstrated through our analysis. We also conclude that our log-average approach is highly versatile, providing round key rate estimates swiftly and efficiently, ready implementation in practical scenarios. Our research, lastly, showcases that the Fast Random Encryption protocol is capable of attaining the maximal key rates with non-uniform seeds under an average condition, as specified in the paper, when the average is calculated using the logarithm base of $2$. It further establishes a relationship between Faulhaber numbers and Bernoulli polynomials via the derivative operator in the context of algebraic binomial theory. The contribution of the first $n$ terms in the Bernoulli polynomial $B_n(x)$ to its value at $x=1$ is represented as the sum of the first $n$ elements in a recursive series, which is related to the Faulhaber numbers, a concept studied in a recent publication by B. O. Ogoringo. At the close of this note, we prove that the coefficients in the expression of $B_n(1)$ can be alternately represented as the derivatives or faulhaber numbers, which correspond to the binomial coefficients when $n$ is even. This reveals a relationship between Bernoulli and Faulhaber numbers, which reflects the underlying identical structure of these coefficients. Furthermore, this relationship enables the derivation of a closed-form expression for the faulhaber numbers and confirms George Washington's conjecture that the sum of the first $n$ odd numbers is equal to $n^2$. Lastly, this proof showcases the equivalence between the derivative operator and the closed-form expression for the faulhaber numbers, which is achieved through an extension of the recursive series used in the derivation of Bernoulli polynomials in algebraic binomial theory. In this research, a comprehensive study of proton and neutron form factors has been undertaken within a noncommutative space-time framework. Initially, a formalism for describing nucleon structure was developed in noncommutative space, which led to an equation of proton and neutron form factors. Subsequently, the form factor equations were tailored to accommodate the principles of time dilation and relativistic velocity. The applicable regimes for this form of form factor equations were also determined. Furthermore, an analysis was conducted to illustrate how noncommutativity affects the geometric dimensions of nucleons, which is analogous to an electron in the QED theory. An essential comparison was also made between our research findings and an analogous study published by S. Antachkow et al. in 2018. Finally, GPD calculations were performed for all the relevant form factors, revealing that proton sizes remain unchanged but contract in the direction of velocity. Conversely, neutron sizes were found to remain unchanged in the z-axis but grow in the x and y axes. Moreover, a fascinating relationship was established in the context of noncommutative space-time between nucleon geometric dimensions and form factors. Detailed graphs illustrating the impact of noncommutativity on nucleon geometric dimensions were also constructed. An additional discovery was made about the correlation between nucleon charge radii and noncommutativity at a dimension-five level. Consequently, a relationship was established, connecting the fifth-dimensional Planck scale to the nucleon energy scale. Our research findings indicate that the LHC's energy threshold is insufficient to detect noncommutative effects in nucleons, whereas existing experimental data on form factors from lower energy collisions are also insufficient to deduce noncommutativity in nucleons. Nonetheless, it was discovered that precision measurements of form factors at a higher rate than currently accomplished can reveal noncommutativity in nucleons. Our primary suggestion is to conduct precise measurements of form factors over a wider range using a deep-inelastic scattering experiment at a Fermilab facility, which would potentially reveal noncommutativity in nucleons at a certain energy level. Our research findings suggest that the threshold for detecting noncommutativity in nucleons at a rate of $\sim 10^{-15}$ meters could potentially be achieved through a deep-purple regime of energy, which was estimated to be approximately $\sim 1$ TeV. Our research findings could be verified through experiments at a customized, high-energy deep deep-pink proton-proton collision experiment designed to measure proton form factor at an exceptionally high accuracy over a wide range.

To establish trust and ensure fairness, as well as safeguard privacy, algorithmic transparency is crucial. This requires not only explaining the reasoning and properties of models, but also assessing their understandability to humans. However, a key challenge lies in evaluating how understandable a model is to humans, in terms of its interpretability. Existing research primarily explores mathematical formulations of interpretability, but leaves the essential human perspective underwhelming. In response, we take a more comprehensive approach by combining human learning theory and cognitive science to develop a measurable, learning-based algorithmic interpretability standard. This standard, known as the Human-Learning-Based Algorithmic Interpretability (HBAI), leverages cognitive science to evaluate how hard it is for humans to learn a model's logic, and how complex the necessary cognitive processes are to reach such understanding. Furthermore, HBAI's effectiveness is demonstrated through comparison on three datasets. HBAI's source code is available at https://github.com/dhinton/HBAI. Our study offers a new, learning-centered perspective on algorithmic transparency, and with its associated metric, the Human-Learning-Based Algorithmic Transparency (HLBAI) cube, facilitates precise measurements of a model's transparency and understanding from human perspectives. HLBAI's code can be found at https://dhinton.github.io/HLBAI. Visual search algorithms for massive image databases rely on efficient indexing systems that allow for rapid retrieval of relevant visual data, no matter the query type. Current leading systems, like Google's k-NN Search, are restricted to static image collections and utilize fixed indexing structures, necessitating separate indices for various image collections. This results in a substantial storage overhead due to the duplication of indexing data and computationally costly matching procedures. In contrast, our proposed Dynamic Image Indexing technique allows a single, flexible index to be used across diverse collections, dramatically reducing storage and query time costs. The Dynamic Index is built by combining static local indexes to create more general ones, enabling dynamic additions to the index with minimal disruption. We introduce methods for smoothly updating the index, including partial re-building and online refinement, and demonstrate better search performance with the Dynamic Index compared to traditional techniques. Notably, the Dynamic Index can be built in near-linear time with a small constant factor, surpassing the performance of static methods without significant increases in storage. The techniques have been successfully applied to Google's k-NN Search, leading to substantial performance improvements in both query time and overall time efficiency. Recent research has shown the potential of hyperbolic space in handling growing text and its implications on text analysis infrastructure. We have developed FGNET-RH, the first named entity recognition model that leverages hyperbolar space to address the complexities of modern text. FGNET-RH operates directly on characters, producing fine-grained predictions on any topic, and does so without requiring labor-intensive labeling processes. We have implemented a refined approach that captures hierarchical relationships through negative sampling in constant curvature hyperbolic space. This is combined with local aggregation and adaptive refinement techniques to enhance performance. We have evaluated FGNET-RH against leading models, both in hyperbolic and flat spaces, and demonstrated its superiority through both quantitative and qualitative assessments. Critical infrastructure such as power and water systems require monitoring to ensure safe and efficient operation. However, traditional Bayesian monitoring methods often rely on detailed models and prior knowledge of system parameters, which may not be feasible in attack-exposed networks. These systems are also vulnerable to stealthy attacks that manipulate measurements, making traditional effectiveness questionable. We utilize machine learning to create an effective monitoring system that uses normalized residue methods to detect anomalies. Our approach, implemented using an autoencoder, can function without knowledge of the corrupting process. Specifically, we apply the Wasserstein distance to measure the residue distribution and calculate residues through subtraction of estimated and actual values. Since the distribution of residues is unknown, we employ a autoencoder to train a normalized residue feature extractor and a monitor. These components work together to achieve optimal detection and minimize false alarms. Our method, which uses a Bayesian approach to calculate the monitor settings, outperforms existing Bayesian monitoring methods that fail in attack scenarios. Additionally, our method can adapt to changing system states, something the Bayesian monitor cannot do. These benefits come with minimal assumptions about the attack type or likelihood model. We also propose an unsupervised approach to calculate the test statistic and threshold using Kullback-Leibler divergence, which does not require labeled data. Our experimental results demonstrate the monitor's ability to perform effectively in attack scenarios and adapt to changing system states. Furthermore, our methods are robust against model errors that affect the Bayesian monitor's performance. In fact, our method's effectiveness is comparable to the top methods in the field with near optimal results. A document summary is a condensed version of the original content, typically comprising the most crucial ideas, that directly reflects the source text. In recent years, neural networks have been successfully employed to generate summaries from English documents. However, there is a significant knowledge gap in this area when it comes to Indian languages, despite being extensively used in social media platforms and English-Arabic translation tools. This research paper addresses this gap by proposing an unsupervised method for generating summaries in Indian languages, leveraging a graph-based approach. The experiment shows that the proposed model GAE-ISumm consistently produces high-quality summaries that surpass other models, including Lead, GraphLead, Lead-ISumm, and GAE. Furthermore, an exploration of BERT, XLM-R, and GAE-ISumm model combinations reveals that the GAE-ISumm model retains its efficacy even when trained on a limited English-Arabic dataset, demonstrating its strong rolex classification capacity. In extension, the study introduces an Indian language dataset, enabling future studies to analyze and generate summaries in multiple Indian languages. The results demonstrate that the GAE-ISumm model produces higher ROLEX values than the Lead and Lead-ISumm models, while the XLM-R-enhanced GAE-ISumm model exhibits improved performance compared to the basic GAE-ISumm model. Consequently, the GAE-ISumm model presents a promising indication of being a reliable choice for generating high-quality summaries in Indian languages. Upward planarity is a type of planarity that focuses only on upward angles between crossing edges in a given graph. Due to the lack of efficient algorithms, it's used as an alternative to 2-planarity, which includes all angles, for certain theoretical graph models. We've developed multiple parameterized algorithms for checking if a graph is upward planar based on the size of crossing pairs. Two of our algorithms focus on the number of crossings in a single layer or across multiple layers, while a third algorithm targets the overall number of layers. We've also tested the complexity of these parameters through experimental studies, finding that the number of crossings across layers significantly drives the complexity of our problem and is relatively easy to calculate. Additionally, our research revealed that the parameter we've targeted, known as the forward degree, significantly correlates with the complexity of our problem and is relatively easy to calculate. Ultimately, our algorithms demonstrate the efficiency of specific planarity tests, while showcasing the importance of considering angles in planarity tests. They also illustrate the usefulness of parameterized algorithms for coping with the limitations of certain graph models. Our research appears to be the first effort to explore upward planarity through parameterized algorithms in the literature. Furthermore, we've provided a detailed overview of existing research in the field by conducting a comprehensive study on various upward planarity tests. While our algorithms have certain limitations, our research aims to contribute to the development of efficient tools for checking upard planarity in certain graph models. Our methods have also inspired us to investigate parameterized algorithms for 2-planability, revealing interesting correlations between the parameters we've studied and the complexity of our problem. Ultimately, our research aims to stimulate future studies on upward planarity and related topics. Our theoretical analysis demonstrates that our approach is valid under mild assumptions and discuss its applicability to a variety of real-world scenarios where treatment effects vary depending on the given conditions. Our method has been validated through a simulation experiment that compares positively with current approaches to FDR control under strongly heterogeneous data. To accommodate online data streams where data is streamed in real-time, we modify our approach to greatly reduce computational and memory demands, making it run time-compatible with existing methods. Our modified approach achieves an equivalent error rate and performs significantly better than the state-of-the-art approach working under identical conditions. Software developers who are not domain experts often struggle to formulate relevant questions during software maintenance tasks, which impedes their ability to take advantage of available documentation.  There is a growing research interest in employing natural language processing and software engineering knowledge to support these developers, however current solutions are limited as they either solely rely on the programmers' own knowledge or offer general advice only.  To address these challenges, we propose a new technique called QUICKAR, which uses crowdsourced data and software engineering knowledge to support these developers.  By leveraging this approach, QUICKAR enables the reformulation of programmers' imperfect ASRS questions into improved versions that accurately reflect the researchers' understanding.  Experimental results conducted across five systems and twenty-five system concepts demonstrate a significant 51% increase in the quality of the reformulated questions compared to the original ones.  Furthermore, using these improved questions, the performance of the concept location technique significantly surpassed traditional methods in supporting these developers, with EPL and NLP combined outcomes exceeding traditional methods by 52%.  Our research findings highlight the role that software engineering knowledge can play in supporting these developers, which is available for further exploration at: http://tinyurl.com/QUICKAR-Knowledge.  Using this knowledge repository, we employed the Knowledge Nearness Distance metric to develop a recommendation system that categorizes relevant entities for the concept location task, which showed promise with a nearness score of 52% compared to the gold standard entity.  Our innovative approach represents the first time crowdsourced data from platforms including Wikipedia, Wiktionary, and Wiktsources has been integrated with software engineering knowledge to support these developers, which marked a 27% improvement compared to the technique's performance in identifying the gold standard entity.  Additionally, the integrated approach helped to reduce the impact of noise in the entity link mapping, which was observed to contribute to a nearness score of 30% in some cases. As entrainment operates on a nuanced level, its measurement is typically restricted to controlled environments within research settings, requiring intense data collection processes. In contrast, this study focuses on developing an entrainment metric for free conversations between strangers, unaffected by setting constraints, through a large-scale dataset analysis. A novel approach combining deep neural networks and an adaptive measurement technique is proposed to quantify entrainment in actual conversations by incorporating an adaptive threshold to overcome the challenge of limited training data. Results from a discussion among strangers gathered through a chat platform in a real-world setting reveal that this method successfully identifies entrainment between conversants despite the absence of supervision, demonstrating a substantial correlation with human-generated labels regarding the feature each speaker adapts in the conversation. Overall, the study yields the first known attempt to measure entrainment in unsupervised settings through conversational data, opening up new possibilities to analyze and understand entrainment in real-world conversations. Furthermore, this method could be applied to other adaptation features, such as speech production, by adapting the method to the specific characteristics of the feature in question. As the collection of speech data is becoming increasingly difficult, particularly with the rise of end-to-end devices, the proposed method offers a crucial perspective on the operational environment of speech interactions. The development of modern astronomy relies heavily on computing and representing precise spatial representations and spectral analysis.  Due to the rapidly evolving technology, astronomers can now access vast amounts of data, but the lack of standardization in representation and lack of suitable tools have become significant obstacles that hinder research from being translated into functioning software or tools.  This work presents a suite of freely available web-based tools that utilize modern astronomy datasets to learn about spatial and spectral representation.  By providing users with flexible geometry support, support for up to 8 layers of imaging and spectral data, and an extensive list of available processing algorithms, this framework aims to bridge the gap between raw astronomy data and usable information.  Each tool is documented with a sample project, complete with a GitHub repository that includes documentation, sample datasets, and the full deployment process.  This work evaluates the effectiveness of these tools through two key metrics: a representation learning experiment to assess their performance and a user study to gauge their practicality.  Our tools outperformed existing solutions in representation learning and surpassed industry standards in user satisfaction, exceeding expectations with a GSR of 4.73 and a 95% confidence interval of [4.47,4.99] on the Shapley Value for Python Astronomy Libraries Evaluation metric.  This work issues a call to action for researchers to collaborate and provide accurate and standardized protocols for representation and integration of astronomy data into suitable tools.  Furthermore, this project proposes an independent evaluation mechanism to ensure the performance and protocols of tools are in line with industry standards.  Ultimately, this work highlights how modern astronomy data can be leveraged to develop innovative solutions in representation learning and functional programming, paving the way for new perspectives in Abstractor and Equivariant learning, as well as new opportunities in astronomy representation and symptom detection. Classifying every video frame into its respective action can be a labor-intensive task, particularly on long-duration videos at high frame rates. To streamline this process and eliminate the need for costly annotated datasets, we present a novel unsupervised segmentation technique that identifies consistent patterns across separate segments of a video. Our proposed method uses a self-supervised framework to derive stable, frame-to-frame representations from raw videos. Following this, a novel graph-based clustering approach is employed using temporal relationships between these frames to generate coherent action segments. To further enhance stability and co-occurring actions within videos, we integrate a specific node connection constraint during the clustering process. This constraint and a modified clustering score that incorporates connection edges significantly improve our method's accuracy. Comprehensive experiments demonstrating the state-of-the-art performance on JHMDB, 50Salads, Sun Action+RGB, Sun Action+RGB-D, Kinetics-Seg, UCF Sports and Human3D datasets have validated the effectiveness of our proposed technique. A modified version incorporating both RGB and depth frames is implemented for the Sun Action+RGB-D dataset. Current educational technology-based assessment tools provide instant feedback to students; however, their limited capacity restricts the amount of feedback they can offer. In the field of education, a new method of giving feedback has emerged, where small pieces of feedback are provided to students in a sequence. These incremental feedback mechanisms are intended to engage students more deeply in the learning process, increase problem-solving efficacy, and boost satisfaction rates. An experiment was conducted to evaluate the efficacy of this approach in education, specifically in the realm of software testing for students. The study compared the outcomes of two methods of providing feedback: one offering detailed, comprehensive feedback and another providing conceptual and incremental feedback grounded in the specifications for design. The results showed that students receiving the conceptual and incremental feedback outperformed those with the comprehensive feedback option in terms of exam performance, using a paired test with a significance level of.007. Furthermore, students provided the conceptual and incremental feedback also reported higher levels of satisfaction with the assessment process than those given the comprehensive feedback option, using a repeated measures design with a significance level of.001. The study suggests that using this novel approach to feedback in education can yield favorable outcomes for students. Future research recommendations are provided at the end of the article. The data collected from this research was made publicly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/2018RGCISchools/FeedbackComparison. The source of funding for this research was listed on the OSF website at https://doi.org/10.5014/c.2019.234035.07.005.

Domain adaptation has been used primarily for adjusting models to test on one label distribution, but our research explores a more complex problem: adapting models to a completely different type of label distribution than those initially trained with. For instance, instead of just adjusting to a shifted distribution, we aim to adapt a model so that it predicts probabilities rather than hard classes. This new domain, which we call "Hypothesis Shift", requires a novel and challenging adaptation task. To tackle this new domain adaptation task, we introduce a solution method that doesn't need access to the original training data and instead utilizes pseudo-models trained on the target domain without the need for temporary labels. By combining our pseudo-models with unlabeled target data, we create a semi-supervised "label distribution shift" problem that needs to be resolved. Our approach to resolving this problem is a simple two-pruning algorithm that significantly boosts performance on a variety of HSL scenarios (including ImageNet, CIFAR-100, and CIFAR10-100). Additionally, we introduce a range of challenging scenarios that outdo existing methods of domain adaptation by a margin of 6% or more. Our findings demonstrate that domain adaptation can successfully occur even when there are large shifts in both the domain and the label distribution, leading to a whole new realm of possible research in this field. To address this, we must first define what constitutes a quantum resource theory (QRT) and understand the initial conditions for a general QRT. An initial condition for a general QRT must be a convex set of states that can be maintained indefinitely without utilizing the presumed resources. Assuming the initial subset is closed under positive operator scaling (POS), we can determine the complete class of initial sets within the cone of positive semidefinite matrices. These results not only enhance our knowledge of certain QRTs, such as the jamiołkowski-Pielinowski state set, but also demonstrate the significance of POS in quantum resource theory. Additionally, we illustrate the relation between initial conditions and the theory of quantum Markov processes. We obtained a unique observation of a jet-driven piston blast in the low Earth solar corona through Long Baseline Array observations, covering a frequency range from 110 to 140 MHz. This event wasn't associated with significant solar activity and featured a prominent 10-second radio burst followed by a fading type IIb continuum. The burst and continuum spectra exhibited a fundamental and a harmonic frequency component. Their association with a coronal shock driven by a jet became apparent after spatially processing the data. The shock wave triggered a piston front that initiated the 10-second radio burst. This initial shock also gave rise to a forward shock, which the continuum emission followed. It produced a forward-reversed structure characterized as a jet-driven piston blast. The forward-reversed emission was influenced by the forward shock, while the reverse side remained unperturbed. This event supports an shock-driven piston scenario and serves as an exemplar of low-coronal extreme type IV radio bursts, likely triggered by a jet-like disturbance propagating through low coronal regions. This interpretation correlates with findings from other observers, who detected a coronal shock using high-resolution large-field-of-view observations and tracked its progression from low to high altitudes. Furthermore, it aligns with white-light observations of a similar event on another occasion. By treating the vortex circulation as a stochastic process, the equation of motion is derived using Ito's formula and the energy estimate from Campana and Fadin, along with the Cameron-Martin-Maz'ya theorem, to demonstrate the existence of a unique solution. Furthermore, the work is extended to incorporate the impact of random external noises, and an example is provided illustrating the application of the theory to Euler equations, with a specific consideration of vortex motion within a circular domain. However, it is noted that that while the methods are similar, the integration method in this work differs significantly from the method in Eyink and Suley, and the work can be easily extended to model 3D statistical fluid dynamics using functional stochastic differential equations. Nonetheless, it is observed that while the methods are equivalent in 3D Euler equations, the consideration of circulation is non-trivial and introduces novel difficulties in 2D and 3D incompressible Navier-Stokes equations, along with physical and mathematical implications that require separate investigations. Finally, the work is considered an initial step towards developing a theory for 2D statistical fluid dynamics via functional stochastic differential equations, with a corresponding reduction in the dimensionality of the problem at its highest level. The work is considered an advancement over prior research in this field. The concept of entanglement in systems comprising an indefinite number of particles is still not thoroughly understood. Specifically, it is not clear how to measure entanglement in cases where the entanglement of pairs of particles is non-zero but the entanglement of smaller groups within the system approaches zero. In this paper, a method for determining entanglement in such systems is proposed using the idea of entanglement of approximation. We apply this approach to the concept of boson sampling, creating a boson sampling device that starts with a certain level of entanglement and demonstrates the relationship between its efficiency and the amount of entanglement. We also examine the state vector of a boson sampling device using Fock basis and Fock space Fubini-Study polynomial, quantifying the entanglement of its individual components and measuring its overall entanglement. We find that the entanglement present in the whole system cannot be determined solely by the entanglement within its individual parts. We further demonstrate how different types of entanglement can affect the probability of a boson sampling device and a single-photon experiment. Our findings suggest that post-selected boson sampling does not solely rely on the entanglement of its individual parts. We also propose a method to measure entanglement in cases where the entanglement of its whole and partial components approaches zero. Our approach utilizes the relationship between entanglement and uncertainty, using uncertainty as a measure of entanglement in cases where the entanglement of its whole and partial components approaches zero. We apply our method to the $N$-photon maximally entangled state, which is a special case of boson sampling device. Our approach can measure the entanglement of this special case using the von Neumann entropy or the relative entropy. We also demonstrate that our measure of entanglement is consistent with the entanglement of its whole and partial components. Experiments using single-cell RNA-seq data and fluorescence microscopy images demonstrate the success of the proposed method in extracting relevant temporal information. Reinforcement learning strategies that do not rely on the environment being fully observable must make their own assumptions about the state, relying on a value that reflects the confidence in those assumptions. A particular form of this type of learning is based on the Kalman filter, which helps to mitigate the impact of noise. However, conventional wisdom suggests that using this type of approach outside of the context of dynamic systems with continuous variables leads to underperforming results. We have seen this underperformance evidenced in our research, which involved testing a neural network-based Kalman filter in the context of a simple Pacman game. While using a Kalman filter can lead to suboptimal performance in traditional partially observable learning scenarios, our research showed that when the underlying dynamics are complex and difficult to model directly, using a neural network-based Kalman filter can be an effective solution. This has significant implications for the use of such an approach in similar scenarios. We have outlined the key factors that must be present in order for such a method to be effective, starting with large action and state spaces that cannot be easily defined due to their complexity. While the high dimensionality of these spaces can make it difficult to directly model the dynamics, using a neural network-based Kalman filter can help to improve performance, particularly if there is some degree of continuity within the environment. A key benefit of using a neural network-based Kalman filter is that it does not make any assumptions about the form of the environment's dynamics, which means that it can be used to solve a wide range of problems, from predicting the most recent state based on the agent's actions, to more complex problems, such as predicting the location of enemies based on the agent's movement. In this work, a framework is introduced to address the challenge of action detection within videos, starting with limited identification of key actions or their locations. This framework relies on a network known as graph convolutional learning, which utilizes information about a video's temporal structure to recognize critical moments. It also leverages a feature representation spanning the entire duration of a video, focusing on spatial and temporal context. Tests conducted on the ATHLET dataset reveal the proposed approach equals or surpasses the performance of previously developed methods in accurately detecting key actions. Additionally, a context-aware video analysis tool allowing for the visualization of learned graph representations has been created. It becomes apparent that the learned model effectively grasps the overall video content with high precision, even when only a small number of key actions or their locations are identified. This research has important implications for fully understanding videos, especially in the context of weakly-supervised detection of key actions. It seeks to bridge a significant knowledge gap related to interpreting the importance of individual video frames and nodes within a graph representation of a video. Importantly, this research showcases the potential of learning video context through a graph representation, which holds great promise for future innovations. Code for this project is available on the link: https://github.com/AaronGao/spot-what-counts.

This involved mapping the FUV emission within the complex using 23.5 x 21 arcmin^2 images and 1.5 arcmin pixels, which were then beam-corrected and filtered to subtract the quiescent sky emission. FUV spectra from 151 counts/s/arcmin^2 and 301 counts/s/arcmin^2 were also extracted from the brightest areas, allowing for the identification of atomic and molecular lines. Three FUV brightness zones were found within the complex: zones A and B, characterized by high-pressure FUV emission (up to 60 times the local background), and zone C, marked by moderate-pressure emission (three times the local background). These FUV emissions act as resultants of pulsations in dense cores within the cloud, which transition from the ionized phase to the molecular phase over centuries. Furthermore, pulsion activity in this region is tied to similar dynamical processes as those observed in dust emission, revealing a primary function of pulsions in regulating the molecular core's lifecycle. Over the past ten years, substantial advancements have taken place to minimize the occurrence of incorrect positive results in data retrieval systems. These developments led to the creation of novel systems such as skip lists and Bloom filters. This work presents a brand-new approach to compressing filters without the presence of false positives, which enables efficient querying on binary arrays using a logarithmic amount of storage with nearly ideal error rates. The introduction of the Free Free Set concept, where a subset of a binary array contains no relevant elements, allows our method to provide the lowest known storage requirements for maintaining a false-free collection to this day. The method's performance is facilitated through the integration of two innovative technologies: a fast construction algorithm and an efficient structure that can be quickly evaluated. These technologies, known as FF-Bloom and Free-Free Data Structure (FFDS), respectively, significantly contribute to the performance improvement of the system. The FFDS leverages a novel evaluation routine that utilizes a specialized collection to effectively mitigate false positives during query processing, resulting in a high false positive rate resistance of $O(\log^{ - 1.7}_{m})$. This work introduces Hopper, a multi-hop spatiotemporal deep learning model, 
designed to improve forecasting accuracy by mimicking a human forecaster's 
approach. Hopper combines innovations such as a novel transformer architecture, 
a specialized attention mechanism, and an efficient learning strategy, along with 
leveraging external climatic data such as meteorological and geographical information. 
In particular, Hopper focuses on generating precise predictions for target locations 
considering neighboring stations with varying spatial and temporal relationships. 
To address this challenge, Hopper efficiently encodes complex geostationary 
rainfall data and integrates external climatic features through an interdependent 
structure. Comprehensive experiments utilizing 23 datasets demonstrate Hopper's 
superiority over existing models, highlighting its ability to effectively generalize 
across target stations and preclude overfitting. Furthermore, Hopper's source 
code is made available to the research community. 
An update to this work is provided in https://dx.osc.mg/hopper2023-revision. 
Additionally, the associated paper can be found at https. IJCAIS2022/Hopper. 
The preliminary version of this research was presented at https://dx.osc.mg/aaai2021p-1211. 

Key highlights of this research are:
1. Developing a multi-hop transformer model, Hopper, for spatiotemporal deep learning.
2. Introducing a novel transformer architecture, parallel multi-hop transformer (PMMH-T), and an efficient learning strategy to improve forecasting accuracy.
3. Creating a multi-hop interdependent structure (MHI) to combine the strengths of local and global climatic features.
4. Leveraging external climatic data, such as meteorological and geographical features.
5. Demonstrating Hopper's superiority over existing models using 23 datasets and showing its ability to effectively generalize across target stations and preclude overfitting.

Our research proposes a new method for measuring the $W$ mass using data from proton-proton collisions. By analyzing the production of a $W$ boson paired with a $b$ quark and its antiparticle, researchers can accurately identify the $W$ mass despite its event statistics being lower compared to those of $W$ bosons produced alone. A key advantage of this approach is its ability to mitigate uncertainties related to the Allen precision, thereby enhancing overall precision. Furthermore, this method allows for easier tracking of systematic errors related to parton distribution functions, a critical aspect when dealing with limited event statistics. It has been demonstrated that utilizing the CMS detector at the High-Luminosity LHC, researchers can achieve $W$ mass precision of approximately 100 MeV. Consequently, this method offers significant potential for determining the $W$ mass across a wide range of collision energies.  Recent Run-2 data from the CMS experiment have been used to validate the effectiveness of this method. With the expected dataset from the HL-LHC, this method is poised to yield highly precise $W$ mass measurements in the range of 150 MeV to 200 MeV. Furthermore, this technique is also applicable for making precise measurements of other heavy bosons like the top quark. [Note: This article's contents supersede an earlier one published in 2019]

Several exoplanets with unusually large masses have been discovered, up to 10 times the mass of our planet Jupiter. However, observations reveal that massive star birth places are characterized by thin protoplanetary disks. As a result, our model prevents massive planets from achieving masses comparable to that of our planet Saturn. When factoring in the effects of massive binary stars on the planet formation process, our model reveals that massive planets in such systems rarely achieve masses above 4 times the mass of our planet Jupiter. Our research also indicates that massive planets in these systems tend to strip away gas from around them, contributing to a thin appearance of the protoplanetary disk. That is, planets forming from the gravitational collapse of the disk may have a limited range of possible masses between 0.3 and 4 times the mass of our planet Jupiter. This discovery, rooted in the principles of gas behavior in the disk, is consistent with the observed population of massive exoplanets. Our research also led to a new understanding of the structure and properties of protoplanetary disks, revealing the true population of planets should exhibit a particular pattern when plotted against the area they occupy. This plot should reveal a distinct bimodal distribution, with a resulting ratio of 50% showing planets in a particular mass range and the remaining 50% appearing at higher masses. That ratio can be used as a means of detection, with a possible failure to find planets in the higher mass range serving as an explanation for thin protoplanetary disks in massive star environments. This work delves into the relationship between the multiplicative structure of chip-firing games, Jacobian groups of curves, and elliptic curves represented by non-Higman curves. Initially, it examines initial prime divisors of the symmetric group $G_n$ of degree $n$, whose action on $\mathbb{Z}_p^m$ defines the chip-firing game of dimension $m$, and establishes criteria for these primes based on $m$ and $p$ that aren't too conservative. The researchers then show that for odd primes $p$ not dividing $n$ a specific number or multiples thereof, the group $G_n$ over a sufficiently large field of characteristic $p$ is an elliptic curve defined over the fraction field of $k[tn]$. Further findings reveal additional connections between the multiplicative structure of these games and a particular type of curve called "weakly singular curve of type (n,p)" which extends the concept of a non-Higman curve. Ultimately, this work places the relationships found in the context of the theory of tameetons for these games, identifying a specific type called "weakly multiplicative tameeton" and establishing that a certain group associated with these tameetons is an elliptic curve when the characteristic of the field is a specific prime. During the investigation, interesting properties of the Jacobian group of a certain type of curve called "Prym variety" and a specific collection of finite groups called "Higman groups" also arose. The researchers hope the results obtained in this work inspire further investigation into these games, their relationships, and their connections with algebraic geometry. The work raises numerous open questions and challenges for future research. The proof of a key finding relied on an unusual approach to chip-firing games, specifically the examination of the "extended game" whose action is defined not just on $\mathbbakZ_p^m$ but also on $\mathbb{Z}_{p+1}^m$. The researchers acknowledge the helpful feedback they received from multiple sources, including a specific conference where the initial findings were presented. The work concludes with a thought-prove statement regarding its generalizations. The main body of this work was completed in 2019; an investigation into weakly multiplicative tameetons was carried out in 2021. The work concludes with a list of its authors' current research interests, which include the theoretical computer science of games defined by groups. The document is completed with two appendices that provide additional context and related information.

In quantum theories with globally symmetric fields, certain symmetries must be intact at infinity. However, the presence of global fields in a quantum gravity context is contentious, largely due to the lack of measurements describing cosmic large-scale structure at quantum gravity conditions. A notable exception is the phenomenon of double refraction observed in fast astronomical objects, which provides data on the topological properties of quantum gravity space. Recent discoveries of double refraction events present new constraints on quantum gravity models, specifically limiting models relying on globally symmetric fields where the symmetry group is subgroupged into two distinct subgroups. One subgroup governs geometric properties of the space, while the other impacts the physics within that geometry. Upon applying these constraints to commonly discussed quantum gravity models, it became evident that the data from double refraction events imposes significantly stricter requirements than similar analyses based on the cosmological principle. The analysis also identified a previously unrestrained region in the parameter space associated with the models in question. The models where the symmetry is completely broken and the ones where the symmetry is partially preserved both exhibit distinct geometric properties on the boundary of their respective domains of validity, describing the geometry of the quantum gravity space. The models of partially preserved symmetry appear particularly appealing since they offer a chance to align the data from double refraction with the theories of cosmic large-scale structure, thus creating a more consistent picture of the physics involved. A potential experimental path exists to further refine the constraints derived from double refraction analysis and to test quantum gravity models, focusing on the measurement of the gravitational slip angle. Such an experiment could involve analyzing astronomical objects moving at speeds close to the speed of light within our galaxy or using advanced simulation technologies to generate highly relativistic particles. The proposed measurement could significantly lower the current uncertainty threshold related to that angle, thereby providing more precise constraints on quantum gravity models consistent with double refraction data. Deep learning research often focuses on the transferability of models, which involves using a pre-trained model on a small dataset to predict outcomes on an unrelated dataset. While some studies indicate that model architecture significantly affects transferability, others suggest that the impact is negligible. We disagree with this consensus, arguing instead that two widely accepted principles are flawed. Instead, we propose that the underlying data should be the primary focus. We utilize various metrics to measure the impact of data on transferability, and our findings confirm that data structure is crucial. We also introduce a method to analyze the impact of data on the predictions of deep learning models, providing new insights into the world of model transferability. The code used in this research is available at https://github.com/AIresearchers/Rethinking-Transferability. Our research is the first to scrutinize two widely accepted principles, which has real-world implications for how researchers approach data and model design. We anticipate that our findings will motivate more studies examining the impact of data on transferability. Furthermore, we expect that our research will encourage the development of models tailored to the specific requirements of target datasets, rather than relying on one-size-fits-all architectural policies. Ultimately, the outcomes of our research may lead to a deeper understanding of the factors influencing transferability in deep learning. We hypothesize that the structure of a network can limit the efficiency of information dissemination. Furthermore, we examined the effects of different network configurations, such as ring, lattice, geographically-inspired, and random networks, on the spread rate, discovering that a network's modularity (a measure of its clusters/communities) is a key determining factor. By incorporating a simple delay into a widely-used spreading model, we identified an inverse relationship between modularity and efficiency, where higher modularity results in a significantly slower spread rate. Moreover, the efficiency of information dissemination also depends on the size of a network's weakly-interconnected boundaries. Specifically, we found that a network's weakly-interconnected fraction and modularity are jointly responsible for the efficiency of information dissemination. The reliability of time-domain models used for analyzing signal distortion in communication systems is a serious concern. At the heart of conventional time-domain models for unamplified links is the regular perturbation model, which relies on a key assumption that the channel response is weak compared to the pulse shape. While this assumption has been thoroughly investigated in continuous time domains, a corresponding discrete-time domain assessment is missing. As a result, we undertake a reliable method of pairwise analysis in this discrete domain. Our approach suggests that the conventional time-domain models will exhibit convergence for pulses of any finite length as the channel impact tends towards zero. Moreover, we propose an enhanced time-domain model in discrete form that is particularly efficient for pulses of short lengths. Our approach involves dividing the open infinite signal path into a series of successive approximations, which enables us to derive an iterative resolution valid for arbitrary pulses. By applying a specific discrete version of our method, we are able to validate the discrete regular perturbation model and show that it matches the output obtained from a parallel direct approach for pulses of any finite length. Our analysis is further validated for various channel impacts in both numerical and graphical forms. Ultimately, we apply the discrete regular perturbation model to a range of baseband and passband modulation techniques to derive an analytical expression for their respective bandwidth efficiency. Our model is found to be highly accurate when compared to corresponding direct simulations. It is anticipated that the reliability of our discrete regular perturbation model will facilitate a better comprehension of unamplified communication systems, which may involve a wide variety of discrete pulse shapes resulting from band-limited Galerkin or Nyquist-Fejér expansions. Moreover, this model may offer a useful approximation even in cases where the channel impact is not negligible, which expands its practical applications to various passband modulation techniques. Specifically, in the passband, this model has the potential to greatly improve the performance of specific modulation techniques such as minimum band-limited energy per symbol, minimum band-limited power per radiated power, or minimum band-limited power per band-limited energy. The corresponding performance enhancements have already been validated in numerical and graphical forms. Interestingly, in some instances, this model has the potential to greatly improve the performance of certain bandwidth efficient modulation techniques by as much percentage as several orders of magnitude. Despite this, the Thakurta metric actually corresponds to a singular, conic-shaped spacetime, characterized by the condition $\alpha < \gamma$. Furthermore, even when a surrounding "medium" is present, its influence is insufficient to stabilize such spacetimes against further collapse. As such, the Thakurta metric is unable to provide insight into cosmic black hole behavior, a fact that the original analysis failed to address adequately. The original analysis also mistakenly attributed a "standard model of cosmological black holes" to Horuda et al (2020) - in actual fact, that work sought to rectify a oversight regarding the lack of dynamical evidence supporting primordial black holes in that specific model. This work addresses two key challenges in the theory of Bohr sets. Firstly, it establishes a way of "counting" the places where certain Bohr sets overlap when their underlying groups are comprised of numbers of a finite or infinite but quantifiable magnitude. Secondly, it demonstrates that a specific, anticipated relationship between the size of Bohr sets and their "sums" does indeed hold true in any group that can be represented numerically, thus building on a previous finding that relied on a manual, "brute-force" approach to checking for set membership. By achieving this, we gain insight into the nature of "countable" groups and make progress towards understanding how to identify the largest possible sizes of Bohr sets within them. Furthermore, we use a mathematical concept known as the Fourier transform to divide sets into their individual components, thus allowing us to explore relationships between these pieces and their associated "Fourier transforms." In doing so, we are able to establish a series of complex, step-by-step logical connections between the sizes of sets, their "sums," and a certain mathematical property that describes the distribution of "frequencies" within these collections. These relationships, which are shown to be consistent even when considering infinite "collectives" of sets, form the foundation of a sophisticated network of interconnected ideas that underpin a comprehensive theory of the sizes of Bohr sets. Ultimately, we use a combination of mathematical reasoning and insight to effectively "measure" the largest possible sizes of Bohr sets within these numerical groups, thus bringing the "Bohr sets problem" to a successful conclusion in the context of these numerical groups. Furthermore, we uncover a series of intriguing and fundamental questions that remain unanswered within this area of research, representing opportunities for future exploration and advancement. This study addresses the dial-a-ride problem within large urban settings, focusing on the scheduling of a fleet manager who needs to schedule vehicle trips to maximize profits by serving customer demands while considering drivers' working hours and the vehicles' capacity limitations. A solution approach involves developing a range of tight inequalities aimed at minimizing the cost of the objective function, which arises from due to demand uncertainties. Additionally, the dial-a-ride problem is transformed into a mixed-integer linear program using these tight inequalities. However, solving this new program directly can be challenging due to the introduction of additional constraints. As a result, the authors propose a novel Branch-and-Cut method to solve the transformed program efficiently. The effectiveness of this method is illustrated through computational experiments conducted using 12 test cases derived from a study on urban dial-a-ride problems. The test cases were based on real-world data and involved varying numbers of clients, vehicles, and time periods. The computational results demonstrate that the method efficiently solves the transformed program for all test cases within a reasonable time frame. Furthermore, the method was used to select the best solution from a set of generated candidate solutions. A thorough analysis of the computational results highlighted that the effectiveness of the method largely depends on the type of tight inequalities introduced, with which a high quality solution can be achieved, namely a solution that is within 5.3% of optimality. The method also demonstrates the capability to rapidly solve the original dial-a-ride problem, with computed solutions representing approximations of the transformed program's optimal value, namely, a solution that is within 2.2% of optimality.
