A novel approach for solving certain partial differential equations (PDEs) is proposed, primarily focusing on first-order and second-order equations with linear, nonlinear, and certain quadratic terms. This method can also be adapted for Neumann boundary conditions. A key aspect of this approach is the use of cell-mean based approximations, leveraging a specialized neural network architecture that incorporates a hidden layer with a ReLU activation function. For a wide range of the specified equations, theoretical convergence rates are demonstrated, ranging from suboptimal to nearly optimal rates depending on the equation type. Notably, this method is the first to achieve convergence for certain nonlinear PDEs without small parameter restrictions. Furthermore, numerical results and theoretical estimates indicate a high probability of convergence for most cases. Notably, experiments show that these estimates are overly conservative in many instances. Extension possibilities for this approach are also discussed, including applications to more advanced mathematical models and even systems biology equations. Notably, additional research is needed to address potential issues related to numerical instability and spatial bias in some cases.  A related movie can be accessed at https://youtu.be/UhMWsCwBvSs. Moreover, further investigations have revealed several promising extensions including the application of our method to systems of higher-dimensional PDEs with boundary conditions as well as Ginzburg-Landau and reaction-diffusion systems of equations. Notably, future work aims to improve the method's adaptability to a broader range of equations, potentially without requiring modifications to the neural network itself. A related movie illustrating the method's performance on the 2D Ginzburg-Landau system can be accessed at https://youtu.be/7A2k13EoDO8. Moreover, another related movie illustrating the method's performance on the reaction-diffusion system can be accessed at https://youtu.be/7Uu9gY2Hgfc. Furthermore, our group is currently exploring the application of our method to the steady 2D Ginzburg-Landau-Van der Waals system, which describes the behavior of a system of magnetic vortices in the presence of a singularity. The Unruh effect can only be observed directly by measuring the gravitational influence on a contained space, as explained by its connection to the angular momentum of a two-dimensional sphere. A novel approach has been considered where the Unruh effect is interpreted through the shift in the phase of a complex field within a bounded region. Although this phase shift, known as the Berry phase, occurs within a space-time scalar field system, it cannot be measured by following the time-dependent behavior within a bounded area under linear coupling, as this would result in a second-order effect. Rather, a self-consistent method for determining the phase shift is derived from the response function of the system, which includes terms representing infinite past and future radiation, as well as a term representing the interaction between these two. As this result appears to be inconsistent, a consistent method for determining the phase shift is derived from the angular momentum of a two-dimensional sphere, specifically from its connection to the mass of a gravitating black hole. By applying the Peierls method, the self-consistent result can be expressed as the expectation value of a specific operator within this system, known as the topological operator. By comparing the results from this approach and the previous one based on a boundary, it becomes clear that the Berry phase can serve as a marker for identifying the Unruh effect within a bounded region. Furthermore, it is considered how the Unruh effect within a bounded region may be observed through its connection to the gravitational influence on a contained space, as well as the effect that this has on the possibility of directly measuring the Unruh effect. Specifically, it is considered the effect that this has on the relationship between mass and angular momentum in the context of the Berry phase. As this approach stands in contrast to a commonly considered method for interpreting the Unruh effect, it is considered for the common ground between this new interpretation and the common one, particularly in relation to the role of horizons in the Unruh effect. However, in this approach, the concept of horizons is not utilized. Rather, as an alternative view of the Unruh effect, the connection to a specific quantum system is sufficient. In addition to this, the mathematical framework of the approach is similar to that of a commonly considered model in the literature, known as the Schrödinger-Villars model. However, in this approach, the reason for the phase shift is clearer and is connected to a specific physical observation, rather than a guess as is the case with the Schrödinger-Villars model. This study introduces the Multilingual Incident Extraction Evaluation dataset consisting of 1,000 articles in English and eight other languages, spanning news content from 69 countries between 2014 and 2020. Composed of 16,685 paragraphs annotated to represent violent incidents, the dataset reveals that information dissemination is unevenly distributed across languages. In relation, we examine the effect of language on knowledge diffusion, observing that fewer than one percent of American readers will, through news media, learn about incidents occurring in other countries. Conversely, readers residing in countries experiencing local conflicts are more informed. To establish a benchmark for multilingual information extraction tasks, we develop a two-pass annotation process and outline a range of evaluation experiments, in addition to making the MEE-E dataset freely accessible to the research community. Both the dataset and the annotation scheme are available on our website at https://mee-e.org/. We will present the remaining portion of this research at NAACL-HLT 2022 in the form of a paper.

Research on universal grammar suggests that human language is guided by innate grammatical rules. Although the prevailing parsing models rely on statistically learned grammars, neglecting the inherent linguistic rules. We propose a novel approach where both a rule-based model incorporating universal grammar and a statistical model are simultaneously employed to predict syntactic structures and semantic interpretations. By integrating the outputs of both models, the accuracy of the overall parsing system is improved. We support our method with experiments conducted on the SRL framework, demonstrating that our joint algorithm outperforms traditional algorithms in enriching predicate-argument relationships. Additionally, our results show that the combined model performs better on various parsing tasks, even when the rule-based model is subpar. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the logical explanations provided by the joint algorithm for parsing failures are more effective in identifying incorrect annotations compared to sole statistical parsing. We have made our source code available on https://github.com/yilundong/jusp_linguistic_grammar/blob/master/jusp_linguistic_grammar/jusp_linguistic_grammar.py. Our research is the first to incorporate both linguistic rule-based models and statistical models into a joint framework, aiming to mitigate biased annotations that may exist in popular parsing datasets. The findings of our study have significant implications for jointly analyzing syntactic structures and semantic interpretations. Importantly, our research sheds light on a potential data bias discovery and suggests a novel method for correcting inaccurate annotations, thereby contributing to the development of high-quality parsing datasets. We hope our method can serve as a general framework for parsing various types of language. Finally, our study is closely aligned with the idea of joint development of syntax and semantics proposed by Gibson and Fedorenko (2019). Importantly, our research is practiced successfully in the field of semantic role labeling. Our current work is an initial step towards applying this idea to other complex linguistic tasks and we are exploring its extension to other areas, such as natural language inference, a sentiment analysis technique and so on. Ultimately, our research is an attempt to make a meaningful contribution to the performance of linguistic rule-based models and simultaneously mitigate potential biases in widely-used parsing datasets. By combining data from the James Peery telescope, the collaboration set a limit on any delayed activity from FRBs, including constraints related to repeat bursts and activity levels. Finally, the study considers the potential for extragalactic and in-situ background radiation to influence the observable patterns of FRBs, including constraints related to repeat bursts and activity levels. By exploring these topics, the research contributes significantly to our understanding of FRBs, which may involve complex astrophysical phenomena.

We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, resulting in Delegated RingCT.
The Delegated RingCT scheme is comprised of an integrated signature and encryption framework, combining a public key encryption protocol and two types of signatures along with linkable ring signatures, alongside non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs.
A comprehensive description of Delegated RingCT, along with security evidence and an implemented prototype, are presented, which we subsequently test through benchmarking analysis.
While Delegated RingCT may not possess the same level of anonymity compared to other RingCT implementations, we seek to establish its potential as a faster alternative.
In particular, our Delegated RingCT implementation exhibits improved performance compared to previous studies on Delegated Proof of Stake with RingCT transactions.
Moreover, our Delegated RingCT initiative can be applied to a range of other cryptocurrencies employing the RingCT protocol.
We anticipate Delegated RingCT to contribute significantly to research on combined Payment and Consensus Layer systems. 
Finally, a security-related study, which considered various Delegated RingCT linkable ring signature constructions, was conducted and led to the proposal of two novel schemes: Full Linkable Cross Generic Construction and Internal Round Functions Linkable Cross Generic Construction. 
The FCRC and IRFLCRC schemes represent the first instances of linkable ring signatures that satisfy the requirements of $\mathcal{R}_1$ and $\mathcal{R}_2$, respectively, which were initially suggested by Chor et al. and Hwang et al. in prior research. 
A particular advantage of the FCRC linkable ring signature scheme lies in its capacity to be applied within a setting characterized by round efficiency, which contrasts with the Internal Round Functions Linkable Cross Generic Construction scheme. 
A distinct attribute of the IRFLCRC linkable ring signature scheme lies in its capacity to be applied within a setting characterized by full linkability. 
Both the FCRC and IRFLCRC linkable ring signature schemes achieve a level of security that corresponds to the $\mathcal{R}_1\cap \mathcal{R}_2$ security level, which was defined by Chor et al. and Hwang et al. in prior research. 
A particular security-related achievement of the FCRC linkable ring signature scheme lies in its semantically secure status, which was confirmed via a constructive proof in related security research.

Unified beam dynamics remains a top priority for both research and industrial particle accelerators.  Among the numerous sub-disciplines of beam dynamics, beam diagnostics stands out as particularly crucial because they provide the only means of monitoring beam performance.  Traditionally, beam diagnostics have primarily consisted of monitoring the beam charge through electric measurements, beam trajectory through optical systems, and accelerated beam intensity through calorimetry or emittance by scanning around the beam periphery with various optical devices.  Given the complexities of accelerator systems and the inherent difficulties of simulating all possible operational scenarios, reliable and direct measurement tools become indispensable.  This work will offer an overview of modern beam diagnostic techniques that have emerged in recent years, specifically examining "brightness" scans which have become a vital means of assessing the quality of high-brightness beams.  The discussion will encompass the fundamental principles and applications of brightness scans across current and proposed radiofrequency systems, including traveling wave cavities, linacs, and superconducting cavities.  The associated mathematical representations and underlying assumptions will be examined, in addition to the crucial aspects of implementation and measurement.  Finally, future outlook and challenges will be addressed, with an emphasis on the vast potential of brightness scans that has yet to be fully realized.  The associated mathematical representations and the related technology development will be the primary focus of this discussion, with an exploration of promising areas for future work and implementation.  The discussion is tailored towards engineers and researchers working in particle accelerator design and development, with the aim of inspiring further development and application of this important beam diagnostics tool. Specifically, we utilize generative adversarial networks to develop a collaborative data-driven model that can learn and predict patterns from the data sources. Our proposed approach is supported by theoretical evidence, which showcases its ability to closely approximate both conventional models' performance and more informal learning methods' predictions. Ultimately, we demonstrate the effectiveness of this model on two real-world examples, namely domain adaptation in video surveillance and predictive maintenance. This paper presents a novel optimization technique called AskewSGD for efficiently training quantized neural networks. Initially, we transform the quantization problem into a continuous subproblem tailored to each network layer. Carefully designed constraints ensure that the proposed optimization method generates points that closely resemble the results of the quantized approach, thus improving the final performance of the network. AskewSGD's performance is evaluated on a range of benchmark datasets, achieving a mean square error reduction to 1/100th that of the plain SGD optimizer on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets. AskewSGD achieves significant performance gains over traditional approaches such as Straight-Through Estimation and Learned-Codebook Quantization, leading to a 70% reduction in training time for the ResNet20-L1 benchmark on CIFAR-10. Moreover, AskewSGD's results demonstrate a high degree of generalizability, with minimal performance variability observed across multiple independent trials. AskewSGD's success stems from its ability to extract dense patterns within sparse codebooks using the plain SGD optimizer, combined with its application of constrained optimization to generate codebook vectors that closely resemble the results of the quantized approach. This approach enables AskewSGD to substantially outperform competing methods and achieve superior generalizability while maintaining a simple and efficient architecture. AskewSGD's efficiency is further highlighted by its adaptation in edge-deployment settings where the AskewSGD performance superiority is even more pronounced. Interestingly, when performing binary quantization on the MNIST dataset at bit costs exceeding 0.9, AskewSGD's performance superiority over the plain SGD optimizer became apparent with a result that was only 3% away from the performance achieved using 16-bit floating point representations while reducing the model size to 50% of its original size. Consequently, when applying binary quantization to the MNIST dataset at a bit cost of 0.85, AskewSGD's result that was only 3% away from the performance achieved using 16-bit floating point representations was accompanied by model size reductions of up to 50%. Ultimately, AskewSGD's performance and generalizability superiority over the plain SGD optimizer suggests its utility in settings where model size reductions and performance enhancements are sought after such as in edge-deployment settings. Most advancements in Generative Adversarial Networks have focused on improving performance, but the paucity of research on model interpretability is significant. Unlike other fields where interpretability is a top priority, the primary concern in GAN research has been generating high-quality samples. We aim to address this imbalance by proposing a novel approach to uncovering hidden state information within a discriminator, thereby enhancing model interpretability. By developing this method, we hope to establish a platform for studying interpretability in GANs and setting a benchmark for future research. In our study, we employ the approach to uncovering hidden state information to reveal insights about visual representations, discriminator modules, and the relationship between them. Through experiments on CIFAR10, LSUN, and CelebA, our findings confirm that the structure of a discriminator affects its representation, and that our method is effective in identifying important visual features in representative samples. Uncovering the discriminator's module structure is also possible with our approach, and we obtained some explanations for the visual bias in GAN learning. Finally, our results demonstrate that improving interpretability in one stage of a generative model can have a positive impact on other stages, revealing the potential for a positive and negative interrelationship between generative and discriminative learning. Nested sampling is a computational strategy that's found a range of applications from bayesian inference to the simulation of cosmological surveys. Its performance is heavily influenced by a step selector, which determines which samples to remove and add at each iteration. High-quality choices can lead to significant gains in computational speed. This study evaluates and compares various step selectors, including a new proposal distribution, at the analysis of CMB Planck data. It shows that a flexible, k-dimensional tree-based approach outperforms others, particularly in terms of overall efficiency and time spent in acceptance/rejection operations. This method not only excels in practical terms, but also offers a straightforward implementation without the need for complex techniques. Furthermore, an open-source implementation of nested sampling has been introduced, which allows for the easy exploration and comparison of different step selectors in practical applications. This code can be found at github.com/jmculbreath/PyInference. It enables users to specify custom step selectors and run an algorithm for a given problem, in addition to incorporating a range of default selectors and problem types. Moreover, its structure mirrors that of the emcee sampler, making it simple for users to switch from emcee to PyInference and back again for side-by-side comparisons. This kind of head-to-head comparison revealed that PyInference's default selectors performed worse than expected, leading to the identification of a bug in its kernel implementation. Following this analysis, the code was revised to fix the bug, which in turn led to improved performance for its default selectors. This study's findings and code are expected to aid in the evaluation and comparison of different sampling based techniques to determine their relative merits. Such comparisons could ultimately lead to the development of a comprehensive benchmark suite to aid in the efficient and effective design of bayesian sampling algorithms. Our investigation focuses on the temporal and frequency domain characteristics of the fluctuations in the particle number and relative phase of a simulated, forced Bose-Hubbard crystal. As the crystal is subjected to a constant driving force, it exhibits periodic behavior that is linked to the occurrence of Hopf bifurcations. Furthermore, an alternative method for determining two-particle correlation functions in real-time and real frequency space has been developed and implemented. The method, which relies on the numerical solution of a first-order Maxwell equation, allows for efficient correlation function computation without the need for a large data storage capacity. Our results indicate that the frequency domain correlations provide a valuable, quantitative insight into the periodic dynamics of the system. Specifically, the technique successfully identifies and distinguishes between up- and down-conversion processes induced by the forced dipole dissipation and Rotating Wave Excitation. However, the method's application to the total particle number correlation is left as a topic for future research due to the predicted significant numerical difficulties. The findings presented here serve as a first steps towards exploring quantum many-body systems through $s$-wave scattering. They also highlight the potential of combining time- and frequency-domain correlations to gain a deeper, systemic understanding of condensed matter phenomena. Ultimately, the technique developed in this work has the potential to contribute to a more in-depth, microscopic analysis of quantum correlations in highly dissipative environments. To identify data points that fall outside expected patterns, we rely on out-of-distribution (OOD) detection, which is particularly challenging for classical Gaussian Process classifiers. They tend to overconfidently predict a normal data point is part of the training set's distribution. Building upon the success of Bayesian Neural Networks in OOD detection, a new method called DGOS has been developed to tackle this issue for Gaussian Processes. The approach utilizes a posterior sample from an uncertainty-calibrating Bayesian formulation of Gaussian Processes to create a layer of uncertainty thresholds. This allows the classification system to be divided into two parts: one containing data that clearly falls within the predicted class, and another consisting of data that lies outside these thresholds. OOD detection is then simply a matter of identifying any data points that fall within the latter strata. The new method, $d\gamma$GOS, achieves this by leveraging a distributional Gaussian Process framework that assigns samples to specific distributions. This approach enables the creation of a confidence layer that pinpoints points with high uncertainty, making it possible to accurately identify OOD data. The new methods have demonstrated significant improvements in identifying OOD data while maintaining high classification accuracy for in-distribution data. Our research shows that incorporating uncertainty into Gaussian Process classification can lead to improved performance in OOD detection. Metric learning's pair-wise loss technique is centered on developing an embedding that maximizes similarity between images in close proximity. Various forms of pair-wise loss strategies have been proposed. One such method, triplet loss, has been praised for its ability to consider a variety of image relationships. This research reveals, however, that triplet loss is not superior to other methods, and their perceived performance disparities, in fact, result from variations in hyperparameter settings. Furthermore, experiments demonstrate that more effective configurations of pair-wise losses can be achieved using Reinforcement Learning-based loss functions. These customizable losses yield performance enhancements across multiple image datasets. Furthermore, these improved losses yield better security against adversarial attacks compared to traditional methods. Ultimately, these findings illustrate the value of evidence-based model optimization techniques to develop robust and efficient machine learning systems. The research supports claims with comprehensive model comparisons spanning 9 state-of-the-art pair-wise loss techniques, and includes code and configuration details for reproducibility on the public CARLA dataset. A companion project is available on GitHub here: https://github.com/andreergaifas/metric_learning.git. The research is the first to scrutinize and standardize the configuration of metric learning pair-wise losses, and thus contributes significantly to the field. We investigate non-stochastic multi-armed bandits in the presence of an advisor that suggests primary arms. While selecting the advised arm is preferable, the bandit might choose an alternative arm. Nevertheless, the advisor's preferred arm may be suboptimal; consequently, balancing short-term benefits from the preferred arm with long-term benefits from alternative arms is crucial. In such scenarios, choosing the advisor's arm only when it is optimal results in a optimal regret. Our work applies this concept to the All-Pay auction system, where the advisor's suggestion corresponds to the auction of a specific arm and the advisor's income from that arm affects the bandit's probability of choosing it. A new statistical approach to modeling the stresses in offshore wind turbines using Gaussian processes has been developed, taking into account the lack of data encountered in path-dependent analysis. This method utilizes Gaussian processes to create an initial prediction and a sequential probabilistic refinement. The refinement estimates the uncertainty in the stress levels more accurately, based on the actual stress data. The proposed technique has been successfully tested on two simulated scenarios and an actual offshore wind turbine, showcasing its ability to provide a more precise indication of uncertainty without relying on stress data from the entire entire sequence. The method also enables the simulation of stress levels that may have occurred but are not present in the dataset, offering a way to virtually recreate past events. Furthermore, the technique has been applied to the simulation of an offshore wind turbine's service life, allowing for a deeper understanding of its degradation dynamics. The approach enables the identification of sequences with significantly higher probabilities of occurring and may serve as a basis for developing informed maintenance strategies in the future. This paper presents SceNDD, a novel naturalistic driving dataset focusing on common driving situations. In the context of boundary/conformal field theory, a reflected entropy proposal recently emerged, suggesting that the ratio of reflected entropy and entanglement wedge cross-sectional area can serve as a measure of string tension within a dual AdS setup. Focusing on boundary CFTs/BCFTs, we're investigating the underlying reflected entropy through the lens of interval Markov chains. Interval exchange maps, which generate Markov chains, naturally involve reflection in this context. We show that, in a certain scenario, the reflected entropy scales with the square of Steiner partition exponent $\theta$ for interval exchange maps where Steiner's parameter $q$ exceeds 2, and we note that $\theta=2$ when $q=2$. Furthermore, for a specific transformation related to M\"obius maps, we find that the reflected entropy remains constant, illustrating the potential for a cap on reflected entropy. These findings simultaneously validate and challenge the proposed relationship between reflected entropy and string tension. As examples, we're analyzing the Majid-Swezchuk fusion model relevant to $A_{2-1}$ conformal field theory, the Dittje-Mueller-Bruant model, and the random matrix model. The global COVID-19 pandemic has led governments to implement contact tracing programs as a tool to contain the spread of the disease. These programs primarily rely on mobile device data such as location, time stamps, and mobile app identifiers which are typically aggregated and released to support public health efforts in de-identifying contact data. Despite this, the integration of mobile COVID-19 tracking apps with general location data, as seen with Google/Apple's COVID-19 Exposure Notification, has raised concerns about patient privacy. Recent cases of COVID-19 patients having their identities compromised raises questions about the effectiveness of de-identification methods employed in contact tracing programs. A recent instance of exposing university students' identities through their Android location data further underscored these risks. These incidents prompted our research into the de-identification risks of national contact tracing programs and whether the use of location data exposes the identities of COVID-19 patients. Our research revealed a simpler approach to de-identifying COVID-US instance, as well as an exposed location data risk for Google/Apple's COVID-19 Exposure Notification. The simplicity of our method is what makes it concerning, given that the de-identification of location data for contact tracing purposes has become a public health priority. Our research protocol is also capable of being expanded to accommodate other contact tracing programs based on mobile apps, a more complex undertaking. A prototype implementation of our research protocol has been demonstrated, showcasing its practicality and effectiveness. A thorough analysis of relevant ethical, legal, and social implications was conducted, taking into consideration recent COVID-19 pandemic-related measures as a primary point of reference. A comprehensive policy-related survey was conducted, targeting 18 countries representing the four continents of North/South America, Europe, Asia, and Australia. Our research survey showed that participants were not aware of any COVID-19 related data breach in their country, highlighting participants' confidence in government efforts to manage the pandemic. Our research was conducted to raise awareness among contact tracing program administrators about the importance of identifying the source of the COVID-US instance and similar breaches to prevent similar breaches from occurring in the future. A set of recommendations was proposed at the conclusion of our research, aiming to enhance the privacy of national contact tracing programs and contribute to a more effective pandemic response. These recommendations were aimed at various stakeholders, including government entities, mobile operating system providers, data providers, and pandemic management officials. Our research was conducted in an effort to mitigate the consequences of a COVID-19 pandemic and promote a more collaborative pandemic response through the integration of our research findings into relevant pandemic management

By applying the principles of quantum filtering and quantum Bayes' theorem, we demonstrate that a neural unit with two states can effectively process light signals coming from a solar cell, which is represented by a quantum operator. This unit can also be in a superposition state, facilitating the resolution of ambiguous light intensities and enabling the neural system to adapt to changing environments over time. In addition, we show that a neural network consisting of such units can be used to solve classification problems, and its ability to process quantum information can contribute to improved performance compared to classical approaches, especially when faced with complex or dynamic problems. In contrast, a neural system relying solely on mean field theory is less effective in high light conditions and may not be able to solve more intricate problems. In order to quantify the benefits of quantum effects in neural networks, we propose a measure called Q-score, which indicates the proportion of quantum information present. When Q-score is high, the neural system is more efficient; in this case, the additional quantum information has greater impact; otherwise, the difference is minimal. When the quantum annealing schedule is large, the latter shows better performance, and as it decreases, the former outperforms it. It's worth noting that the quantum effects in a neural system described in this model are different from those seen in quantum computing systems, which use unitary transformations to resolve ambiguities, as opposed to the more realistic non-unitary approach employed by the former. This paper outlines a proposed research initiative where we apply algebraic topology and machine learning together to tackle problems in physics. We argue that the combination of two techniques, persistent homology and machine learning, could lead new breakthroughs in understanding the geometric properties of discrete quantum matter, such as quantum clusters. By exploring homology through image representation learning, we aim to establish a new foundation for analytical tools in physics that can also be applied across materials and contexts. Furthermore, this approach has the potential to create novel methodologies that can aid in understanding the underlying structure of point defects in materials, and we expect it to open up new research avenues at the intersection of algebraic topology, machine learning, and physics. The initial phase of the project will focus on developing the foundational techniques of persistent homology from a learning perspective, and on creating a first prototype that can incorporate symbolic constraints to isolate specific topological features relevant to quantum clusters, where existing methods have struggled. The longer-term objectives of the project involve representing underlying lattices as graphs, exploring the connection between geometric and topological properties, and employing machine learning-based methods for symbol detection. The potential beneficiaries of the research initiative include the Italian physics community, particularly those working on understanding the elastic properties of van der Waals materials and their topological structure, and those working on defect structures and their application to quantum computing materials and physics. The general public can also benefit from the potential applications of the research in fields like biomedical imaging and understanding the structure of materials at an atomic level. The research initiative will be led by two principal investigators, one with expertise in machine learning and algebraic topology and the other with expertise in physics and quantum computing, and they will be joined by three further team members with expertise in AI, physics, and materials science. The team plans to achieve their objectives through a range of activities including workshops, conferences, open courses, publications in top journals, and by establishing collaborations with institutions in the Italian physics research community. The specific evaluation metrics for the research initiative and its potential impact will be determined through a systematic analysis of its outcomes and effects on the community and the team. The research initiative is proposed for funding of $231,000 over two years. The application includes a project outline, curriculum vitae of the lead researchers and team members, and a comprehensive public outreach plan. The project is supported by a reference letter from one expert in the field. The application is submitted by the University of Bologna, a public University in Italy. The project can potentially be submitted for renewal after two years with renewed funding.

For a solar panel, the energy it produces follows a non-linear relationship with the intensity and angle of the incident sunlight. To accurately determine the total energy output, we need to integrate this nonlinear function over the possible input conditions, which involves integrating a trigonometrically-dependent function over a specific interval. A suitable method to perform this integration is Gaussian quadrature, and we've developed a way to optimize this method to account for the specific integration requirements. By doing so, we've developed new rules for selecting input points for the integration, and our method converges more quickly and precisely than other methods for integrating solar-panel energy output. We've tested our method against known solutions for integrating trigonometric functions and found that it produces the expected results, even when precision is extremely high. Additionally, we've applied this method to simulate the energy production of a solar panel under various real-world scenarios and found that it produces realistic results under these conditions. Finally, we've demonstrated that our method can be generalized to apply to more complex integration requirements. A related appendix has been added to provide supporting information.

The task of category-level object position estimation involves determining the $y$-coordinate of an object in an image, representing its classification into a particular category and its elevated or ground-level position. This task was previously studied by Huang et. al. in 2019, where results showed significant improvement over the more complex task of object semantic segmentation. This paper presents an approach that surpasses the current state-of-the-art performance in zero-shot category-level object position estimation. The proposed method starts by identifying the binary classification of an object's ground-level position and a preliminary semantic segmentation. By conditioning the latter on both the object category and a map of the image's semantic segments, this method achieves superior results on the COPOPE dataset by exhibiting accurate zero-shot semantic segmentation scores and increased discriminative power. By combining zero-shot semantic segmentation and binary classification, this method achieves improved performance compared to previous methods, which only considered category-level information. Additionally, exhaustive experiments were conducted to study the influence of two key factors: the zero-shot nature of the task and the presence of a class imbalance in the data. These experiments revealed the predictive power of semantic segmentation features and the significant disadvantage of zero-shot methods lacking access to class labels. Furthermore, this investigation demonstrated the severity of class imbalance's impact on zero-shot methods and the efficacy of addressing it through the use of balancing techniques. By presenting a comprehensive analysis of these factors, these results significantly contribute to understanding the specific characteristics of the task of zero-shot category-level object position estimation. By leveraging the identified insights through a step-by-step breakdown of the proposed approach, we successfully enhanced the estimated $y$-coordinate by approximately 4.8% relative to the previous state-of-the-art method. Furthermore, our approach is versatile and can be applied to more complex object semantic segmentation by introducing additional bins in the classification process. Consequently, this method achieves a new state-of-the-art performance on the more complex task of semantic segmentation. By evaluating the relevance of the proposed method to real-world applications, we estimate its potential error rate in such scenarios. Ultimately, the proposed method achieves superior performance in zero-shot category-level object position estimation, surpassing the current state-of-the-art performance by approximately 4.8% and setting a new benchmark for future research. Furthermore, this method's performance on semantic segmentation tasks indicates its potential as a benchmark for future research. Predicting traffic conditions is a widespread issue. Current methods use a complete spatio-temporal dataset to train models that anticipate traffic conditions at any given location and time. However, measuring traffic density is severely hampered by a lack of data. To address this challenge, a novel forecasting task known as traffic density forecasting, which requires determining whether a road section will be heavily or lightly congested, is proposed. Due to the scarcity of data and the substantial number of roads, this problem poses significant difficulties. To tackle these obstacles, a model called SpaNet (from scarcity to similarity) is presented. It employs an encoder-decoder structure, using an encoder to derive feature representations from the input images and matching them with analogous images from historical data to generate predictive information. To enhance model performance during training, unannotated road sections are also utilized as positive examples. The model's stability is ensured through the implementation of a similarity metric. The results of the experiments show that SpaNet surpasses the performance of the existing state-of-the-art methods both qualitatively and quantitatively. This work introduces VACA, a variational graph autoencoder designed to generate counterfactual queries and model interventional data through the integration of causal graphs. VACA uses a causal graph to define interventions on its input graph, a variational autoencoder to learn an underlying graph representation, and another network to generate counterfactual data by applying interventions to this representation. By learning a multi-faceted graph, VACA can generate counterfactual data by predicting interventions on its internal structure, as opposed to simply changing its labels. We demonstrate the effectiveness of VACA through counterfactual queries on various datasets. 

Key aspects of our method:
Our method is based on a variational autoencoder with a Gaussian mixture router, allowing our model to switch between generating counterfactual data and learning a multi-faceted graph.
The integration of a causal graph allows us to generate counterfactual data by applying interventions on the internal structure of the graph.
As opposed to existing methods, our model does not assume causal graph accuracy and allows for partial specifications of the graph.
Our method's ability to learn a multi-faceted graph allows us to generate counterfactual data by applying different interventions.

Our method's performance is evaluated through a qualitative analysis of a benchmark dataset. 

Key results:
Our method's performance is comparable to state-of-the-art approaches when tested on interventions and outperformed existing methods on counterfactual queries.
The quality of our method's counterfactual data was outperformed by existing methods but still generated high-quality data.
Our method's counterfactual data was characterized by lower entropy, indicating higher quality.

The motion picture industry is a significant cultural and economic force. To enhance our understanding of this sector, we examined the grand opening box office revenues of movies from the past three decades using a larger dataset than has been used in similar research. Our work relies on a 608-movie dataset that includes 131 attributes, such as financing and casting information. We investigated multiple output variables, including worldwide box office revenue, domestic revenue, and worldwide minus domestic revenue. Our research revealed that certain pre-release attributes have a significant impact on the commercial success of movies. We discovered that factors like the director's previous success, the lead actor's popularity, and the presence of well-known actors or directors in supporting roles significantly influence a movie's domestic and worldwide box office revenues. We also explored the effect of marketing expenses on revenue, but our results indicated an inconsistent relationship. Our conclusions are consistent with current industry practices, highlighting the importance of pre-release attributes in determining commercial success. We also emphasized that predicting revenue requires an in-depth analysis of these factors. Finally, our research demonstrated that relevant factors can be applied to predict revenue at any stage of a movie's lifecycle, making this a valuable tool for assessing a movie's commercial potential. Federated learning allows multiple clients to cooperative train a shared model while preserving their privacy. Several recent studies have explored the challenges of fairness in FL, focusing on ensuring individual groups' classification outcomes aren't discriminated against. Our research involves the first assessment of privacy risks in discriminatory FL and an evaluation of a developed metric to quantify the trade-offs between fairness and privacy in FL. Ultimately, our results underscore the importance of addressing the trade-offs between fairness, privacy, and consistency in the context of differential privacy for federated learning. They also motivate the adaptation of general differential privacy methods to the context of heterogeneous, discriminatory data. Based on these findings, we introduce a novel technique to ensure privacy while promoting fairness in FL, which is compatible with a range of consistency objectives. Our approach, called the Consistency-Aware Privacy Preserving Federated Learning (CAPP-Fed), extends the existing federated learning process by integrating two key operations - training on a transformed dataset and generating a representative model, required for communicating the transformed data to a central server. By analyzing the data transmitted to the server, our algorithm, CAPP-Fed, is able to provide a precise measurement of the trade-offs between privacy, consistency, and fairness. We have designed a novel control method that utilizes a learning algorithm to develop complex policies for complex control systems, even with limited data availability. This algorithm models the control system as an optimal Markov Process to identify the sequence of actions required to achieve a desired goal, and it formulates this problem as a series of decision-making tasks when only partial data is available. This method addresses one of the significant challenges in reinforcement learning, which is how to efficiently collect data to effectively train a policy. To better utilize available information, we have introduced side constraints that represent the physical constraints of the system, and we have developed a complementary optimization algorithm to integrate this side information into the model. We have evaluated our approach against existing methods through numerous real-world simulations, and it consistently outperformed traditional reinforcement learning and adaptive methods, achieving up to 300% better results in tasks such as flying, walking, reaching, and swimming. Furthermore, our approach successfully utilized available information to streamline the learning process, resulting in a 90% reduction of the required data in some instances. In addition, our results demonstrate that our control method can effectively transition between different tasks with minimal adjustment, saving valuable time and resources in system development. In a similar manner, our approach successfully applied a pre-existing model to control a previously untested system, enabling the adaptation of a validated model to new systems without the need to relearn the policy, thereby reducing the time and resources required to effectively train a policy. In conclusion, our research successfully addressed one of the critical challenges associated with the reinforcement learning and adaptive methods, thereby providing a robust and efficient solution to complex system control and optimization. In a practical test, our approach successfully controlled a real helicopter model, bringing us closer to efficiently utilize data-driven control in real-world applications, and marking a breakthrough milestone in data-driven control. Training a generative adversarial network often involves a high-dimensional, non-convex space search due to its advocate's nonlinear classification, often causing optimization difficulties. To address this challenge, we present relation GAN, a variant of traditional GAN that employs relation networks in its discriminator. This choice is motivated by relation networks' ability to reason about relationships between pairs of elements in their input, potentially enabling them to utilize higher dimensional input, such as feature maps, to make more informed decisions. Furthermore, we improve this relation GAN model by introducing a triplet loss into its training protocol. This combination of a relation network-based discriminator and enhanced training procedures enables the model to reason about the similarities and differences among a larger number of elements, resulting in improved training performance. Specifically, experiment results demonstrate that relation GAN outperforms its predecessors, including advanced variants like progressive GAN, in a variety of tasks. Furthermore, we reveal that its superior performance is largely due to its ability to reason about multiple reference points during training. Lastly, we exemplify the model's capability to reason about multiple reference points through a few key visualizations. This research contributes a method to tackle optimization challenges in high-dimensional spaces, such as training a GAN, by equipping the model with the ability to reason about relationships among sets of data. It also presents an efficient approach to leveraging this ability through clever utilization of a readily available deep learning framework. The research's findings validate that utilizing the reasoner's ability can greatly aid optimization, and confirm that utilizing multiple reference points can aid stability during training. Object Detection, a long-standing problem in Computer Vision, has received considerable attention recently, particularly on accelerating knowledge transfer from a limited number of annotated samples. This study enhances knowledge transfer by identifying a known object's category when provided with a sample image and a collection of labelled images. To accomplish this, it suggests a straightforward data augmentation approach for constructing numerous pseudo labels of bounding boxes from a limited set of annotated images. This technique is then tested and proven effective on the Open Vocabulary Object Detection task, significantly reducing computation time by 93% when compared to traditional methods of training from scratch. Moreover, the experiment's results show that with pseudo labels generated through a residual convolutional neural network, the accuracy of the Open Vocabulary Object Detection task can approach that achieved through full supervision, yielding an mAP of 52.3% compared to 51.9% under equal computation time conditions. Finally, the proposed method is found to outperform state-of-the-art models of Cross-View Retrieval and Open Vocabulary Object Detection benchmarks. The research code will be made available on the TerraFowl GitHub repository.

The concept of veracity in data is similar to its accuracy, but differs in how a dataset is classified as being correct. A dataset can be considered veracious when it is considered accurate yet inconsistent. In contrast, a non-veracious dataset is considered incorrect yet can be corrected. Inexact datasets can also be considered non-veracious. This area of study, veracity in data, is a relatively new and emerging field that focuses on the reliability of machine learning models and data quality. Recent studies have demonstrated that data inconsistencies can significantly impact model accuracy, pointing to the need for assessing model veracity instead. Data verification is essential for understanding a model's strengths and weaknesses, allowing for targeted data augmentation and variables optimization for this end. This work identifies key areas of investigation for veracity in data, outlining specific tasks and outlining the steps needed to develop datasets, models, and optimization techniques for this purpose. Furthermore, we explore tasks and methods associated with transformers and their corresponding adaptations in veracity in data. Our analysis investigates the need for a standardized metric that can gauge the veracity of both data and machine learning models. Ultimately, we examine existing research in veracity in data and highlight areas for further study.

This research aims to develop an advanced predictive framework for mortality models. Building on previous studies by complete life models, we expand our analysis to cover the entire life span from birth to complete life. Similar to actuarial work in the past, actuarial professionals currently rely on simplified assumptions such as constant population growth rates, non-fluctuating interest rates, and stable immigration levels. In contrast, this paper uses advanced econometric techniques to create a sophisticated model for forecasting mortality rates under the influence of various economic factors. Our model differs from earlier work such as that of Dahlberg and Sandstrom in that it incorporates simultaneous factor analysis to account for interactions between different factors and features a flexible pricing system that allows for variable government discount rates. Furthermore, this paper suggests a number of potential factors that could affect mortality and outlines a quantitative method for determining the mortality prediction interval. Additionally, we found that a model with a low number of common factors can produce more reliable outcomes than a model with individually calculated factor loadings. Our research found that combining economic variables can lead to a better representation of mortality trends than using demographic variables alone, with variables such as unemployment and inflation providing significant additional insight. Finally, as an application of our model, we used scenario analysis to simulate the effects of two economic crises on mortality and found that mortality outcomes depend heavily on the specific characteristics of the crisis. Our research systematically explores how multiple novel mechanisms affecting valley behavior in two-dimensional materials interact with existing processes, such as intravalley and intervalley friction, and linear and quadratic spin-scattering. These new interactions stem from the adaptation of molecular and metallic coupling mechanisms in two-dimensional materials. Among these new interactions, the ferroelectric mechanism has the lowest intensity, followed by the van der Waals mechanism, which has a comparable intensity to linear spin-scattering. The adaptation of a doping mechanism is notable for its high intensity, while the adaptation of a traditional Fröhlich mechanism is notable for its weak intensity. Notably, the cross-terms among these new and existing processes are negligible, suggesting they can be separately influenced. Furthermore, our analysis highlights the significant effects of the ferroelectric and doping mechanisms in valley Hall effects, causing increased conductivity along the edge, whereas the van der Waals and Fröhlich mechanisms lead to directional, diagonal, or minimal conductivity. The van der Waals and quadratic spin-scattering mechanisms, on the other hand, are associated with conductivity patterns that are far from diagonal. The interplay of these novel and existing valley coupling mechanisms offers vast possibilities to control valley states, which may be exploited in two-dimensional semi-conductor materials with ferroelectric or p-n junction layers. Additionally, the mechanisms could be controlled by doping or intentionally introduced as an intrinsic property through the placement of dopants within specific regions of the material. Valley control may also be achieved in two-dimensional materials with metal or molecular coupling mechanisms, which are less dependent on doping but more dependent on layer stacking, making them more fragile to environmental disturbances but also providing a higher degree of stability to valley states. The last part of the research demonstrates that the concept of intrinsic ferroelectricity may be combined with valley behavior in two-dimensional materials, resulting in a new category of materials referred to as ferroelectric valley couples. Auditing financial records is a crucial but labor-intensive process that is typically performed by human experts after which they synthesize their findings into a concise report. Due to the sheer volume of documents associated with financial transactions, both experts and non-experts face significant difficulties during the auditing process. One particular challenge arises when categorizing documents, which is equally crucial for both experts and non-experts. While financial transaction data can be effectively visualized through techniques like clustering and singular value decomposition, current methods are only suitable for data analysis and lack the ability to provide confidence intervals for categorization decisions. Therefore, a novel framework has been proposed that leverages formal concept analysis and Dempster-Shfer theory to categorize financial documents. Specifically, the framework starts by applying formal concept analysis to obtain an information concept space, before selecting the most relevant set of attributes for categorization and evaluating the uncertainty associated with each category using Dempster-Shfer theory. The framework's effectiveness has been validated through a case study involving a real-world dataset obtained from a Turkish company. Compared to existing methodologies, the framework has demonstrated superior results by accurately categorizing 90.0% of documents with a higher confidence level of 0.964, while also showcasing its adaptability using a second case study involving a dataset from a real-world forensic investigation. 

Key words: financial auditing, Dempster-Shafer theory, formal concept analysis, document processing, attribute selection, uncertainty measurement, logarithmically robust normalized framework.

To address reliability issues in Internet of Things devices, software updates have been proposed as an alternative to repairing individual components. However, these updates pose compatibility and security risks if not properly executed. Moreover, the current protocols largely ignore the complexities of large-scale network performance and choose a representative node for update purposes. Nonetheless, these updates can cause problems for other network devices as well. This research investigates the impact of Linux updates on a router's network, focusing on its ability to maintain connections with other nearby IoT devices, especially on the local mesh network of Luos operating at 2.4 GHz. The study's main objectives involve evaluating the performance of an IoT router after an update, comparing its functionality with the expected results after the update, and examining the effects of update mechanisms on the surrounding IoT network. To achieve this, a comprehensive experimental design was conducted, involving statistical analysis of three key performance indicators: data transmission speed, packet loss rate, and network cycle duration. The resulting data was verified by conducting 54 distinct updates in three different settings, mirroring the type of behavior expected from an auto-update mechanism. The results showed that while updates can cause initial difficulties for nearby IoT devices on the mesh network, these difficulties dissipate rapidly, returning to normal within a few minutes, and the router recovers efficiently from any disturbances it may encounter during the update process. Furthermore, the results revealed that the update mechanism itself, specifically the Drop Least Recently Used (DLRU) update mechanism, rather than the update itself, is the primary factor influencing the update process. The results have also shed light on the impact of update mechanisms on the surrounding IoT network, and it appears the update process is unaffected by the size of the surrounding network. The resulting work presents a new perspective on reliable large-scale wireless network performance, and it raises important considerations for the creation of dependable IoT firmware updates. The data collected during these experiments is also being made available to aid in achieving dependable and efficient large-scale wireless network performance. The code used for this project is also being made available to facilitate replication of the research's results. The study's findings have also inspired a new project focused on exploring efficient large-scale wireless network performance, which is being led by the study's researchers. The research's results have been successfully applied to various fields, including dependable IoT updates and efficient large-scale wireless network performance. This lack of analysis is concerning because quantum deep learning is now being explored as a potential enhancement to future AI systems. Our primary goal is to investigate the robustness of quantum deep learning models to universal perturbations. We achieved this goal by adapting a method originally designed for classical models, successfully demonstrating the existence of these perturbations in quantum scenarios as well. In addition, we found that the robustness threshold for quantum models generally matches that of their classical counterparts. Interestingly, our results also suggest that the same principles apply to universal instances, where the sample complexity of quantum and classical models converge in a broader sense. Finally, we found that manipulating quantum states through the application of unitary transformations can actually make quantum models more resistant to perturbations, an outcome that highlights the potential advantages of using universal perturbations in quantum systems. This study marks the first major investigation into the robustness of quantum machine learning models, emphasizing the value of further research in this area. We examine Steklov eigenvalues in nearly round domains of n-dimensional Euclidean space. Building on work by Betti, Blanchard and Pinsky, and Sha-Krause, we establish a detailed estimate of the asymptotic behavior of these eigenvalues as the domain approaches a sphere geometrically. This achievement is bolstered by a novel spectral stability theory for normal families of eigenvalues, complemented by an exhaustive analysis of normality criteria applicable to various functional classes, including analytic functions, bounded Calderon-Zygmund measures, and Lebesgue and Sobolev functions, all defined on the (n-1)-dimensional boundary of the described set. This theory has the added benefit of being applicable to nearly minimal surfaces as well as nearly Euclidean domains, while also leading to new findings regarding the Steklov eigenvalue problem. Specifically, we prove the Hilbert's 17th Problem for nearly Euclidean domains and provide new insights into the inverse problem of spectral theory in nearly Euclidean domains. These advances are further secured through the use of a convenient new functional that generalizes the average value operator, applicable to nearly Euclidean domains and (n-1)-dimensional boundaries, respectively. This is achieved through the fusion of classical ideas, including those presented in the works of Scheuer, with the principles of nonlinear functional analysis and, notably, Michael's compactness principle. Furthermore, we establish a distributional Steklov eigenvalue problem on the (n-1)-dimensional boundary of the described set and demonstrate its application to the nearly Euclidean case, thus expanding the existing theory of distributional eigenvalue problems by Fischer and Griebel. The novel contribution here is to relax a traditional assumption requiring the electric potential to be subharmonic, which is typically assumed in prior works. Instead, it is shown that when the potential has a suitable growth rate, perturbing the Vlasov-Poisson model results in well-posed solutions within bounded domains. Moreover, the obtained results can be applied to a broad classification of such modified models. The key strategy employed in this work is to develop and utilize certain estimates that rely on the maximum principle, combined with further generalizations of classical estimates. Ultimately, the results of this study are illustrated through two examples, namely the Vlasov-Poisson system itself and a model primarily studied in the context of planetary atmospheres, known as Rao and Tsipras' model. The latter is shown to be effectively reduced to the Vlasov-Poisson model. Furthermore, the study adds to the existing body of work focused on global analysis in various systems described by the Vlasov equation. A more reliable solution involves leveraging pre-trained language models to evaluate summaries via direct text comparison. We introduce SummScore, an English summarization assessment dataset that solely utilizes original articles and final summary scores provided by professional editors. Unlike other datasets, it excludes translated scores and focuses on the entire summary rather than separate components. A cross-encoder model is used to develop a two-part assessment metric. It first evaluates the coherence of the summary using an external knowledge graph to fill missing narrative gaps, and then gauges coherence and fluency via an ensemble of models. The conventional approach to 3D detection, where camera and LiDAR data are combined, is either to use a straightforward feature fusion or a more structured fusion through coordinate transformations and integrated representations. Although the latter method is considered superior due to its structured fusion, it poses significant difficulties in implementation and is often prone to errors. This research attempts to bridge this gap with BEVFusion, a simple yet powerful liDAR-camera fusion framework that selects the most relevant LiDAR features in relation to 2D bounding boxes directly from the LiDAR beam space, thereby avoiding the complexities associated with structured fusion approaches. By selecting only key features, BEVFusion accelerates computation by reducing from 30K to 64 Flops for car instances and facilitates training without LiDAR labels. Experimental results show that the model attains a mAP of 82.2% on Waymo Open Dataset, outperforming other comparable fusion approaches and highlighting its efficiency as the most straightforward and effective liDAR-camera fusion technique. The code for the model is available at https://github.com/rg212/BEVFusion.

This has largely been due to the predominantly one-frame-based approach taken in the field, where the temperature fluctuation is typically treated as passively adapting to the flow field. This one-frame approach simplifies the dynamic interaction between the temperature disturbance and the pressure-correlation term in the temperature equation, but is at odds with DNS data. The latter is known as a primary driving mechanism in atmospheric weather systems. Both types of disturbances are to be studied via a proposed thermal sub-filter stress term in the two-scale framework. The proposed method demonstrates particular adaptability in the zero-shot setting but delivers consistent enhancements in both settings. We also highlight the pre-training of neural models on vast graph datasets as a promising area for improvement. The advent of continuous learning neural networks has made possible the creation of autonomous driving systems that automatically adjust vehicle parameters to meet the latest safety standards. However, ensuring the accuracy of these networks for various situations is a challenging task due to the difficulty in evaluating their behavior across a wide range of scenarios. This problem is similar to assessing the behavior of a control system with unknown dynamics, where input outputs are observed without access to internal state information. This work introduces novel neural networks called Control Consistent Deep Networks that can learn a continuous safety-critical property known as control continuity. Essentially, this property ensures that adjusting a control's parameters within a certain range results in a stable and acceptable behavior. Control Consistent Deep Networks achieve this by integrating a dynamic function that simulates the system's state over time with a constraint that ensures the network's predicted outputs align with actual outputs under certain conditions. This allows the development of a validation tool to verify the control continuity property for any Control Consistent Deep Network through the analysis of a finite set of data collected from experiments. This validation demonstrates that adjusting the network's parameters within certain bounds always leads to a stable and acceptable behavior. The process is applied to a real-world scenario where a vehicle's steering and throttle parameters are adjusted to meet the latest safety standards while ensuring a control continuity property. This guarantees that the network's predictions during learning remain stable and accurate. Moreover, this research demonstrates that using a specific neural network known as Linear Gaussian State Space Singular Value Decomposition is an efficient method to simulate the system's state over time and ensure a control continuity property. Ultimately, this research provides tools to both create and validate neural networks for control systems that can be tested through simulation tools. This is particularly useful in cases where evaluating a system's behavior across a wide range of scenarios is difficult due to the presence of obstacles or risks to human safety in real-world environments. The problem of reconstructing missing data from tensor-composed images, such as those found in medical or hyperspectral imaging, is usually solved by decomposing the data into its constituent tensors. Two methods for achieving this compression are subset of features reconstruction and latent component reconstruction. However, these methods have their limitations. Subset of features reconstruction can handle high compression ratios, but its lack of contextual information hinders its performance. Latent component reconstruction, on the other other hand, yields improved results but with a limited number of possible substitutions. To address these challenges, this research introduces the Patch Tracking-based Streaming Tensor Loop Completion model, which applies iterative learning and patch tracking to enhance compression ratios and contextual information. Additionally, PT-STL can learn end-to-end and can be executed in real-time, making it suitable for real-time data recovery applications. By leveraging a vast collection of artificial and real-life datasets, this paper demonstrates PT-STL's ability to outperform competing methods across various testing conditions. Moreover, PT-STL is shown to successfully restore missing data in real-life applications such as super-resolution and denoising. To support and facilitate research using PT-STL, a companion repository has been developed, including source code, the dataset used in this research, and the pre-trained models. The underlying problem is formulated as an iterative process aimed at reaching a state where removing the nodes with the fewest degrees from the graph results in a maximum value for the sum of the products of incoming edge weights of the remaining nodes. The study introduces a concept known as BOLDE (Branching on Local Maximums of Edge-Weighted Centrality), a search-based technique that approximates this state. However, most animation tools display only the mesh, hiding the skeletal structure and limiting the ability to create detailed movements. To address this, we developed ANR - a system helping users create realistic animations on high-resolution avatars - by pairing a cutting-edge browser-based viewer with our advanced visualization tools. The advanced visuals include methods for displaying joints, skin weights, and geometric deformations, as well as automatic mesh splitting techniques to show each piece's contributions to the final image. Additionally, our system integrates tools for adjusting animations, attaching arbitrary objects to the model, and making automatic adjustments to improve visual quality. All this is achieved with a simple file format change, allowing users to create more sophisticated animations and accurately fine-tune the behavior of their avatars. The core innovation of ANR lies in its advanced visualization methods, which showcase the intricate details of animations not previously accessible to animators. As a result, ANR significantly aids animators in helping them understand how their animations work and how they are implemented, particularly when working with complex, heavily deforming models. Our capacity to understand and process visual information arises from 
the interplay between our innate visual capabilities and the experiences we've had 
in the world. These experiences, which shape our visual perceptions and abilities, 
can be categorized into those that occur naturally, like varying lighting conditions, 
and those that we've intentionally engineered, like the filters used in many image 
datasets. There's a notable disparity between how humans and machines are affected by 
these different types of experiences, which has significant implications for how we 
collect, label, and evaluate visual data. In this work, we delve into these disparities 
through a series of studies involving severe transformation of images across three key 
aspects: the patterns of variation in datasets and real-world datasets ($\mathcal{X}$), the 
accuracy of models trained on these datasets ($Acc(X)$), and the ease of use for human 
annotators ($HU(X)$). These investigations reveal that models trained on these datasets 
($T_{D} = \{X\}$) exhibit a notable disparity in their accuracy ($Acc(T_{D}(X))$) 
across naturally occurring and engineered datasets. Moreover, we find that models and 
human annotators prefer engineered datasets, which have been severely transformed in 
various ways, demonstrating a notable disparity in their preferences as well. These 
disparities highlight the need to understand and explore the differences between these 
datasets and their implications for the models, the humans, and the visualization tools 
we design. Ultimately, we conclude by considering the potential applications of 
these insights, which can lead to the development of new, diverse datasets that expand 
our visual knowledge and capabilities. These potential developments are the focus of 
our discussion in Section 7.3. The associated code for our studies can be found at 
https://github.com/asharaidi/severe-image-transforms. A video discussing our work 
can be accessed at https://vimeo.org/362265998. Its corresponding manuscript was 
published at the CVPR 2021 workshop on Understanding and Demonstrating Visual 
Biases.  In this work, we are exploring additional biases that are present within 
visually extended datasets, which have not been previously examined. The findings of 
our study, which identify preferences for severe image transforms that are 
visually-extended, shed new light on these biases and their potential impact on 
visually-biased models and interactions. Furthermore, we make the case that these 
biases can be mitigated

Transformers, the basis for contemporary text processing models, concentrate solely on surface patterns by incorporating all past language inputs, leading them to be ineffective at interpreting the meanings of infrequently used words. Cutting-edge language comprehension models, such as GPT-3, suffer from a similar shortcoming despite their exceptional fluency. They lack a separate component that evaluates the meaning of phrases. We have developed an innovative interpreter model called Universal Semantic Interpreter that operates independently of language generation. Its unique feature is the ability to infer unseen word meanings while maintaining accurate sentence comprehension. Our language-generation system, Lexicalized Choice Module, combines the interpreter with other skills to produce coherent and meaningful outputs with just a short training period. The results demonstrate that it surpasses performance of GPT-3 and other models in understanding and responding to complex, open-ended commands. Additionally, our findings highlight the significant reduction in inaccuracies resulting from the interpreter's ability to infer unseen word meanings. The full source code for these innovative models is now publicly accessible on the Gitee platform, facilitating integration with the GPT-3 model developed by OpenAI. Users can obtain the interpreter only by answering a few simple questions about each unusual word as it is used, a task far less difficult than the one required for training the GPT-3 model. This study presents an entirely new pathway for natural-language processing model development. The substantial source code is now publicly accessible on the Gitee platform.

We demonstrate that two continuous minimal actions of the infinite dihedral group on an infinite compact Hausdorff space can be uniquely defined if and only if they are orbitally equivalent. This criterion also applies to other virtually cyclic groups, such as the trivial extension of the integer group and the trivial extension of the modular group. Additionally, our findings lead to the discovery of distinct orbit equivalences for certain minimal flows associated with the integer group and the modular group. We further prove that continuous minimal actions of the integer group on a specific type of space are uniquely defined by their properties and that continuous minimal actions of the modular group on a certain type of space fall into distinct classes based on their properties. This reasoning relies on previous work by B. Weiss and the second author, as well as a recent paper by S. Gol\'ezar, B. Miller, and T. Tseng. Furthermore, our work reveals that continuous minimal actions of the integer group on a specific type of space exhibit rigidity, meaning their properties cannot be altered, and that continuous minimal actions of the modular group on a certain type of space fall into distinct classes based on their properties. This reasoning utilizes the theory of leaf spaces developed by E. Gottschalk and the space filling theory developed by T. Ellis. Finally, our work is extended to the general linear group and its various subgroups by combining our findings with a recent paper by A. T. Mattner.
