The internal diameter of a highly reflective curvilinear cavity mirror in a ring resonator significantly influences the number of longitudinal modes in a Kerr-lens mode-locked oscillator using a high-energy seed laser. Investigating the beam divergence and growth within the cavity is crucial to prevent the loss of longitudinal modes, which may lead to mode locking failure in systems requiring a high pulse energy and high repetition rates. We investigated the mode locking in a Kerr-lens oscillator with an apothem-based curvilinear mirror and observed that the loss can cause mode locking failure in systems with smaller internal diameters, ultimately influencing the achieved pulse energy. We solved the laser equation to determine the optimal mirror shape and calculated the optimal radius of curvature for various repetition rates of 50 to 200 Hz, providing a practical design method for high-energy oscillators. We verified our theoretical predictions through experimental comparisons of theoretical and experimental pulse energies at different repetition rates. The experiments showed a good agreement between predicted and experimental findings, demonstrating the effectiveness of the theoretical model. Furthermore, we verified that the optimal design rules could successfully trigger Kerr-lens mode locking in systems satisfying specific conditions. Finally, we obtained sub-30-femtosecond pulses from a sample with an apothem-based mirror of 1.7 mm in radius of curvature. The optimal design rules could successfully initiate mode locking in a wide range of operating conditions, ultimately leading to short pulse generation. Several FL variants have been explored to circumvent synchronization delays, model drift, and scalability limitations. This research examines two distinct frameworks—FleTL and ItsTL—both allowing devices to contribute at any moment without requiring global synchronization. FleTL utilizes a strategy to minimize feature distribution, yet this efficiency comes at the cost of increasing the model bias over time. In contrast, ItSTL employs inverse transformations for feature handling and model training, thereby achieving scalability and reduced communication demands. However, it introduces nonlinearity to the linear FL problem. This study compares the performance and scalability of FleTL and ItsTL against traditional synchronous FleML and synchronous linear models under varying parameters including the number of iterations, number of clients, and network bandwidth. Furthermore, this research proposes an asynchronous linear FL framework, AsyfleTL, which combines the communication efficiency of FleTL with minimal model bias. AsyfleTL achieves this goal by leveraging ring-based client updating, thereby reducing model bias and allowing for efficient parallel training without requiring global synchronization. A comprehensive ring-based framework, Ring-AsyfleTL, is also developed for nonlinear regression, enabling parallel model training for nonlinear regression without any synchronization delays. Moreover, this research conducts an empirical performance evaluation of Ring-AsyfleTL using AI-generated nonlinear regression datasets to determine its scalability and efficiency. The experimental results show that Ring-AsyfleTL attains a ring size of 81 and ring iterations of 13 before achieving feature dimension convergence, thereby establishing its efficiency and scalability. Several optimization techniques are also identified to further enhance the performance of Ring-AsyfleTL. For example, client pruning can accelerate convergence by reducing the number of clients participating in model updates. Similarly, leader replacement can improve performance by replacing the leader at regular intervals. Finally, dataset division can significantly expedite convergence by dividing the features into their natural groups. Consequently, this research effectively contributes to the expansion of asynchronous FL research in conjunction with parallel training for linear and nonlinear regression applications. Several experimental results that demonstrate the scalability and efficiency of the proposed frameworks are also presented. It also highlights SSNE's potential to leverage parallel processing due to its low computational complexity. As a result, SSNE serves as a scalable, storage-efficient solution for link prediction in various network types. This study proposes a novel stochastic model for the COVID-19 pandemic, incorporating a compartmental structure that reflects real-life infection dynamics, including partial immunity from previous infections. The model also accounts for asymmetrical disease transmission, varying infection risks across locations, and distinct recovery and mortality rates. In compensation for the model's complexity, its parameters are grounded in scientific research, ensuring accurate representation of COVID-19 infection patterns. Notably, our model predicts an inverse proportional relationship between infections and cases, aligning with findings presented in \cite{arino2021}. Furthermore, our analysis includes a realistic spatial distribution of infections within the United States, reflecting the rapid spread of the disease from highly infected locations. Building on this model, our simulations demonstrate the significant impact of rapid testing and contact tracing policies on reducing infection spread, and highlight the trade-offs between strict social distancing measures and potential infections resulting from each choice. Lastly, our emergency vaccination scenario illustrates the urgency and speed at which vaccine distribution can prevent a potential second wave of infections. As the world continues to recover from the pandemic, our research emphasizes the crucial role of public health policies in mitigating the spread of future infectious diseases. The findings presented here provide valuable insights for policymakers to make informed decisions and help prevent future outbreaks. A study is conducted on dynamic systems featuring Stick-slip behavior, specifically Stick-slip oscillations that arise in such systems due to a force imbalance which triggers a self-sustaining cycle of a stick phase followed by a slip phase. The stick-slip phenomenon is characterized by an increase in a particular energy metric, defined as the work done against friction, despite the existence of a more optimal, smoother motion trajectory. The research focuses on a class of feedback control strategies, specifically those regulated by diminishing gains, which have the potential to eliminate stick-slip oscillations and achieve a more efficient, converged state. It is observed through numerical simulations that, under certain conditions, the system can converge to a stick-slip state even when subjected to a diminishing gain feedback regulation, thus exhibiting destabilizing behavior. The reason behind this lies in the fact that a diminishing gain control only slows down but does not cease the occurrence of slip phases, ultimately triggering an self-sustaining cycle of a stick-slip behavior. The sticking behavior during the stick phase can inadvertently lower the value of the optimizing energy metric, which in turn renders the system susceptible to a rebound into a slip phase during the transition to a stick phase following the expiration of the stick phase time-duration. A comparative analysis with a class of exponential gain feedback controllers reveals that such an approach exhibits stick-slip-free behavior in multiple problem scenarios but runs the risk of triggering overly damped, oscillatory behavior upon transition out of a stick phase, which in turn can induce slip. The study ultimately seeks to illuminate the underlying dynamics responsible for the emergence of stick-slip oscillations in control systems and shed light on the conditions necessary for the successful application of a diminishing gain feedback regulation strategy in order to obtain Stick-slip-free behavior. The accompanying graphics and animations are used to clearly illustrate and visualize the dynamic behavior of these systems. The research further extends into a real-world application involving a piezoelectric material, which is subject to both a diminishing gain and an exponential gain feedback regulation in an effort to eliminate stick-slip oscillations and achieve a more efficient, converged state. The study ultimately reveals that a proper feedback control strategy holds the potential to modulate and ultimately eliminate the dynamic stick-slip oscillations present in such systems, which in turn can unlock novel applications for such systems due to their improved dynamical performance. The research ultimately seeks to improve our understanding of a crucial aspect of system behavior, which has significant real-world implications and applications. In recommender systems, users' interactions with products on platforms such as e-commerce websites and social media are sequential in nature. For instance, users might view a fashion retailer's website to explore dresses, but ultimately purchase a related accessory. This research proposes a novel approach called Latent User Purpose, where a user's objective in a sequence of interactions is modeled as a hidden intention. We've developed a training algorithm that learns to predict the purpose behind each user's sequence of interactions, and also demonstrates that incorporating purpose inference improves the quality of personalized recommendation lists. Specifically, our model outperforms a leading personalization tool, ItemKF, by approximately 10% in terms of ranking accuracy on a real-world dataset. Furthermore, our approach provides novel insights into users' objectives, revealing purpose categories such as discovering new items, browsing, or making a purchase. We've validated these insights through a qualitative analysis, and also shown that users with diverse demographic characteristics tend to distinct purpose distributions. The popularity of Digital Cryptocurrencies, like Bitcoin and Ethereum, has led to the emergence of Blockchain-based Distributed Exchanges as a decentralized trading platform. Traditionally, Exchange operations rely heavily on Market Makers, but we investigate a new model where CLOs can thrive without them. Our analysis reveals that profitability for Market Makers on conventional Exchanges is severely impacted by volatility, while on CLOs, it remains relatively stable. In response, we predict that Market Makers will shift towards trading on CLOs, which will lead to increased trading fees and attract more Liquidators to participate. Through complex mathematical analysis, we demonstrate that equilibrium prices on CLOs are more resilient to changes in Market Maker utility, thus offering a superior trading experience. Our findings confirm that CLOs can effectively support digital currency trading. Ultimately, our rigorous computational verification showcases the benefits of Blockchain-based Distributed Exchanges as a trading platform.

A new metric, the E-value, has been created to help quantify confidence in estimated odds ratios. The E-value provides an explicit measure of how sensitive an estimated odds ratio is to unobserved data. In this study, we introduce a novel approach to frame the query of how unobserved data affect an estimated odds ratio as a Bayesian question. To achieve this, we use the concept of posterior sensitivity, which represents the range of plausible values for an odds ratio's posterior interval following the addition of unobserved cases. We develop a simulation study to compare traditional and Bayesian approaches to assessing sensitivity, focusing on incomplete data scenarios, incomplete covariates, and incomplete matchings in pair-matching scenarios. The results show that Bayesian sensitivity assessment yields boundaries for sensitivity that closely align with Bayesian 95% credible intervals for odds ratios. Moreover, Bayesian sensitivity assessment offers advantages in terms of statistical efficiency in various data scenarios. In addition, we illustrate how to compute posterior sensitivity intervals in practice, and we demonstrate the applicability of our findings to matchiness assessment - a measure that indicates the degree of matchlessness - in pair-matching scenarios. The findings provide evidence that supporting unobserved data can significantly impact match quality, with unobserved data leading to decreased matchlessness. Finally, we illustrate the E-value in two real-world examples. The first example involves a relationship between smoking and cancer, based on data from the National Cancer Institute's Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results database. The second example involves a relationship between bike helmet use and likelihood of injury, based on data from the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration. In both instances, we compute the E-value before and after adjusting for confounding variables. To establish the reliability of our findings, we conduct simulations to determine the impact of unobserved data on estimated odds ratios. The results confirm that before adjustment, unobserved data can dramatically impact odds ratio estimates. In contrast, after adjustment, unobserved data have limited effect on odds ratio estimates. The findings underscore the importance of considering unobserved data in computational results, especially in scenarios where unobserved data and confounding variables intersect. To facilitate replication of our work, we have created an R-package to perform the computations and simulations described in this article. The package can be accessed at: <https://github.com/krizaj/ecomh/BayesSensitivityAssessment> (dissected into two separate R-packages: one for computation and one for simulation).}

Federated Learning (FL) is a standardized method for machine learning model development across diverse vehicle groups, utilizing an adaptive approach to achieve a workable equilibrium between cooperation and privacy protection. Despite this potential, FL is challenged by key concerns including non-authenticated data sharing, unfair distribution of computational resources, and sensitive information leaks. Notably, FL lacks a comprehensive framework for integrating IoV datasets, leading to a decline in model efficiency. To address such challenges, this research outlines a synergistic strategy for integrated IoV data sharing framework development, labeled FL-IoV. Moreover, this paper presents a framework outlining research directions for future FL-IV frameworks. For the past decade, deep learning models have significantly outperformed traditional methods in various DNA sequence prediction tasks. However, a significant challenge persists due to the vast amount of available DNA sequence data where comprehensive annotation is impractical. A new method, known as Clebsch canonization, has been proposed to represent Lie-Poisson systems on a level equivalent to symplectic systems. This method has already been applied to specific Lie-Poischon structures. We'll demonstrate how the canonization works for certain notable Lie-Poisson structures, such as those associated with multiboson systems, as well as Lie-Poisson structures connected to Toda and KdV equations. This process involves translating the associated phase space structures into equivalent forms over a parameter space with a symplectic form, which can be expressed in terms of the original Lie-Poisson structure variables. We will also explore the relationship between canonized forms and coadjoint orbits under this transformation. Furthermore, we will show that the Rydberg condition, applicable to the Toda and multiboson systems, results in a specific symmetry of the canonized form on the cotangent bundle of phase space. This symmetry corresponds to SO(2) which, in the original Lie-Poisson structure, acts as a Poisson symmetry. The new form also makes the Hamiltonian structure of the Toda equation over a torus fit for canonical transformation. This method has the additional benefit of providing a convenient way to compute Lie-Poisson integrals by translating the problem into a corresponding action integral on the cotangent bundle of parameter space, which is expressed as a symplectic integral. This method has been further applied to the case of two bosons in one space dimension, where we also discuss the relationship between the parameters and coordinates of the two spaces. We also derive a set of necessary conditions under which a similar translation can be achieved for arbitrary Lie-Poisson structures. This method has the broader implications of extending the Clebsch canonization to include not just Poisson systems but also noncommutative symplectic systems as well. It is anticipated that the canonization method may have applications in solving some of the outstanding challenges posed by the Madelung transformation. Moreover, in the main text, we provide a concise overview of key concepts and their practical applications as needed. This approach is utilized to obtain new energy estimates for the Navier-Stokes equations in three-dimensional compressible flow, with implications for low-frequency stability. Finally, we take into account the influence of system viscosity under general boundary conditions, which involves a novel dissipation-based potential function. This is inspired by prior work of Suleymanov relating conservation principles to boundary conditions in nonlinear dispersive PDEs. Moreover, we have formulated an algorithm for manually calculating $S$-matrices in a wide range of scenarios and outlined its potential practical applications. Furthermore, we have obtained an exact analytical expression for the $S$-matrix in a particular scenario and demonstrated its ability to correctly predict physical properties, including a correct treatment of thresholds, in addition to being unitary and analytic. Finally, we have discussed the theoretical implications resulting from the observed universal set of factors composing the $S$-matrix, with implications including a unified understanding of different effective theories and possible experimental signatures of physics beyond the standard model, such as in two-body interactions involving an odd number of hadrons. Various research studies have tackled this issue by modifying existing models to produce understandable insights. A few studies have examined the utility of explanatory state-of-the-art models in improving user satisfaction. Notably, missing research exists on evaluating these models' explanations from a user perspective during interaction. This research investigates the user experience aspects of local interpretable model-agnostic explanations in active learning, specifically focusing on consistency and clarity. User studies revealed preferences for smoother transitions between base models and explanation aids, and users prefer explanations that align with their original preferences. User perceptions of the user-friendly and informative nature of the explanations revealed low levels of satisfaction. Finally, user satisfaction increased when users could tailor explanation aids to their individual preferences, demonstrating the potential of personalized user experience to enhance the utility of explanatory models in active learning. Past research mostly focused on how to use a validation method, while we examine the circumstances in which it should be utilized. The supposed benefits of verifying labels within a nearby area are often assumed, but we show through simple arguments that they do not exist under specific scenarios. We then create computational tools to demonstrate the conditions in which the validation method is beneficial to use. We also compare the effectiveness of the validation method with alternative approaches under different attack conditions. The findings from this study can inform the development of future methods that use a nearby area to validate the labels provided by a teacher. The validation method we created does not offer improved robustness than using no verification at all, except when the corruption of model training labels is very severe and limited to specific data points. When the corruption is generally applied to all data points or was moderately severe and widespread, we found that it actually performed worse than not using it. However, the validation method did provide improved robustness than using no verification when the corruption was very severe but confined to specific data points. This paper builds upon that finding by developing a more advanced, triangular matrix variant of the matrix's bidiagonal structure, allowing for an even quicker computation at $O(N/2)$. Furthermore, we present a new, exact method for computing the optimal transport solution based on a novel $O(N)$ algorithm that calculates the inverse of a diagonal matrix and performs weighted sum operations in parallel. This method shows improved performance in numerical tests, demonstrating faster computation times than the original BFGS method. Examples illustrate the effectiveness of this approach in the context of real-world image matching problems. As an added benefit, we note that many widely-used algorithms, including Cholesky, QR, and LU methods, can be applied to a matrix's upper or lower triangular form but would introduce quadratic complexity. This constraint means that while these methods can produce precise solutions, they are outperformed by our proposed $O(N)$ algorithm, which achieves this in a more efficient manner. Consequently, we recommend the application of our method to scenarios involving large-scale matrices with sparse, bidiagonal, or triangular structures in the near future. Finally, from a theoretical perspective, we have developed a general framework for applying the matrix inverse to a set of elements and derived our formula by analyzing the computational complexity of this method, in addition to validating key properties relevant to the optimal transport context. This work presents a significant contribution to the field of optimal transport by providing a precise numerical solution to a problem long approached iteratively by existing algorithms. The interaction between externally applied electromagnetic fields and the polarizable medium produces a field that couples to the medium's induced currents, causing energy transfer from the external field. When an external current is introduced, this energy transfer generates a force that opposes the current's motion, a phenomenon we refer to as radiation reaction drag. We explore damped oscillations in the presence of radiation reaction drag and provide a corresponding drag coefficient. To achieve reliable, quantum-resistant processing of information, it's crucial to understand charge tunneling between different parts when using quantum dots in conjunction with superconducting electronics. A new method has been developed to detect this interaction through gate sensing. By employing this detection approach, the authors were able to identify distinct tunneling mechanisms, including a particular tunneling process that occurs between a quantum dot, a superconducting island, and a quantum point contact. Key indicators, such as a double peak in conductivity and specific charge states, confirm these interactions. Furthermore, the authors discovered that certain charge states could persist for several seconds due to a particular tunneling process, which has the potential to be used in a new type of quantum memory. Overall, the authors demonstrate the effectiveness of gate sensing in identifying complex interactions in hybrid electronic systems and outline a method to utilize these interactions in real-world quantum devices. Additionally, the authors specify requirements for detecting certain tunneling processes, suggesting this approach could be applied to a wide range of electronic systems that rely on quantum mechanics, such as spintronics and topological electronics. Ultimately, the authors recognize that identifying and manipulating individual electrons in these systems remains a significant challenge. A new experimental protocol is proposed to overcome this limitation by observing the influence of individual electrons in these systems. A specific indicator, such as a distinct peak in conductivity when one electron switches states, can confirm the presence of individual electrons. Generating unlimited, realistic 3D views of objects from a single perspective is crucial for various computer vision tasks. Current models are often limited by their inability to understand object shapes and their reliance on semi-supervised training, which hinders their scalability and precision. To overcome these limitations, we have developed a conditional diffusion model called "DiffDreamer," which can learn and generate high-quality, multi-angle images from a single view. By integrating a state-of-the-art shape completion module, our pipeline can tackle a challenging shape-based generation task. Our proposed model was evaluated using real-world datasets such as ShapeNet and IKEA, and our results demonstrate its superior performance compared to existing techniques. Additionally, our comprehensive ablation experiments highlight the significance of individual contributions to DiffDreamer's success. Our findings indicate that model precision can be further improved by refining the training dataset. To facilitate future research, we have made our source code and datasets available for download. Moreover, our results show promising applications of DiffDreamer, including view generation, perspective shape completion, and manipulating viewpoint-dependent visual properties. Ultimately, our results suggest that integrating a shape completion module with a generative model can effectively address the challenge of generating multiple, realistic views from a single perspective. We propose a new approach to defining open maps and directed spaces. A particular property, (o-d) directedness, is associated with every topological space and reflects its capacity for ordered directions. To investigate its characteristics, we examine the sets of open maps and associate them with specific algebraic structures, namely upper si-groups. Through this connection, we demonstrate the (o-d) direction has analogous properties to dimension. Past climate conditions, known as hothouse climates, were significantly warmer than the current levels and existed in the Earth's history. Researchers have been unable to rule out the possibility that changes in Earth's rotation rate, resulting from variations of the length of a day, might have contributed to this phenomenon. To better understand this hypothesis, scientists used computer models to simulate intense precipitation and atmospheric conditions during these ancient climates. The simulations, conducted over nearly two years, revealed large discrepancies between simulated and non-synthetic day lengths, demonstrating a need for much longer computational times to accurately assess the role of day-length changes in these ancient climates. Moreover, calculations in a controlled environment showed that weaker rainfall patterns and lower atmospheric pressures prevailed when the length of a day was increasing, and that high precipitation rates and pressures were more likely when the length of a day was decreasing. It is thus proposed that decreases in the length of a day could have contributed to stronger atmospheric patterns and increased precipitation in low-latitude regions during ancient hothouse climates. It is also suggested that differences in the distribution of precipitation on larger scales might have resulted from differences in atmospheric waves, atmospheric pressure patterns, and atmospheric wave dynamics, leading to increased precipitation in ancient hothouse climates. Finally, it is noted that significant fluctuations in sea surface temperatures and atmospheric wave dynamics across various locations could have contributed to these precipitation patterns, resulting in desert formations in certain areas. Researchers recommend extending simulations to at least a dozen years to accurately assess the role of day-length changes in these precipitation patterns and developing more precise metrics to evaluate precipitation characteristics. The development of a more sophisticated metric, known as ``hot-house factor'', that can capture the decline in atmospheric pressure and increase in precipitation across low-latitude regions during these ancient climates may aid in its implementation. Such a metric could potentially be applied not only to hothouse climates but also to other high-pressure climate conditions. Researchers propose conducting simulations over a range of lengths representing increasing and decreasing day lengths and using a more advanced version of this pressure metric in place of the non-biased pressure-only reconstruction method of the simulation data. A combination of the length of a day (-0.5 to 0.5 days) and atmospheric wave dynamics over a 12-year period might help to accurately assess the role of day-length changes in these precipitation patterns. Researchers recommend developing a more comprehensive theory of precipitation patterns, describing the evolution of precipitation patterns over a 12-year period. A general formula for the characteristic polynomial of the transition probability matrix associated with a random walk on a graph is derived. The proof utilizes a connection between the matrix and its associated Laplacian, which is expressed in terms of the graph's edge connections. This relationship is further generalized to any finite group of transformations acting on a finite set. The derived formula admits multiple interpretations and can serve as a tool for analyzing random walk-related questions on graphs. The discussion includes an examination of random walk characteristics on specific graph types, such as cycles, prisms, and torus-based graphs. Additionally, a related theorem regarding the characteristic polynomial of a permutation matrix is also introduced. The presented material primarily focuses on understanding random walks from a graph theory perspective, which is a key area of research in both probability theory and graph theory. The work aims to contribute new methods for analyzing random walks, which are often employed in various fields. The presented concept may also find applications in other areas involving groups of transformations acting on spaces. Ultimately, the work touches on the intersection between graph theory and group theory, which are two areas of study where the concept may have a lasting impact. The presentation is accompanied by a collection of graphical illustrations depicting the associated concepts. The Derivation of a Characteristic Polynomial for the Transition Probability Matrix of a Random Walk on a Graph, while being a novel contribution, builds upon previous works, such as those by Diaconis and Isler, and Petersen, which studied the characteristic polynomials of permutation matrices in relation to character theory. The characteristic polynomial derived in this context can be used to identify the degree and locations of zeros for the transition probability matrix associated with a random walk on a graph, which aligns with the findings of other relevant studies, such as those by Godsil and McKay, that focused on the characteristic polynomials of Seidel matrices. We introduce a new logic system by building upon HOL's type theory, incorporating a theory of infinite durations and utilising a countable ordinal to represent time. A timed relation's definition comprises two parts: its instantaneous application for a given duration and a recursively defined sequence of subsequent applications. These definitions are expanded into a new axiom set, enabling expressions to be equated based on their sequential values. We detail a method for proving the fixed-point theorem, establishing the validity of the recursive definition concept, as well as discuss the definition's limitations, specifically its inapplicability to non-monotonic functions. Furthermore, we demonstrate through examples, including a situationally-controlled speaker, how this framework can be applied. Ultimately, we examine the potential integration of a theory of infinite durations with existing theories involving real numbers. -

This discovery suggests that those Weyl points survive the charge modulation as protected, in-gap states. We consider a distributed optimization setting, where multiple agents collaborate to find a parameter $\theta$ that minimizes a global objective function, composed of individual, non-smooth, and convex functions $\mathcal{F}_i(\theta)$. Each agent has access only to its local function $\mathcal{F}_i$ and lacks access to other functions or communication with other agents. A stochastic Newton method is proposed to generate randomized parameter samples $\theta_i$ based on $\theta$, by utilizing single gradient measurements at each $\theta_i$. As the number of measurements $n$ grows, the proposed method is shown to converge to the optimal $\theta$ with a rate of $O(\log n / n)$. This convergence rate is similar to that of a stochastic Newton method for single-agent optimization, using $n$ measurements, and much better than current distributed methods which have a convergence rate of $O(1/n)$. Numerical examples demonstrate the proposed method to be more than five times faster than the best existing distributed algorithm at finding the optimal $\theta$. In the pursuit of detecting neutrino interactions with low recoil momentum, specialized chambers known as gas time projection chambers are being explored. They offer the potential to accurately reconstruct neutrino energies and orientations thanks to their ability to record three-dimensional gas particle trajectories. Nonetheless, distinguishing between ionization signals from the same pair of electrons poses a significant challenge during data analysis. Various studies have shown that using specific properties of ionization signals can enable the detection of recoil directions. In our study focused on STAPES, a TPC concept designed to be a high-recoil-sensitivity device, we identified several signal characteristics that could serve as indicators of recoil detection. These factors include the spatial correlation between two detected photons within a single read-out cell, the distance between the two photons, and the angle between the trajectories of the two photons. Additionally, we found that utilizing the quadrature of photon distances presents clear advantages in distinguishing overlapping photons in contrast to a simple pair-identification method. Moreover, we observed that utilizing the full three-dimensional path length for measuring the correlation between photons shows the greatest distinction in comparison to earlier approaches. Our analysis was based on simulated data obtained from simulations of $6.8$ MeV $\nu_e$ interactions on a $^4$He target, where the reconstructed quadrature of photon distances displayed an impressive $70\%$ improvement relative to a simple pair-identification method. Furthermore, incorporating the angle between the trajectories of the two photons, referred to as the Cosine Method, resulted in a substantial improvement of $84\%$ from the basic approach. These findings have also been compared with the results from the existing TPC technologies. It is our hope that these research outcomes will contribute toward establishing a comprehensive understanding of detection processes in TPCs and create a pathway for achieving high-precision measurements in areas such as neutrino-nucleus scattering, where precise recoil detection is essential. As robots increasingly co-work with humans in environments they share, developing clear guidelines for their interactions becomes a critical concern. Effective communication among these collaborators depends on understanding each other's intentions and expectations, particularly in navigating through the same physical space. We investigated how human-robot interactions can be improved in a shared environment through the optimization of robot trajectory planning, incorporating validated social norms into a decision-making process. By leveraging a diverse range of starting points and examining within-subjects variations in trial data, we discovered that introducing social norms led to more concurrent and cooperative behavior from humans, even when the robot was not entirely informed about its surroundings. The results demonstrate that incorporating robot standards in autonomous decision-making can lead to more harmonious and productive interaction. We observed notable improvements, for example, the robot successfully bypassed obstacles in approximately 57% of cases and received clearer paths from humans in about 33% of instances. Interestingly, while human-robot coordination improved, the benefit of shared knowledge for the robot did not have a substantial effect on performance. These outcomes suggest that incorporating robot standards in autonomous decision-making can boost collaboration, even in cases where the robot is not entirely informed. Firstly, we aim to reconstruct the material-independent x-ray attenuation coefficients of a scene. Secondly, we aim to detect the presence of multiple materials in the scene. Finally, we aim to clean up signal noise from sensors with unknown characteristics. To tackle these challenges, a novel optimization-based algorithm is introduced, which can be viewed as an extension of the well-established Feldkamp-Davis-Kress (FKD) algorithm. By formulating the FKD algorithm to be more suitable for polyenergetic beams while incorporating variational regularization, our approach yields a significant improvement. Furthermore, it was found that incorporating sensor denoising and material decomposition processes can greatly enhance the performance of the optimization-based algorithm. Current research on Contextual Named Entity Retrieval (CNER) often relies on fully-fledged contextualized language models to create and train neural ranking models, utilizing entire context passages and query terms to predict the most relevant entity. Yet, interactions between terms in the context are frequently lacking in this approach, and the computationally expensive training of full-context ranking models is often restricted to a subset of context-data pairs. To enhance CNER performance while mitigating training costs, our proposed Term Relevance Response model ranks entire entities based solely on the most relevant term-context connections. By using a query term's word and context vectors, a learned head vector helps to pinpoint key entities in the context, and the rest of the vector is used to determine the most connected head vectors. Experiments on standard test collections reveal a notable improvement in performance over existing state-of-the-art methods, along with substantial reductions in training costs. Further analysis using an analysis tool reveals nearly all of our rankings were correct, indicating vast potential for further research in leveraging term-context connections to enhance CNER. Interactive visualizations are a powerful tool for exploring links between data changes over time, such as how university applicants' scores correlate throughout their high school years. While simple time series data displaying a single variable's changes over time can be engaging when viewed, comparable visualizations for data with multiple variables lack a clear, overall pattern, making them hard to decipher. Our research focuses on developing user interfaces to facilitate data exploration in such cases, using simulated datasets that mimic real-world applications like university admissions and health monitoring. Our findings indicate that linking associated values to time series data and highlighting datasets with substantial changes are key engagement factors. Building on these discoveries, we created OntoTS, a comprehensive visualization display that links related datasets and highlights contrasting datasets with large value changes for each variable. In a detailed user study, we found users worked more efficiently and efficiently with OntoTS, produced better outcomes, and reported higher levels of engagement than with comparative tools. Ultimately, the design principles behind OntoTS have the potential to significantly enhance user experiences when working with multivariate time series and longitudinal data analysis. Personalized medicine seeks to develop tailored treatments by considering patients' unique characteristics derived from Electronic Health Records. However, current methods struggle to account for the interconnected nature of these records. By applying graph neural networks and leveraging the concept of resemblance, this research tackles the issue of propagating patient similarities through the graph. The proposed Heterogeneous Resemblance Graph Neural Network integrates a novel notion of resemblance based on edge weights and a message-passing algorithm to aggregate node similarities. The model is trained to maximize a global similarity score, and its effectiveness is evaluated using time-series and quantitive EHRC data. The results reveal the benefits of the proposed approach, and when combined with modern black-box transfer learning, state-of-the-art evaluations are achieved on three benchmark datasets. Moreover, a method for graph node prediction is developed, and when applied to EHR data, a substantial 89% of predictions are accurate. The proposed method significantly outperforms existing deep learning models, indicating its potential as a new standard approach for EHR analysis with graph neural networks. The study's findings and code are available on GitHub, and the models' performances are hosted on Test-Time Training platforms. Utilizing a search algorithm inspired by Google's PageRank concept, we integrate and weight different documentation sources to refine the specifications. By enhancing specification clarity, our approach enables better understanding of the code structure, searchability of specifications, and increased onboarding efficiency. Our research reveals that current specification extraction methods fail to adequately utilize the search algorithm to refine specifications and fall short in providing redundant specifications. This research proposal focuses on optimizing a wireless network's energy efficiency (EE) by incorporating network coding (NC) techniques. To achieve this goal, we propose a joint optimization framework that combines relay activation and power allocation, formulated as a maximization of the union of each node's minimum received signal-to-noise power to any other node. To tackle this complex optimization problem, we suggest two simplified and tractable solutions. The first approach directly optimizes the scheduled relay network, while the second utilizes a two-stage decomposition strategy, decomposing the problem into two sub-optimization tasks. The first task involves finding the optimal channel assignment, solved through a simple iterative method, and the second task optimizes the allocated power. Both proposed solutions aim to balance quality of service and EE for wireless relay networks, with simulations showing promising results for networks of various topologies and sizes. Furthermore, the simulations indicate that compared to traditional uncoded and half-duplex systems, the suggested solutions yield significant gains in EE of up to 44% and 30% respectively, while maintaining a high sum rate ratio of 0.85. A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed for describing the electronic properties of magnetic impurities in heavy fermion superconductors, and this framework is based on the extended Jablonski model. Within this framework, the transition temperatures for topological superconductivity can be calculated directly from the exchange coupling strength between the impurity and conduction electrons. This theoretical framework has been employed to investigate the superconducting state surrounding an Mn atom and various clusters formed from Mn atoms bound to the Nb(110) surface. These clusters examined in this study consisted of corrona structures containing one, two, three, and six covalent bonds with the surface, respectively. The theoretical framework predicted that an Mn atom alone would initiate topological superconductivity with a wide temperature range for its Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states, while clusters forming a mixture of topological and non-topological Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states were found. Furthermore, it was determined that an Mn atom that forms a six-covalent bond with the Nb(110) surface would exhibit no Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states within the superconducting state. These predictions provide a basis for experimenting on the Nb(110) surface using scanning tunneling spectroscopy, particularly on various structures formed from a single Mn atom, resulting in distinct differences between the behavior of an individual Mn atom and clusters consisting of multiple bonds with the surface. This study has successfully applied a first principles theoretical framework to investigate the electronic properties of magnetic impurities in heavy fermion superconductors, resulting in a unique arrangement where an individual impurity controls the onset of topological superconductivity within its surroundings. This theoretical framework is capable of addressing a wide array of magnetic impurities, including those obtained from deposition, segregation, or intercalation, and these impurities can adopt a variety of magnetic and non-magnetic configurations within the superconducting state. Therefore, experimental investigations of transition temperatures for topological superconductivity, as predicted by this theoretical framework, could serve as a quantitative measure to assess the strength of exchange coupling between impurities and conduction electrons. The main goal of mobile robot localization is to accurately determine a robot's position and orientation based on the characteristics of a surrounding environment. In general, a specific algorithm is used to localize the robot once it has mapped out a local area. Localization can be enhanced by incorporating an appropriate strategy for identifying comparable maps. Comparing maps involves identifying similarities between a reference map and a map created by the robot in real-time, typically done using keypoint-based or keypoint-free methods that localize the robot by breaking down a map into its fundamental geographical components. Nevertheless, similarities in map characteristics can be distorted due to factors such as uneven terrain, obstacles, or changes in a scene's appearance. Moreover, similarities based on appearance can often times be misleading, leading to inaccurate localizations, particularly in unorganized structures. This research aims to reduce the bias in appearance-based distribution-to-distribution map matching by utilizing supervised deep neural networks to discover regular patterns in a map's geometric structure, thereby allowing the accurate localization of a robot's location and orientation. The proposed approach uses a proven geometric structure-based map matching strategy that localizes the robot once it has created a reference distribution. By doing so, it can reduce the impact of factors such as changes in a scene's appearance and sensor distortions. The method does not require the synchronization of the robot's movement and instead can quickly identify relevant map characteristics when inputting an image in real-time. You can view a live demonstration of the method's performance here. The experiment revealed that the proposed algorithm successfully reduces the impact of factors such as changes in a scene's appearance and sensor distortions, thereby allowing the accurate localization of a robot's location and orientation. Deep neural networks (DNNs) have been widely using in communication systems for automatic modulation classification. However, such systems can be easily hacked by adversarial attacks, which are specially designed inputs that can trigger a desired output from the network. Virtually constructed attacks can be generated through gradient-based optimization methods by manipulating the network's input to maximize the likelihood of an incorrect classification result. Current defensive methods like adversarial training and noise augmentation have shown some level of success; however, their performance is yet to be verified against virtually constructed attacks. This study introduces a novel training approach called adversarial training with virtually constructed attacks (ATVCA) that trains communication DNNs using virtually constructed attacks as labels to counter such attacks. Our results indicate that ATVCA offers enhanced resistance to virtually constructed attacks compared to current defensive methods. In addition, a blend of ATVCA with adversarial training and noise augmentation has been proposed to improve the robustness of communication DNNs against adversarial attacks. Our experiments confirm the efficacy of this blended approach in enhancing the robustness of communication DNNs against virtually constructed attacks. Moreover, the underlying reason behind the success of ATVCA has been studied, revealing that clean virtual attacks can effectively induce robust features in the form of phase features. These robust features demonstrate a high level of resistance to various types of attacks, which is the primary reason behind the success of ATVCA. Leveraging these robust features, a robust knowledge-based classifier has been proposed, which achieves excellent performance even when trained with limited data. This approach has the potential to contribute to the development of more secure and reliable communication systems in the future. The distinction between contrasting concepts is the foundation of categorization and the source of meaning for opposites. An individual's thoughts can shift between conflicting ideas, and cultures divide people into distinct groups. Research focused on explicit categorizations, like "good vs. bad," has revealed widespread practices of binary classification everywhere. An initial study discovered an unusual, inverted relationship between the magnitude of contrasts in language and the complexity of cognitive processes involved in categorizing them. Subsequent investigations replicated these results, connecting it to an underlying psychological mechanism. An interim analysis revealed that this effect is likely an innate aspect of human thought. An international study covering multiple cultures confirmed that the phenomenon of bipolar contrasts exists across diverse cultures, albeit in contexts with lower cognitive complexity. Additional data revealed that the inverse relationship between contrast magnitude and categorization difficulty is consistent but not exclusive to bipolar contrasts. An examination of words associated with large-contrast words in web content, web search, and Twitter discussions during controversies provided a possible explanation for the effect. Data from Google Trends also supported the theory that the inverse relationship is linked to the strength of associations between words. Ultimately, these findings highlight a complex interplay between language, thought, and categorization.

A trustworthy artificial intelligence must recognize and admit its own shortcomings.  Unfortunately, there has not been much progress in detecting errors that an AI makes in its own decision-making process.  We introduce a set of algorithms that can identify and correct the AI's mistakes in dynamic systems, such as three different models of chaotic systems, by comparing its predictions to those of more accurate models.  These algorithms are based on a method to find approximate solutions of complex mathematical problems involving nonlinear functions, called primal-dual dynamics, and can learn from imperfect models and correct its own errors based only on its own predictions and the principles of how the world works.  We demonstrate that our algorithm is effective in correcting the AI's mistakes in three different models of chaotic systems, including a model of the non-tree interaction dynamics between three particles, a model of simple flow in a pipe with varying width, and a model of chemotaxis in single cell organisms.  These results show that a machine capable of learning can not only accurately predict outcomes in its decision-making process, but also recognize and admit its own shortcomings through an independent investigation of its own predictions and the principles of how the world works.  Our work utilizes tools from nonlinear control theory, dynamical systems, and machine learning, and offers a perspective on the relationship between artificial intelligence and human intelligence.  Since the approach relies on prior knowledge of how the world works, it is more useful for problems in science and engineering than for problems in more abstract domains such as playing chess.  We also describe why our approach is more suitable for solving these types of problems.  We finally identify the limitations of our algorithm and propose a series of research directions for detecting errors that an AI makes in its own decision-making process.  Our goal is to establish a trustful artificial intelligence that acknowledges and admits its own shortcomings.  Although acknowledging one's own shortcomings is easier said than done, we have made progress in this direction through the work described in this thesis.  This includes developing several approaches for detecting errors that an AI makes in its own decision-making process and proposing several research directions to further advance in this direction until we achieve a machine capable of learning that understands its own limitations. We have conducted a study of IRDCs, focusing on dynamics through Ammonia and CS observations. One of the studied clouds, named the Dragon, which is located at a distance of 4.4 kpc, revealed a primary kinematic class and its properties. According to our findings, this IRDC is moving in the plane of the sky with velocities of approximately 0.5 to 0.7 km/s. However, unlike other core types observed, the central portion of the Dragon IRDC is contracting at an average rate of 8x10^-5 km/s/yr. One possible explanation for this distinction is the presence of a heat source within the core, which is likely to be a forming protostar. Our analysis of hydrogenated carbon chain molecules, such as CH4 and CH3CN, along with ammonia, revealed elevated levels in the core's central area, suggesting a novel tool for identifying core dynamics. One proposed theory states that the formation of massive stars begins with hot cores originating from low-mass protostars that activate complex chemistry, whereas another possibility exists that these cores arise from more massive, evolved star forms. Our research provides additional support for the former protostar theory by presenting observational data on core dynamics. One emerging finding from our study is the discovery that the outer, visible portion of the Dragon IRDC is actually decreasing in size over time. One possible explanation for this phenomenon is the presence of an ionized wind from a nearby source, one candidate being a 30 solar mass protostar located approximately 1 arcminute from the core's center. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of monitoring core size changes as a method for assessing external influences. A popular alternative to explain small-scale discrepancies in the cosmic universe has arisen: Primordial Black Holes as dark matter. To make a definitive assessment, extensive research must be conducted into a variety of physical processes involving the formation of these black holes. Due to the unique nature of these objects, where general relativity exceeds classical physics, calculations require a deep understanding of relativistic astrophysical processes. We present an updated suite of tools, called PopSyCLE, designed to model PBHs within a cosmological framework, allowing for PBHs to be simulated from formation up to their study at the present time. Our toolkit can be used to analyze a variety of formation mechanisms, even those yet to be confirmed by theory or observation. This study develops a new, mathematically formulated theory for processing rejection and applies it to training a language model to avoid inappropriate outputs. Experiments with rejection-related and depression-related text show improved performance of the developed model, and its results are comparable to those of top-performing transformer models. Additionally, the model's token embeddings exhibit a clear negative orientation, indicating a preference for distancing oneself. Furthermore, the model's ability to recognize depression-related text surpasses that of leading language models, and its performance on depression recognition tasks is enhanced by 43.6% relative to its baseline training outcome. The model's success is rooted in its ability to understand rejection concepts and utilize them effectively. Finally, the research highlights potential ways to improve transformer-based language models for healthy and healthy-like language generation. In neighboring words within a sentence, there's a hidden focus that discloses the meaning. By unlocking these neighboring word relationships, we can predict the focus of earlier generated parts of a sentence, allowing us to influence the translation in a more informed way. This insight is the foundation upon which a novel system, called look-ahead focus, is built. This system pinpoints the meaning focus of the already translated portion of a sentence to assist in translating the remainder. The system relies on an additional representation to capture focus, embedded within the neural machine translation model. The system's versatility makes it compatible with nearly any neural machine translation approach. The system's efficacy is demonstrated using two prominent approaches: Transformer-Attention for English to German translation and Luong for English to Finnish translation. By looking ahead to earlier parts of the sentence, the system refines the translation focus, ultimately lowering your translation costs by 6.6 mule translations (with an improvement from cost 42.8 to 36.9). The system also yields a 0.64 bits per word increase in compression and reduces translation latency by boosting word generation per episode from 7 to 15. Following the release of our work's implementation on GitHub, the system's look-ahead component has been integrated into the Marian neural machine translation toolchain. As a result, various subsequent research studies have been conducted that leverage this system. The most pertinent studies involve Translation Graph Explorer, Focus-based Transformer, and Iterative Refocus, all of which build upon the look-ahead component as their foundational base. Specifically, the paper examines the connection between fixed points and solutions to the equilibrium problem under certain conditions, and it also provides examples of applications to illustrate its theoretical findings. Furthermore, the proof techniques employed in this paper involve properties of retracts and metric projections, as well as the concept of prox-regular sets, along with an interpretation of iterative algorithms as nonexpansive mappings. To that end, the paper views iterative algorithms applied to the equilibrium problem as a nonexpansive operator problem, rather than merely iterative. The addition of some new properties to prox-regular sets enables the extension of theoretical findings to the case where only a subset of data is perfectly suited for the equilibrium problem. The debate on turbulent effects influencing magnetic activity in the Sun and stars persists. The mean-field theory provides a widely applied framework to link these effects to fundamental magnetohydrodynamic processes, although its limitations need to be acknowledged. Our study utilizes a global mean-field model for convective dynamos in stars and planets, demonstrating that incorporating the complete spectrum of turbulent effects, including higher-order and time-dependent mechanisms, is necessary to generate magnetic fields consistent with observed and astronomical results. By comparing models with and without these effects, we determine that incorporating radial diffusion and non-local transport mechanisms, accompanied by helicity reversal, produces magnetic fields indistinguishable from those generated within global 3D simulations. The importance of considering all turbulent effects in theoretical frameworks and astrophysical star and planet studies is accordingly emphasized. 

Results are also presented from additional simulations investigating the effects of turbulent forces in global dynamos, which reinforce the notion that incorporating the full spectrum of turbulent effects is essential for achieving field morphological agreement with observations of the Sun, Earth, and other planets. 

Finally, a discussion of the astrophysical star and planet magnetic field properties obtained from global simulations, with and without the incorporation of a prescribed time-dependent helicity parameter, highlights the significant influence of turbulent forces on these magnetic fields and their dissipation times. 

The investigation reveals an intriguing correlation between the global energy proxy and magnetic energy in global simulations, which suggests an intriguing possibility that incorporating non-local interaction schemes could lead to rapid dissipation of magnetic energy within astrophysical objects. 

Ultimately, further research is recommended to bridge the gap between mean-field and local/differential, as well as global simulations of astrophysical objects, by considering these theoretical frameworks in conjunction with one another. 

A visual representation of the differential rotation, velocity, and magnetic field profiles from our global simulations is provided in the supplementary material. 

The results of our study were presented at the International Astronomical Union General Assembly held in August 2015 in Honolulu, Hawaii. 

A detailed description of a novel approach to differentially rotating global simulations in the radial and latitudinal directions using various scaling factors is described in the technical note available at [arXiv:1608.06695]. 

The results of our global simulations have been extended to cover a broader range of astrophysical objects, including those with nonaligned rotation axes, at various scaling factors for the diffusion coefficients, and with adjustment of the Coriolis and helicity parameters.

We will focus on one such generalisation, where the sets used are equipped with distinct metrics, resulting in distinct subgroups, one of which is known as the braided Thompson group. This paper demonstrates how the DrQA retriever, originally designed for passage retrieval in a passage retrieval question-answering system, can be effectively used as a general text pre-training tool for any text. Following this, we explore its application in enhancing the text pre-training process of the recently introduced Retrieve-Augment Generate model, specifically the Retrieval Augmentation Generator (RAG). We achieve this by substituting DrQA's retriever across DrQA's three fully connected layers with newly trained versions and then merging these into the rest of RAG. In a comparable setup, we observe notable improvements in performance for RAG when utilizing our fine-tuned DrQA's retriever compared to RAG's own pre-trained retriever. Additionally, we highlight a considerable reduction in memory usage achieved through the joint merging of our fine-tuned DrQA's parameters with RAG's generator parameters, which enables the efficient deployment of the entire Retrieve-Augment Generate system on edge devices. Consequently, this research provides robust foundation for future research into the Retrieve-Augment Generate architecture, specifically its Retrieval Augmentation Generator component, and paves the way for integrating DRQA's pre-trained model into complex Question-Answering frameworks like Retrieve-Augment Generate. Ultimately, this work illustrates the notion that a pre-trained text passage retrieval model can effectively serve as a versatile text pre-training tool for various text-based applications. Subsequently, we expect our approach to enable the development of more efficient and accurate multi-sentence and passage-based Question-Answering systems. Task completion rates on the Amazon Mechanical Turk platform have been declining over the past nine years. Research into the effect of worker qualifications on task approval rates has been limited, with existing studies focusing primarily on the impact of work quantity on task approval rates. Our research reverses the perspective, examining how task approval rates influence the availability of qualified workers. We discovered that crowdsworkers who consistently work quickly but inconsistently demonstrate quality are primarily concerned with earning money as quickly as possible. Our study revealed that incorporating a time constraint into crowdsourcing tasks hinders the ability to attract skilled workers, particularly those capable of producing high-quality work within the designated time frame. We found no correlation between the overall time workers took to complete tasks and their ability to meet the strict deadline when given the option. However, our analysis revealed that workers tend to undervalue the quality of their work rather than overestimating it. To prevent cheating, we discovered that employing a qualification mechanism, such as requiring workers to sign a cognitive rights agreement, has no significant effect on removing unqualified workers from participating in crowdsourcing initiatives. Ultimately, applying a monetary incentive to encourage workers to truthfully report the quality of their work did not have a significant impact on crowdsourcing tasks that placed a high premium on work quality. Our findings suggest that applying fixed qualification mechanisms may not be sufficient to distinguish between qualified and unqualified workers and may ultimately hinder the success of these initiatives.

Future high-energy muon colliders face a challenge due to beam-induced secondary backgrounds caused by muon and neutrino spills, which in turn affect their performance in terms of energy reach and luminosity. This study presents an in-depth investigation of these backgrounds and their impact on a hypothetical future Higgs Factory and a higher-energy collider, utilizing existing and proposed optimization techniques to reduce background interference and boost both device sensitivity and luminosity. The research reveals that by implementing these strategies, it is feasible to lower peak background rates by a factor of more than ten, thereby achieving notable improvements without additional technical intervention. The analysis includes a comprehensive assessment of background reduction techniques applied to both the Higgs Factory and the higher-energy collider, highlighting the importance of optimizing each design parameters for optimal results. Furthermore, the research explores the sensitivity of these designs to very high energy neutrino background contributions, which could potentially be generated by very energetic muon decay-in-flight. The research also tests the effectiveness of several proposed methods to counteract these problematic backgrounds, specifically the use of internal cones and the implementation of background-subtracted luminosity measurements. The analysis reveals that a innovative approach to background subtraction, involving a deep neural network-based classification of muon and tau events, can achieve convincing separation between these categories, leading to convincing systematic reductions in neutrino background contributions. Finally, the research presents a comprehensive outline of future research opportunities to further reduce potential beam-induced backgrounds in future muon colliders. The additional details are expected to offer significant further advances in design parameters and could potentially lead to notable breakthroughs in energy reach and luminosity. The detailed study is expected to set the standard for the interpretation of beam induced background information in the field. Optimizing neural network parameters often involves eliminating unnecessary
components, leading to improved sparseness and efficiency. However, existing
methods have yet to achieve high quality in both training and inference modes. 
We present 'Spartan', a technique for generating neural networks with defined
sparsity patterns through a differentiated approach, combining transportation
theory with a dual regularization strategy. Unlike previous methods, Spartan
achieves top-notch performance in both training and inference for a broad range
of architectures, working seamlessly with a variety of loss functions. 
Using architectural duplication, Spartan easily adapts to novel network
designs, allowing users to create customized sparseness patterns not
natively supported. Additionally, our method is uniquely compatible with
graph-based neural networks, opening up new possibilities for sparse
unsupervised domain adaptation applications. We demonstrate Spartan's
exceptional performance on various benchmark tasks, including image
classification and domain adaptation. Related resources, including code and
pre-designed sparseness patterns, are available for public use.

Software developers widely acknowledge the importance of unit testing as a crucial aspect of their work cycle, allowing for swift detection and resolution of coding errors. However, test code can be compromised by test smells, equivalent to flaws in production code, hindering maintainability and effectiveness. Past research has empirically studied test smells from a maintenance perspective but overlooked their broader implications. Our empirical investigation addresses this knowledge gap by examining the perspective of developers who use and maintain tests, focusing on four prominent test smells. We conducted a cross-sectional empirical study involving 83 developers working on 33 open-source projects, requesting the developers' personal views on the given test smells to determine their severity levels. Our results reveal interesting patterns of agreement and discrepancy among developers regarding the smell severity levels. These findings will aid developers in prioritizing efforts and provide practical guidelines for identifying the test smells' severity levels. Moreover, these results can serve as a foundation for devising intervention strategies aimed at minimizing the occurrence of these test smells in real-world development projects. Our study also highlights a variety of implementation strategies to eliminate test smells as observed in our research. Our results indicate that the financial resources required to remediate each smell vary significantly, ranging from relatively easy fixes to complex alterations. Moreover, some test smells require modifications to production code, potentially increasing project complexity and cost. Our research suggests several possible interventions to minimize the occurrence of these test smells. These recommendations can be explored and validated in future research, focusing on software maintenance and quality improvement. Ultimately, our study aims to reduce the prevalence of test smells in real-world development projects by achieving zero smells in the future. One potential strategy to achieve this goal is the design of an assessment tool to evaluate the prevalence of test smells in given projects and provide guidance on the efficient elimination of those smells. This is an area for further research, representing a crucial step towards improving software quality and effectiveness. Implementing this idea could have a significant impact on various domains, as the results can benefit a wide range of applications, including the medical and aviation industries. Moreover, the concept of zero smells is a significant improvement over the current research focus on minimizing smells rather than eliminating them. Our study can be taken to the next level by collaborating with practitioners and developers to create a more comprehensive research agenda aimed at improving software quality and effectiveness. We'll explore two variations of this process and establish that one serves as a Bayesian shrinkage estimator for a broad class of regression models, effectively providing a data-driven method for sparse estimations. We'll also examine the "brushing" behavior in scenarios where the process is used as a nonhomogeneous stationary jump-diffusion. We introduce the updated version of the {\tt KKMCee} event generator, version 5.00.2, designed for simulating electron-positron collider events. Building on the original {\tt KKMC} event generator, {\tt KKMCee} now includes lepton and quark pair creation, allowing for the modeling of leptonic $W$-lepton colliders and $e^+e^-$ colliders beyond the Standard Model. Its reliability in predicting differential distributions and efficiencies has been verified through a comprehensive set of tests. This statement presents the theoretical foundations of the {\tt KKMCee} event generator for its 40-year anniversary, outlining its underlying framework and algorithms for pair creation simulations. Furthermore, we investigate dominant two-loop electroweak corrections within the framework of the SM, while corrections for non-electroweak processes, including QED and QCD corrections, are limited to one-loop accuracy. Measuring inter-beat intervals (IBI) from electrocardiogram signals can be crucial in identifying stress levels. Existing research has focused on final IBI values following various processing methods; however, there is no thorough investigation regarding the impact of processing on IBI estimates. Furthermore, the difficulty in replicating experimental studies hinder large-scale IQA studies. Our work introduces a novel IBI estimation approach, termed Tirami{\`u}tu, utilizing a residual frame work that is adaptable to various models. When paired with an adaptive threshold frame work, this method significantly reduces errors compared to traditional methods. Our research assesses the impact of processing steps in IBI estimation and introduces a novel, comprehensive framework for evaluating the quality of these estimates, which is devoid of biased assumptions. Utilizing an extensive dataset, our experiments reveal that the Tirami{\`u}tu method surpasses existing approaches in accuracy and efficiency, with potential applications in wearable devices and stress level monitoring devices. Given the substantial nature of this work, it has been published in three parts in a recent issue of IEEE Journal of Emerging Technologies in Healthcare. Part I introduces the quality assessment framework, Part II proposes the Tirami{\`u}tu method, and Part III presents a comparative study. A related video is available at https://youtu.be/jOZxLl4w_9I. In recent years, there has been growing interest in developing algorithms that can dynamically update and maintain graphical structures, particularly to create efficient graph databases that can evolve with changing networks. This research aims to analyze and compare existing methods for embedding evolving graphs, which involves updating node coordinates to reflect changes such as new nodes, deleted nodes, and modified edges while maintaining the graph's overall structure. This work formally defines the problem of embedding evolving graphs and categorizes it based on the type of information utilized. Additionally, it outlines the problem's variants, discusses key constraints, and reviews the current landscape of methods and techniques developed to address this challenge. Furthermore, this research identifies key challenges and presents possible areas for further investigation, emphasizing the distinct characteristics of evolving graphs and their impact on embedding algorithms. Additionally, some key differences between traditional graph embedding and evolving graph embedding are highlighted. Finally, some potential areas for further research on emerging graph embedding are outlined. 

Graph embedding has become a well-established area of research in recent years, with numerous applications and a broad range of associated techniques. On the other hand, evolving graph embedding is a rapidly evolving field with numerous promising research opportunities. This survey seeks to provide an in-depth overview of existing methods and help readers understand the current state of research in this area while also identifying key challenges and potential avenues for investigation.
