A new method for learning a deep, adaptive metric to quantify data representation variability is proposed. Unlike traditional deep metric learning approaches that employ fixed distance measures, our framework relies on the Sinkhorn divergence, a parameterized metric that accounts for correlations within data subsets. We introduce a dual Sinkhorn constraint to limit representation variability, preserving the original nearest neighbor identities. Although the Sinkhorn divergence makes optimization challenging due to its non-smooth and non-differentiable nature, our paper provides an innovative dual regularization constraint, enabling efficient training of deep Sinkhorn metrics via gradient-based optimization. We further conduct comprehensive experiments to evaluate the learned metric under various data representation scenarios, and demonstrate its applicability to both unsupervised and semi-supervised classification tasks, where it enhances neighbor discriminativeness compared to traditional deep metric learning approaches. Moreover, our framework offers a flexible platform for integrating data representation with clustering optimization, yielding better clustering results compared to using fixed distance measures. We test the effectiveness of our approach with datasets such as CMU PASCAD, where the Sinkhorn divergence- based metric captures the diverse poses of human images. Our work offers a novel contribution to metric learning as the first to introduce a trainable metric that accounts for data correlation, opening up new possibilities for deep metric learning and data representation. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/hjdw2/Deep_Sinkhorn_Metric.

In many countries, local contact tracing efforts have been enhanced by the aid of pandemic response teams, but the effect of combining these efforts with other tracing methods has yet to be explored. We employ a stochastic representation of the transmission dynamic of COVID-19 to measure the performance of distinct and joint local tracing efforts. By assuming that all tracing methods strictly adhere to data protection regulations, we simulate the outcomes of various scenarios with respect to transmission reduction and reproductive number metrics. Our analysis reveals that, in certain circumstances, the incorporation of additional local tracing efforts beyond the initial primary system enhances overall transmission reduction efficiency. We also find that, for the case involving two-dimensional space, the distribution of case findings is shifted towards higher transmission rates when two tracing efforts are present, but the effect on transmission reduction remains unchanged. Ultimately, we find that, for the case of a partially immunized population under multiple local tracing efforts, the number of transmissions is reduced by a factor equivalent to one minus the sum of the respective efficiency factors of each tracing effort. The analysis presented here provides insight into the impact of combining different local contact tracing efforts on the transmission of SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes COVID-19, but highlights limitations in assessing the effects on disease mortality, the global transmission rate, and the efficacy of other non-pharmaceutical control measures. Expanding this analysis to account for these control measures and investigating their interplay could significantly advance our understanding of the effect of contact tracing on disease transmission. The second release of Gaia Data (Gaia DR2) extended our capability to gather these essential data, incorporating a vast dataset of astrometric information on a billion stars. Random polytopes offer a useful tool for studying stochastic systems by analyzing their Betti numbers in the sparse regime. A random Gaussian voyage is defined as the set of vertices within a sphere of radius r, and is generated from a Gaussian mixture model. By demonstrating that the Gaussian voyage's distance distribution becomes increasingly sparse as r approaches infinity, we can apply the tools of extremal combinatorics to establish models for its Betti numbers in this regime. Empirical findings and mathematical analyses suggest that the expected Betti numbers are closely approximated by formulas derived from the extremal limits of related geometric patterns, such as those found in the diameter and similitude configurations. These predictions are further validated by simulations and comparative studies, revealing a good agreement between the expected Betti numbers and those obtained from the extremal combinatorial models. Furthermore, the expected Betti numbers are found to be in line with those obtained from the distance distribution model, particularly for larger values of r. A comparative analysis between the two models reveals that the distance distribution model performs better for smaller r, while the extremal models offer greater accuracy for larger r. A thorough investigation into the convergence times of the two models reveals that the convergence radius heavily depends on the dimension d. Based on these findings, mathematical expressions and formulas derived from the extremal models can be used to generate precise models for Betti numbers in the sparse regime. These models can be utilized to estimate Betti numbers with higher precision than previously achievable. The proposed models are especially beneficial for applications where the radius r exceeds one-fifth of the dimension d. The findings and models presented can likely be extended to other stochastic systems featuring homogenous patterns, such as those generated from Gaussian mixtures, across higher spatial dimensions. It is anticipated that applying the tools of extremal combinatorics to these systems will yield more accurate statistical models for their asymptotic Betti numbers. The proposed models and findings can potentially inspire a broader range of research in homogenous geometric patterns and their asymptotic Betti numbers. The investigation also reveals a significant number of other structural similarities and differences between the distance and extremal models, along with various corrective factors that could impact the accuracy of extremal models at different dimensions. In settings where a robot is instructed by an expert, the task involves transferring the expert's knowledge into a robot policy.  However, unlike in typical reinforcement learning scenarios where goals are naturally objective-based, these instructions are typically communicated linguistically and turn out to be a constraining set of quantifiable performance metrics.  Considering that describing goals usually yields more concise language compared to prescribing performance, we suggest a novel approach called Reverse Constrained Reinforcement Learning.  This method effectively transforms task objectives into the robot's goals by treating the constraining set as dynamic goals and learning a policy that maximizes satisfaction of these goals.  We propose a new model called RCLI, which allows for goal satisfaction to be optimized through a variational approach.  Our research demonstrates that this model can efficiently learn a policy using just one video demonstration and meets the performance requirements.  Our model is successful in translating natural language into the robot's dynamic objectives, which are displayed through still images.  Our model is shown to outperform other techniques both in terms of numerical measures and with real human interactions.  Our code and the model are available for download at http://mml.umd.edu/~case/rcli.html. The European Space Agency's GAIA mission will create a detailed 3D chart of over 1 billion stars within the galaxy's visible volume by mapping their positions, motions, and luminosity variations over time. A companion paper examines the observations and observational results, while this paper delves into the data reduction process, its challenges, and accomplishments. Specifically, this document focuses on the data reduction pipelines developed for the data processing, assuming a successful transfer of the data to the ESA's data processing center on schedule. While some algorithms were chosen based on their maturity and effectiveness, new techniques were necessary to handle GAIA's complex data. A major consideration was to implement these accurately and efficiently enough to process the data within a reasonable timeframe. This paper summarizes the progress made in the data processing effort, including the progress so far and the remaining tasks to obtain the mission's science data products. Furthermore, it outlines the various approaches to validate the data processing results and the accuracy of the reconstructed sky, which will be used to determine stellar parameters and to determine motion patterns. Additionally, this document discusses how to implement and use these results, including an assessment of potential errors. A vertex divider in a graph is defined as an area splitting the graph into two sections, 
where one section's vertex connectivity exceeds a certain threshold or is less than another threshold.
Treewidth, an important graph metric used in various applications, can be determined efficiently 
with certain vertex dividers but verifies the property by examining all possible cuts. 
Researchers introduced more space-efficient methods to calculate treewidth in 2016. 
Here, we propose two new vertex divider testing methods to determine the maximum treewidth 
of a graph with a given treewidth value, requiring O(n) bytes if the treewidth is below a certain threshold 
and an unspecified polynomial amount of bytes otherwise. 
These methods were implemented and demonstrated to outperform existing algorithms in treewidth testing. 
They were also used to enhance the performance of the clique width parameter, used in various applications, 
by reducing the complexity of clique width calculations to on polynomial time given a treewidth limit. 
Moreover, the methods were applied to efficiently solve Boolean Circuit satisfiability, a key problem within #P and NP intermediates. 
Also presented was a new efficient method for computing the minimum treewidth of a graph, used in various applications, 
with treewidth values, requiring only O(n) bytes and verifying the minimum treewidth property. 
This method was implemented and showed significant performance improvement for various treewidth applications. 
Lastly, the methods described were applied and showed effective results in computing the minimum vertex connectivity 
for problems such as vertex cover, a key problem within various applications. 
This method was also implemented and showed significant performance improvement for this problem as well. 
All experiments were performed and shown on various graphs with different characteristics, including graphs 
from the collection of Paul Gadalla, from the collection of Flavia Del Guerra, and from the collection of Nikita Ludkin. 
In addition to these tests, the methods described were applied and shown effective results in computing the minimum 
vertex connectivity for a set of graphs collected by Marcin Mucha. 
Furthermore, the methods described were applied and shown significant performance improvement in 
computing the minimum vertex connectivity for problems such as set cover, a key problem within various applications. 
This method was also implemented and showed significant performance improvement for this problem as well.

Recent surveys have highlighted the significant role played by strength and position-based node grouping in the analysis of complex network structures. This has led to a notable absence of systematic discussion surrounding the interpretations and requirements necessary for applying weighted group detection methods, particularly those that are directed and non-zero weighted. To address this gap, this paper systematically examines various interpretations of zero weights in networks, before outlining the necessary conditions for detecting directional groups within them. Our investigation indicates that zero weights possess unique properties depending on the specific direction from which they originate with respect to the network. Ultimately, we provide essential guidelines for accurately detecting directed groups within non-zero weighted networks. The companion notebook for this paper can be accessed at https://github.com/jaycferguson/Weighted_group_identification_necessity_and_interpretation. As an example of the practical application of our findings, using the Facebook network, we were able to clearly categorise and identify ten distinct groups, in clear violation of the network's zero-weight requirement. The Facebook dataset used in this investigation can be downloaded from Facebook's Open Source Dataset Programme at https://osf.io/ke5zg/. The resulting group annotations presented here represent a first interpretation of the Facebook network's structure, but one which is certainly not the definitive or final insight one might glean. The primary contribution of this paper consists of the identification of the ten groups, and more importantly, the necessity conditions we specified for detecting directional groups within non-zero weighted networks. Subsequently, multiple readers have annotated the Facebook dataset as part of the 'Structure from Motion' workshop held at the ASMLSD 2020 conference, yielding diverse group structures. The resulting insights and interpretations demonstrate a clear understanding of the Facebook network's underlying structure, and the variety of perspectives presented highlights their unique relevance and importance. The present paper represents an initial contribution to the interpretation and understanding of the Facebook network's structure, and the resulting insights and perspectives will undoubtedly continue to evolve. One key factor that has held neural networks back from being used extensively in scientific and engineering problems is the lack of reliable uncertainty quantification. This issue has been partly resolved by methods such as Bayesian neural networks and noise regularization, which allow for approximate uncertainty estimates. Recently introduced approaches like adversarial training and reliability bounds have also made progress in accurately assessing uncertainty. This paper investigates the capability of the neural tangent kernel model in estimating uncertainty in physics-informed neural networks and finds it to be a highly reliable method. Through an approach that combines theoretical analysis with numerical simulation, a precise error bound is derived, which can serve as a certified guarantee of prediction accuracy. Numerical results demonstrate that this approach provides very tight bounds, allowing for the prediction of uncertainties with great precision. It is anticipated that this technique will significantly broaden the applications of physics-informed neural networks in real-world settings where robust and accurate uncertainty estimation is essential. This research further validates the potential of the neural tangent kernel model in becoming a crucial tool for high-confidence machine learning in physics and engineering applications. This study offers a certified, a posteriori mistake estimation that can be employed to construct robust prediction systems in a wide range of essential problems. It is expected that similar techniques could be developed to achieve similar goals in other neural network models, potentially even leading to the creation of more efficient uncertainty quantification methods. Nonetheless, for the particular case studied here, the technique yields remarkably precise uncertainty bounds, enabling promising advancements in the field of machine learning through this novel, certified approach. This research is now being expanded upon to assess reliability in other neural networks, a more challenging problem, as well as exploring its potential applications in optimization through reliability-based design. More details about these advancements can be found in recent publications. This work is related to and has been posted on several online platforms, including arXiv and research gate. As the field of Machine Learning advances rapidly, researchers are exploring reinforcement learning in a machine learning setting. Graph neural networks in particular have gained attention for their broad applications such as predicting node properties and connecting nodes. However, graph data is susceptible to contamination which can mislead machine learning models. We introduce an innovative method where an agent deliberately introduces contamination to outperform traditional graph data sampling methods. Through various experiments with diverse graph datasets, our agent was successfully able to identify the most valuable contaminants and develop an efficient sampling strategy within a designated budget. Importantly, our research reveals that these findings are transferable to downstream tasks, presenting a new perspective in machine learning research. We ultimately aim to make machine learning more adaptive to contamination by establishing standards for evaluating the robustness of machine learning models in this context. Our research code is available online for further investigation.

The process of matching objects between photometric catalogs can be challenged by catalogues of varying brightness measures, such as those based on Johnson $B$ and $V$ magnitudes, and $gr$ bands from the Gaia SAGEN project. By utilizing a combination of both photometric and astrometric data to calculate key statistical values, including the likelihood of source contamination and systematic errors, for each potential match, the authors improve the accuracy of matches by calibrating a weighted ranking system to account for sources at risk of contamination. This approach prioritizes astrometric data when matches are uncertain, mitigating potential biases from photometric data. Furthermore, the authors demonstrate the efficacy of their method by applying it to matching processes in the SRG-AGILE All-Sky Monitor, and Gaia Data Release 2, observing improved matches compared to traditional astrometric-only methods, particularly at higher Galactic latitudes where fewer stellar crowding corrections are available. By incorporating photometric data to assess matches at higher risk, the authors refine the accuracy of the matches, and their technique is seen as particularly valuable for future surveys, expected to be highly sensitive and cover vast areas of the sky. Moreover, the authors' method also offers practical applications in determining the significance of astrometric and photometric discrepancies between catalogues, and in identifying source astrophysical noise. Ontologies are extensively used in various fields for categorizing and grouping information. Researchers and practitioners frequently analyze ontology graphs through interactive visualizations to gain insights into complex data, yet there is a lack of effective visualization tools that show relationships between groupings. To address this limitation, we have developed a novel visualization approach called OntoPlot, which seamlessly integrates into existing graph exploration tools and makes non-hierarchical connections in large ontologies more accessible to notice. We discuss key design decisions, present OntoPlot's implementation, and conduct an evaluation consisting of multiple methods, including user testing, performance assessment, and comparative analysis. The latter focuses on identifying areas in which OntoPlot enhances existing approaches and identifies areas for further enhancement. We believe OntoPlot can greatly aid researchers working with large ontologies and contribute to the development of novel ontology visualization techniques. The project's source code and materials can be found at https://github/onto-plot. The benchmark platform where the experiment took place is available at https://cim3d.vgora.fr. Following the guidelines mentioned in the authors' guide, we conducted an informal user experience study shortly after the initial evaluation to gather users' opinions on OntoPlot. The participants' feedback suggested that OntoPlot effectively facilitates the understanding of large ontologies through a non-overlapping visualization of hierarchical and non-hierarchical connections. We observed, as may be anticipated, users tend to consider OntoPlot's plot labels as visually appealing and informative, whereas the label management could be improved. The users viewed OntoPlot's interactive mode as enhancing their exploration capabilities, although some users found the label management to be the only area in need of further improvement. The project's future enhancements could be to make OntoPlot compatible with visualization platforms not directly mentioned in the authors' guide, such as ConceptNet, as well as to integrate OntoPlot with learning platforms to educate users on ontology visualization. We introduce an innovative training technique for semi-supervised end-to-end automatic speech recognition that combines inter-domain loss and a novel interpolation of CycleGAN-trained acoustic and textual features. The proposed method train an end-to-end model with inter-domain loss using synthetic training data and features from a CycleGAN model that maps text to speech and speech to text. The 3D pre-trained end-to-end model then performs speech recognition by running the decoder only, using the target speech as input, after which the generated speech is passed through the reversed model to obtain a prediction. The proposed method is evaluated on the WSJ, Voxforge, and LibriSpeech datasets and significantly outperforms the baseline model, achieving relative improvements of 9% and 13% on the LibriSpeech test sets, with sample rates of 8 and 16 kHz respectively. Furthermore, the method requires minimal labeled speech data and is simple to implement and train. Therefore, the proposed technique is effective in leveraging both speech and text knowledge to enhance the performance of end-to-end automatic speech recognition. The research is supported by a related GitHub repository: https://github.com/IndigoIndigo/ESRcycleGAN. The findings are expected to motivate the use of inter-domain knowledge in semi-supervised end-to-end automatic speech recognition. The approach is anticipated to facilitate the development of highly accurate speech recognition systems using large volumes of lightly annotated speech data. The method expands the applicability of end-to-end automatic speech recognition to speakers with non-standard languages and accents. The research is expected to inspire the exploration of applications for other sequence-to-sequence tasks. 

Please note that this paper is a revised and expanded version of a conference paper titled "Labeled Speech Guided End-to-End Automatic Speech Recognition" presented at Interspeech 2021. The significant enhancements over the original work include:

* The proposed method was evaluated on multiple datasets, whereas the original method was only tested on the WSJ dataset.
* The method was successfully applied to the larger and more challenging LibriSpeech dataset, which has over 1,000 hours of speech data across 10 genres.
* The research was conducted using data with non-standard languages and accents, which offers a significant advantage over the original work.
* The method was trained using large volumes of lightly annotated speech data, which expands the applicability of end-to-end automatic speech recognition.
* The research is expected to inspire the exploration of multiple related sequence-to-sequence tasks.

The temperature gradient-driven flow phenomenon, or the Soret effect, is a thermal phenomenon that affects fluids with an anisotropic structure of thermal stress. Typically, research into the Soret effect is centered on heat transfer through a fluid's phase, with the thermal diffusion factor being a measure of how much the temperature gradient distorts the fluid's internal structure. However, studies on the Soret effect in polymers are rare, and to better understand how different molecular parts contribute to this effect, we conducted computer-based research using a simulation method. By manipulating the temperature, we measured how particles moved within solution models made from polymer and simple solvent substances. Based on our findings, when a polymer's internal structure is subjected to thermal stress, the distance between different molecular parts changes, and this causes an movement-related contribution to the Soret effect. Furthermore, we discovered that this movement-related contribution depends both on the type of atoms involved and the flexibility of the polymer. Conversely, the type of atoms involved does not affect the distance between different molecular parts when the temperature gradient is considered. Our research reveals that flexible polymers' internal structures play a significant role in determining their Soret effect. As an example, for a polymer consisting of two different molecular groups, the ratio of contribution to the Soret effect is greater in flexible polymers and molecules with large differences in molecular mass, and this ratio is higher for the group with lower molecular mass. These research outcomes may contribute to the development of temperature-resistant materials. They also shed light on the properties of proteins under high temperatures, which could help explain their decreased functionality in such conditions. Ultimately, our studies may lead to the creation of temperature-stable proteins. It is also important to note that although this research may have significant practical implications, it is still limited by its reliance on theoretical simulation methods. Therefore, to confirm these findings and develop efficient methods to detect the Soret effect in polymers and proteins, it is necessary to conduct further research using both theoretical and experimental approaches. Information on the composition of the test solution, such that polyethylene oxide was used, and the characteristics of the NPT method, such that surface tension was used, would be important components of this study. Our simulation methods could be improved by adjusting the coupling parameters between the molecules and atoms to reduce fluctuations in system energy, and increasing the duration and frequency of the simulations to reduce systematic errors. Ultimately, our studies could have significant implications in the development of proteins and polymers with stable structures in various environments. The development of automated essay assessment poses significant challenges 
despite the advancements in natural language processing. To address this issue, 
we introduce two advanced transformer-based models: one pre-trained and one 
customized. These models, built on the open-source Hugging Face Library, 
outperform existing solutions and showcase state-of-the-art performance on 
both classification and ranking tasks. Additionally, we successfully integrate 
these models into a comprehensive assessment framework, effectively 
distinguishing between essays from diverse writers by assessing their language, 
use of grammar, and style. As a result, we achieve promising evaluation scores 
and substantial reduction in computation time compared to previous approaches. 
Lastly, we showcase the potential of our methodology in automated essay assessment 
and discuss areas for further improvement and expansion. The source code and

One of the most significant obstacles in self-driving vehicles is pedestrian detection, which is compounded by false positives causing navigation system delays.  Currently used pedestrian detectors are trained using datasets with negatively marked boxes; however, the majority of these boxes do not contain pedestrians, resulting in a high ratio of false positives.  By reducing these false positives, the likelihood of system crashes being triggered is reduced.  In this paper, we present an unsupervised technique that employs adversarial training to control the ratio of positive boxes (with pedestrians) to false positives.  This method re-evaluates the prediction boxes generated by the pedestrian detector, ranking them according to their likelihood of containing a pedestrian without any supervision.  The ranking is achieved by introducing a classifier that divides the boxes into those with pedestrians (positive boxes) and those without (false positives), with an added constraint that positive boxes should greatly outnumber false positives.  The boxes with a high likelihood of containing a pedestrian are narrowed down in size, whereas the boxes with a low likelihood are both narrowed down in size and have their boundaries adjusted to prevent overlap.  The dataset is then re-ordered based on a ranking that was devised to prioritize boxes containing pedestrians.  The method was tested using the Citypersons dataset and found to have successfully reduced the number of false positives while increasing the detection rate by 5.89%.  The method was also evaluated under real-world conditions using an in-car system that employs the SPPeck pedestrian detector and found that the detection system performed at a level equivalent to that achieved using box filtering, which is the currently employed method.  The method was successful in controlling the ratio of positive boxes to false positives and in detecting pedestrians at a rate equivalent to that achieved by the pedestrian detector trained using datasets with negatively marked boxes.  The method offers a means of reducing the likelihood of the navigation system crashing as a result of false positives. \copyright 2022 IEEE - All rights reserved. Our primary objective is to investigate the impact of a throw motion's initial phase on perceiving the throw's force and accuracy. To achieve this, we create a synthetic throwing motion dataset with variations in intensity, trajectory, and point of release, where the point of release is the instant just before the ball leaves the thrower's hand. Ultimately, we establish that the point of release affects the throw's dynamic appearance more than its static attributes, revealing new avenues for designing believable and immersive throwing motions in virtual worlds. This method linearly links token translations to tree structures, enabling simultaneous decoding of words and syntactic dependencies. By leveraging this tree structure, the method avoids the quadratic complexity associated with previous approaches that utilized syntax-based decoding. Furthermore, the method retains the ability to accurately predict word frequencies, a concern that had posed challenges to previous syntax-based decoding methods. In interstellar chemistry, reactions play a pivotal role in creating and destroying small molecules, and the binding energy distribution (BED) provides crucial information on the microscopic consequences of reactions for the formation of complex molecules in space. Existing research has introduced various methods for calculating BEDs, but a shortage of extensively documented quantum chemical calculations for astrophysical species and reactions limits their application in modeling and prediction. Our new platform, the Binding Energy Assessment Platform (BEAP), aims to fill this void by providing a comprehensive database of EDs based on extensive density functional theory calculations for over 300 astrophysical species and 700 reactions. We incorporate analytical forms of EDs that facilitate rapid predictions and rapid convergence of distributions. Our research also discusses the significance of several factors for the astrophysical community: the choice of analytical form, calculation accuracy, and the impact of hydrogen excitation on water and BEDs. We assess five key factors influencing the formation of complex molecules in two specific reactions and demonstrate the platform's potential to inform modeling and the prediction of distribution shapes. We provide the platform itself at https://beap.as.utexas.edu/. We offer our EDs in a MiDAS+ format, available at https://beap.as.utexas.edu/ed-browse. We release our source code at https://github.com/utexasas/computational-astrophysics-group/beap.

This work begins by providing an exhaustive statistical characterisation of a multiplicative stochastic process, thereby establishing a theoretical foundation for similar studies in the future. Subsequently, employing this results, a novel method for enhancing the lower bound of a specific stochastic process is presented, demonstrating the potential for practical applications, such as reducing the lower bound of a Brownian motion. We explore quantonics, a classical shadow of quantum mechanics, through the eyes of quantum information theory. Our expectation assessment contribution centers around generating expectations of observable values via quantum state inputs to low-depth quantum circuits. These quantum circuits, defined by specific allowable unitary transformations (gates), are classically efficient to implement. Our approach has practical applications in the simulation of quantum mechanics with limited accuracy and for understanding the quantic characterization of classical probabilistic systems. We have developed an algorithm for determining optimal gate sets that minimize confusion between states, resulting in better assessment accuracy with an equal number of quantum measurements. Our research also highlights the role of quantum correlations in expectation assessment and examines the circuit asymptotics under various assumptions. Finally, we outline potential extensions to deeper quantum circuits, albeit less accurately, and discuss the critical role of quantum correlations in expectation assessment. We investigate the one-dimensional planar DII equation in the context of scattering theory. Specifically, we analyze the properties of the scattering matrix and its behavior as the wavevector k approaches infinity from the upper half-plane. We also consider the system's behavior under the action of the group SC(2,2) of Carleman automorphisms. By doing so, we locate the regions where the mean action of the transformation on the space of smooth functions with compact support is minimal or maximal. Minimal action regions correspond to the conditions under which the transformation's effect on the frequency domain leaves the space of solutions unchanged. We investigate these concepts further in relation to the space of smooth functions with a finite speed of variation. This study demonstrates that under certain conditions, the DII equation exhibits a non-trivial reflection coefficient. Notably, these conditions can be combined with those for which the non-trivial reflection coefficient arises in the past, resulting in a new set of conditions where the reflection coefficient shows a non-trivial $|k|$ behavior. This research focuses on the DII equation as an example of a two-component integrable system. The paper concludes by discussing the DII equation in the context of a broader class of nonlinear partial differential equations describing long-wave homogeneous surface waves on a two-fluid layer. By doing so, we reveal a connection between the reflection coefficient's behavior in the upper half-plane and the uniqueness of a solution to the Dirac operator in the two-fluid model. The resulting system's properties allow for the existence of a non-trivial reflection coefficient, which in turn corresponds to the conditions under which the corresponding inverse scattering method is local. Locality of the scattering theory has been established for the DII equation under different conditions; this paper contributes by combining these conditions with those resulting from the mean action of the group SC(2,2) being minimal. The resulting combination of conditions corresponds to the most non-trivial $|k|$ behavior in the upper half-plane. This coefficient function serves as an analog of the coefficient function for the focusing AKNS equation. Advanced machine learning models can be vulnerable to classifications being altered based on the order and combinations of features. This phenomenon is known as a robustness gap, and it can be mitigated through the utilization of dataset permutations as a form of regularization, enhancing models' consistency across varying feature combinations. Our research introduces a set of functions known as sibylvariants, which effectively serve as robust weak learners in combination learning techniques, such as ensembles and bootstrapping. We demonstrate the efficacy of sibylvariants by showing that:
1) They close the robustness gap for most classification datasets,
2) They outperform traditional weak learners in combination learning scenarios,
3) They offer superior data efficiency when compared to traditional weak learners,
4) They successfully train models on highly unreliable data.
Additionally, we provide access to the sibylvariants code, accompany it with experimental results, and make available the corresponding dataset with altered class labels. Furthermore, to promote research into dataset robustness and stability, we suggest utilizing sibylvariants as a tool to develop new classification models based on dataset variants. Ultimately, we offer sibylvariants as a robust weak learner framework for generating robust predictions in combination learning scenarios. High-dimensional data cannot be effectively processed through conventional, linear models. However, incorporating a nonlinear basis risks overwhelming the model with numerous parameters, potentially rendering it less interpretable. A balanced approach is required. Our research focuses on developing a two-stage learning framework that achieves a linear representation of complex data distributions. Our framework combines a gradient-based, linear model initialized with a data-driven starting point to ensure we are learning a linear representation that accurately characterizes the underlying data pattern. Notably, our approach does not necessitate any prior knowledge of the data pattern and works seamlessly without any modifications. Our empirical evaluations on datasets of varying complexity demonstrate that this adaptive learning framework consistently yields superior performance compared to traditional methods, while also being significantly more efficient. Our results suggest that this approach could be applied to related domains such as transfer learning and reinforcement learning with promising outcomes. Furthermore, incorporating a dataset augmentation strategy allows the model to generalize better to unseen data patterns, thus resulting in improved performance across a board of benchmark problems. Developing small language models, especially in low-resource settings, presents theoretical and practical challenges including the trade-off between compact models and their reliability, as smaller models are more susceptible to errors and perturbations. To explore this issue, we investigated two methods for reducing model size: knowledge distillation and quantization. Despite theoretical concerns about the reliability of these methods, we found that both approaches significantly decrease the impact of input perturbations in practice. Notably, distillation, in contrast to quantization, yields a substantial improvement in the robustness of translation tasks, with a notable 93% reduction in sensitivity. While both methods effectively decrease model size, their implications on reliability vary, with distillation outperforming quantization in this context. We have made our code available for replication purposes. The research reveals that, in low-resource settings, distillation, in conjunction with pruning, demonstrates great potential as a method for automating the compression of NMT systems. Ultimately, the research raises crucial real-world concerns regarding the reliability of NMT systems, particularly those employed in sensitive tasks such as diplomacy, as demonstrated by a basic case study. The construction of a hypergraph multigraph, which serves as a visual representation of a hypergraph's edges and their respective lengths, is a primary focus of this discussion. A specific example is examined in this context to illustrate an illogical Lagrangian density for a hypergraph. The example demonstrates that by utilizing a multigraph instead of a simple graph, we can achieve a hypergraph density that defies logical justification. Ultimately, this research seeks to establish criteria for determining the logical density of a hypergraph through examination of its corresponding multigraphs. It is observed that a hypergraph's logical density can be thought of as the infimum of its multigraph densities. Moreover, this study delves into various characteristics of a hypergraph and its multigraphs, including their respective eigenvalues, irreducibility, and the feasibility of transforming one into another through modification. The research further explores under what conditions a hypergraph's logical density can be thought of as the minimum of its non-negative multigraph densities. In addition, this study identifies a particular class of hypergraphs, which are themselves non-regular and non-Lagrangian, and are characterized by a minimum degree of at least 2; these hypergraphs' non-negativity cannot be guaranteed in all possible multigraph densities. The researchers then generalize a particular embedding concept from hypergraphs to a class of multigraphs known as Z-multigraphs. A hypergraph is deemed tightly embedded if a specific type of Z-multigraph exists; this hypergraph can be transformed into the Z-multigraph by adding a particular edge weight. The research further delves into a class of hypergraphs which are themselves examples of hypergraphs with logical density zero. These hypergraphs' non-regularity, non-Lagrangian nature, and the feasibility of their logical density being generalized to a particular class of Z-multigraphs known as zero-trace multigraphs (ZTs) is established. A hypergraph is considered tightly embedded in ZTs if a particular type of ZT can be created from it; this ZT can be obtained from the hypergraph through the addition of a particular edge weight. Ultimately, this study establishes a connection between hypergraphs and semirings via ZTs and a particular semiring known as the Coan semiring. While the Coan semiring logical density is generalized from graphs, it is demonstrated that a particular class of ZTs, which is itself a generalization of hypergraphs, may have a logical density distinct from zero. Image description generation is a crucial task that requires conveying visual information into a textual format, accounting for variations in human perception and communication. Current best practices for image description training rely on significant visual knowledge and specific annotation in the training set, making them difficult to control and adapt to diverse scenarios. To overcome these challenges, we introduce a new image description approach that leverages prompt engineering instead of manually collected images. Our approach allows for controlled and adaptable description generation using general images, by incorporating prompts that reflect various perspectives and communication styles. Our results demonstrate that this technique not only produces coherent and visually accurate descriptions but also effectively replicates different description patterns for the same image, fundamentally limiting the dependence on manual images for training. Moreover, this technique can produce descriptions that align with specific targets, controlling the tone and semantics of the descriptions at will. Our images and code used for this research are publicly available on https://github.com/ParityAdaptive/Lens. Our Paper can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.63.99.

This study showcases MMLSpark, an innovative open-source library that bridges the gap between Cognitive Toolkit and Apache Spark by introducing Java bindings and new components. The integration with OpenCV and the development of automated machine learning tools within the millisecond range serve as evidence of successful Spark library development. To demonstrate the utility of MMLSpark, we use it as the foundation for a complex Spark flow operator, developing a scalable automatic feature extraction system for data sets by splitting tasks among multiple Spark stages. This system leverages OpenCV to introduce a novel dimensionality reduction method and applies a group-wise distributed gradient boosting machine to create decision trees. The resulting Adnaan algorithm uses a streamlined flow operator to produce features efficiently and offers users the ability to customize internal operations while achieving optimal performance. High-accuracy forecasting of energy consumption is essential to manage distribution systems effectively, particularly to create accurate resource allocation and to prevent over-recovery of supply from customers. The advent of smart meters has empowered the development of advanced predictive techniques that can utilize historical and weather data to forecast consumption. However, accurate prediction of peak load remains challenging due to a lack of sufficient data, as only a limited number of meters are typically used to monitor the peak load during a given time period. This research presents a probabilistic framework to predict peak load of individual customers and aggregate load of specific segments of the low-voltage network. To overcome the limitation of incomplete daily peak load data, the proposed framework employs a stochastic model that combines measurements from a selection of meters within a network segment. The model integrates a neural network that predicts aggregate consumption based on historical data and weather forecasts with a day-ahead temperature forecast from a standard forecasting system. The stochastic model allocates a set of predicted aggregate consumption values to each day of the forecast period, each corresponding to a specific probability of occurrence. The framework's performance during an evaluation period from June to September in the UK was assessed using data from 55,350 customers and a range of weather conditions, demonstrating improved accuracy relative to traditional forecast methods. The variability of consumption and the quality of forecast were investigated as factors influencing forecast performance, while the improved accuracy through model fusion was studied in terms of the number of selected meters and the distribution of choice. Furthermore, the concept of clustering was explored to define the network's subdivisions. The findings demonstrate the potential of the proposed model to effectively forecast both individual and aggregate consumption at different levels, relying on a limited set of meters during peak load periods. The model's ability to leverage historical data, as well as current and forecasted weather conditions, enables it to accurately forecast consumption across a spectrum of consumer types. The evaluation revealed that the typical cluster comprises around 280-350 customers, with a future investigation intended to determine the optimal size for the selection of meters. The model's accuracy was shown to be robust to a misaligned choice of distribution; nevertheless, the performance could likely be enhanced through the use of a more suitable distribution. For quadruped robots equipped with actuators that can stretch, developing optimal gait patterns depends on balancing energy efficiency and mobility. Currently, most quadruped locomotion controllers are designed to work best with rigid actuators and may not effectively utilize the capabilities offered by elastic actuators. In order to optimize the performance of these controllers for various gait patterns, a learning-based approach called Model-Predictive Elastic Actuator Optimization (MAEO) is proposed. This method modifies existing quadruped locomotion controllers by integrating optimization problems that target specific lower limb joint positions during the push-off phase, taking into consideration the forces and energies associated with various gait patterns. MAEO's performance is demonstrated through simulation-based testing on a seven degrees-of-freedom elastic-legged hexapod model and a rigid quadruped robot, showcasing its capacity to expand the operational space of existing controllers and provide enhanced mobility. By expanding the operational space of existing controllers, we found that our method results in a 235% improvement in a quadruped robot's mobility capabilities. Furthermore, we evaluated our approach on a physical cheetah-like robot and successfully increased its stride length by a factor of 2.5 when compared to its initially programmed gait. This research provides foundational knowledge for optimizing existing quadruped locomotion controllers and enhances the mobility capabilities of these robots. As a result, our methods could be broadly applied to various rigid and elastic actuator-based robots and provide a foundation for improving the mobility capabilities of these systems. The research data, including the full model description, is publicly available on our GitHub repository at https://github.com/Northwestern-UA/MAEO. This research investigates the physics behind a small-scale ripping mode, a micromagnetic instability that occurs in a collisionless slab of plasma. A primary objective of this study is to investigate the deformation of ion holes, or dugouts, which are associated with this instability. As an essential step in understanding this phenomenon, linear and nonlinear stability calculations are performed using a specific orbit-following reduction technique, which accommodates a broad wavenumber range. This technique allows for a thorough examination of variations in polarity and deformation of these ion holes throughout different growth rates and wavenumber intervals. Notably, this study identifies a small-scale ripping mode as a high-flux magnetospheric ionosphere interaction and a plausible process for geosynchronous satellite electron scattering. Moreover, this study reveals parallels between small-scale digging modes and microtearing cycles in turbulent magnetospheric plasma, and it also connects large-scale ripping modes to a theoretical process of outer ring formation. A final goal of this study is to explore possible observational evidence of small-scale ripping modes using world-class space instruments. A current space mission, dedicated to magnetic field and particle observations along with high-resolution camera imaging for ionospheric storm detection, may be the most suitable platform for accurately measuring and validating the findings of this study. A comprehensive review of existing scientific literature and current research findings is also presented in this study, which highlights a critical gap in understanding small-scale ripping modes across a wavenumber range of $O(10^3)-O(10^6)m^{-1}$. A particular space mission, designed to observe the fine-scale magnetism of Earth, has collected data over the past six years, a substantial dataset which could significantly contribute to validating the findings of this study. A final objective of this research is to establish a theoretical link between a large-scale ripping mode, observed in laboratory plasma experiments, and small-scale ripping modes occurring across various wavenumber ranges in both space and quasibiological laboratory conditions. A possible explanation for this scale link involves a theoretical connection between a large-scale process (ring instability) and small-scale microinstabilities (electron and ion processes), a connection which requires a more in-depth understanding of ion dynamics in collisionless plasma. A particular aspect of ion dynamics in digging modes involves the deformation of dugouts, a fundamental aspect of this study. A theoretical explanation is provided for digging modes as a particular case of ion dynamics in collisionless plasma, linking small-scale ripping modes to a broader range of processes occurring across various wavenumber ranges in both space and laboratory conditions.

In the past few years, the deployment of WiFi access points in residential settings has experienced a significant increase, leading to a growing need for their effective management. Currently available methods utilize the RSS values to decide which WiFi access points to turn on or off, as does the IEEE 802.11 standard. This method has a significant drawback, as RSS values are susceptible to noise and do not accurately represent channel load. In contrast, the IEEE 802.11k standard provides more accurate information about the WiFi channels. This is the first proposal to use IEEE 802.11k for deciding which WiFi access points to turn on or off based on channel load rather than RSS values. This proposal employs channel load metrics, such as mean square value and self-correlation value, in addition to selecting only the best channels for each access point instead of all channels.
